regions.name: Puglia
regions.tagline: The heel of the boot: old bush vines, Primitivo and Negroamaro, and a flat, sunbaked land that once made Europe's blending wine.
regions.summary:
Puglia is the long heel of Italy, about 400 km of mostly flat limestone between two seas. It has about 93,000 ha of wine grapes (third in Italy after Sicily and Veneto, per a 2025 Censis study) and was for a century the tank-wine supplier of Europe, shipping deep-coloured, high-alcohol reds north to bolster thin wines in France and northern Italy. Since the 1990s it has turned toward bottled wine built on its own grapes: Primitivo (the same variety as California's Zinfandel and Croatia's Tribidrag), Negroamaro in the Salento, and Nero di Troia in the north.

The region has four DOCGs and 28 DOCs. The key zones are the Salento peninsula (Salice Salentino, Brindisi, Copertino, Squinzano and other Negroamaro DOCs), Manduria and Gioia del Colle for Primitivo, and the Murge plateau around Castel del Monte for Nero di Troia and Bombino Nero. Rosé has a long history here: the first bottled Italian rosé, Leone de Castris's Five Roses, came from Salice Salentino in 1943.
regions.history: Greek colonists founded Taras (Taranto) around 706 BC and the Messapians grew vines in the Salento before them. In the Middle Ages Frederick II of Hohenstaufen built Castel del Monte. Primitivo was named by a priest of Gioia del Colle, Francesco Filippo Indellicati, who around 1799 selected an early-ripening ('primativo') vine; it reached Manduria in the late 19th century as a dowry of the Countess Sabini of Altamura. Its link to Zinfandel was confirmed by DNA in the 1990s and to Croatia's Crljenak Kaštelanski/Tribidrag in 2001. After phylloxera hit France, Puglia's cutting wine was in heavy demand; the 20th century brought cooperatives, EU vine-pull schemes (many old bush vines were grubbed up) and, from the 1990s, a quality revival led by family estates.
regions.terroir: Mostly flat or gently rolling limestone, often under a thin layer of red earth (*terra rossa*), with sand and clay near the coasts. The Murge plateau in the north and centre rises to about 680 m and is cooler; the Salento is low, hot and windy, cooled by both seas. Summers are long and dry; old vines are often trained as low bush vines (*alberello pugliese*).
regions.grapes: Primitivo, Negroamaro, Nero di Troia (Uva di Troia), Malvasia Nera, Susumaniello, Bombino Nero, Montepulciano, Aleatico, Ottavianello (Cinsault); whites Verdeca, Bianco d'Alessano, Bombino Bianco, Fiano Minutolo, Pampanuto, Falanghina, Moscato.
regions.styles: Ripe, soft reds from Primitivo and Negroamaro; structured Nero di Troia; rosato (Puglia is one of Italy's biggest rosé producers); sweet Primitivo Dolce Naturale; light whites from the Valle d'Itria.
regions.classification: Four DOCGs (Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale and three Castel del Monte DOCGs), 28 DOCs and six IGTs, of which IGT Puglia and IGT Salento carry much of the volume.
appellations: Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva

regions.name: Basilicata
regions.tagline: One volcano, one grape: Aglianico on the slopes of Monte Vulture, aged in caves cut into tuff.
regions.summary: Basilicata, the ancient Lucania, is the instep of the boot: mountainous, thinly populated and poor for most of its history. Only about 740 ha are declared under its DOC and DOCG wines, but it has one great wine: Aglianico del Vulture, from the slopes of an extinct volcano in the north of the region. Monte Vulture (1,326 m) left behind deep layers of volcanic tuff and ash, and the villages of Rionero, Barile and Rapolla are riddled with caves (*cantine* and *grotte*) carved into the tuff, where Aglianico has been aged for centuries. The region has one DOCG and four DOCs.
regions.history: Greek colonists settled the Ionian coast (Metapontum, Heraclea), and the poet Horace was born in Venusia (Venosa), on the edge of the Vulture, in 65 BC. The villages around the volcano were resettled by Albanian refugees (Arbëreshë) in the 15th century, who dug the cave cellars of Barile's 'Sheshë' district. The Aglianico del Vulture DOC came in 1971; producers such as Paternoster (1925) and D'Angelo kept quality alive, and since 2000 Elena Fucci, Cantine del Notaio and others have brought international attention.
regions.terroir: On Monte Vulture vineyards run from about 200 to 700 m on volcanic tuff, ash and lapilli over clay. The climate is continental with cold winters; Aglianico ripens slowly and is harvested in late October or November. Elsewhere, the Matera hills and the Agri valley have clay and limestone.
regions.grapes: Aglianico above all, plus Primitivo, Malvasia, Moscato, Greco and international varieties in the south.
regions.styles: Structured, long-lived Aglianico; some Aglianico sparkling and rosé; Matera reds and whites.
regions.classification: One DOCG (Aglianico del Vulture Superiore, 2010), four DOCs (Aglianico del Vulture, Matera, Grottino di Roccanova, Terre dell'Alta Val d'Agri) and one IGT.

regions.name: Calabria
regions.tagline: The toe of the boot, Oenotria of the Greeks: Gaglioppo at Cirò, sweet Greco at Bianco and a new DOCG in 2025.
regions.summary: Calabria is the toe of Italy, a long mountainous peninsula between the Tyrrhenian and Ionian seas. The Greeks called this coast Oenotria, 'land of vines', and founded Sybaris, Kroton and Locri here. Wine in Calabria today is small (under 10,000 ha, a fraction of what it once was), but it has distinct native grapes: Gaglioppo for reds, Magliocco and Greco Nero, and the white Greco Bianco, Mantonico and Pecorello. The heart is Cirò on the Ionian coast, where a group of young growers, the 'Cirò Revolution', has rebuilt the reputation of Gaglioppo, and in 2025 the Classico core became Calabria's first DOCG.
regions.history: Greek colonies founded from the 8th century BC (Sybaris 720 BC, Kroton 710 BC) made Calabria part of Magna Graecia. A wine called Krimisa, from a temple of Apollo Aleo at Punta Alice near Cirò, was said to be offered to athletes returning from the Olympic Games; the story is popular locally but hard to document. The region was later poor and emigrant, and the DOCs (Savuto 1975, Cirò 1969) did not stop decline. Librandi, at Cirò Marina since 1953, led a research-based revival from the 1990s with the University of Milan, cataloguing hundreds of local vine accessions.
regions.terroir: Calabria is mostly mountains (Pollino, Sila, Aspromonte), with vineyards on coastal hills and terraces. Cirò's hills of clay, marl and sand run from the Ionian shore up to about 460 m, with sea breezes and dry, hot summers; the Sila plateau behind brings cool air. The Tyrrhenian side (Lamezia, Savuto) is greener and wetter.
regions.grapes: Gaglioppo, Magliocco Canino and Magliocco Dolce, Greco Nero, Nerello, Calabrese (Nero d'Avola); whites Greco Bianco, Mantonico, Pecorello, Guardavalle, Montonico.
regions.styles: Pale but tannic Gaglioppo reds and rosés; Magliocco reds; sweet passito whites (Greco di Bianco).
regions.classification: One DOCG (Cirò Classico, registered in the EU on 18 July 2025) and nine DOCs, plus about ten IGTs (Calabria IGT is widely used). Terre di Cosenza DOC (2011) absorbed four older DOCs.
appellations: S. Anna di Isola Capo Rizzuto

regions.name: Sicily
regions.tagline: The Mediterranean's crossroads: Greek alberello, Arab raisins, English fortified wine and a volcano that became Italy's hottest appellation.
regions.summary:
Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean and the largest vineyard of any Italian region, over 118,000 ha of wine grapes (17.8% of the national total in a 2025 Censis study), ahead of Veneto and Puglia. For most of the 20th century it made bulk wine and Marsala; since the 1990s it has reinvented itself twice. First came the Nero d'Avola and Grillo boom, led by estates such as Planeta, Tasca d'Almerita and Donnafugata, and the creation of the island-wide Sicilia DOC in 2011 (about 24,600 ha). Then came Etna, where old bush vines on black lava at up to 1,000 m and more turned a forgotten DOC into one of the most talked-about wine regions in the world.

The island has one DOCG (Cerasuolo di Vittoria) and 23 DOCs, with Etna's application for DOCG status still pending in October 2026. Beyond Etna and Vittoria, its treasures are its sweet and fortified wines: Marsala, created by English merchants; Passito di Pantelleria, from Zibibbo grapes dried under the African sun on an island closer to Tunisia than to Sicily; and Malvasia delle Lipari from the Aeolian volcanoes.
regions.history: Residues in Copper Age jars from a cave on Monte Kronio near Sciacca, published in 2017, suggest wine was being made here around 4000 BC, among the earliest evidence in Italy. Phoenicians at Motya and Greeks at Naxos (734 BC), Syracuse and Selinunte spread vines and the low *alberello* bush training. Pliny praised the Mamertine wine of Messina, served by Julius Caesar at a banquet in 46 BC. Arab rule (9th to 11th centuries) brought the Zibibbo grape name (from Arabic *zabib*, raisin) and dried-grape techniques to Pantelleria. In 1773 the Liverpool merchant John Woodhouse shipped fortified wine from Marsala to England; Benjamin Ingham (from 1806) and Vincenzo Florio (from 1833) built an industry around it. Phylloxera arrived around 1880 and devastated the island, except on Etna's sandy volcanic soils. After decades of cooperatives and subsidised bulk wine, the modern revival began in the 1980s and 1990s.
regions.terroir: Sicily runs from hot, flat coastal plains to the 3,300 m cone of Etna. The west (Trapani, Marsala, Mazara) is low and windy, with limestone and sandy soils and most of the vineyard. The centre (Sclafani, Contessa Entellina) is a high inland plateau at 400 to 800 m with clay and big temperature swings. The southeast (Vittoria, Noto, Pachino) has red sand over limestone (*terra rossa*). Etna's volcanic sands and the volcanic islands (Pantelleria, Lipari, Salina) form their own world. The African sirocco and the sea temper everything.
regions.grapes: Nero d'Avola (Calabrese), Nerello Mascalese, Nerello Cappuccio, Frappato, Perricone, Nocera; whites Catarratto (the most planted), Grillo, Inzolia (Ansonica), Carricante, Grecanico (Garganega), Zibibbo (Muscat of Alexandria), Malvasia di Lipari, Moscato Bianco, Damaschino, Minnella. International grapes (Syrah, Chardonnay, Cabernet) are widely planted in the west and centre.
regions.styles: Ripe Nero d'Avola reds and fresh Frappato; perfumed, high-altitude Etna Rosso and mineral Etna Bianco; Cerasuolo di Vittoria; fortified Marsala; sweet passito (Pantelleria, Malvasia delle Lipari, Moscato di Noto and Siracusa); Grillo and Catarratto whites.
regions.classification: One DOCG (Cerasuolo di Vittoria, 2005), 23 DOCs and seven IGTs (Terre Siciliane IGT is the main one). The Sicilia DOC (2011) covers the whole island and has one UGA, Salemi. Etna DOC (1968, Sicily's first DOC) recognises 133 contrade in its rules (142 on the consorzio's 2022 map) and has applied for DOCG status.

regions.name: Sardinia
regions.tagline: An island apart: Cannonau from the land of centenarians, Vermentino on granite and a flor-aged white older than sherry's fame.
regions.summary:
Sardinia sits alone in the middle of the western Mediterranean, closer to Corsica and Tunisia than to Rome, and its wine reflects centuries of separate history: Nuragic, Phoenician, Roman, Byzantine, Pisan, Catalan-Aragonese and Piedmontese. It has about 26,000 ha of vines, one DOCG (Vermentino di Gallura) and 17 DOCs. Three region-wide DOCs carry most of the volume: Cannonau di Sardegna, Vermentino di Sardegna and Monica di Sardegna.

Cannonau (Grenache) is the soul of the mountainous east, around Nuoro, Oliena, Mamoiada and Jerzu, in the Ogliastra, one of the world's 'Blue Zones' of exceptional longevity, which locals happily link to their red wine. Vermentino reaches its peak on the granite of Gallura in the northeast. The southwest (Sulcis) has ungrafted Carignano on sand dunes, and the west keeps two extraordinary oxidative whites: Vernaccia di Oristano, aged under flor, and Malvasia di Bosa.
regions.history: Grape pips found at the Nuragic site of Sa Osa near Cabras and at other sites, dated to around 1300 to 1100 BC, show that grapes were cultivated on the island in the Bronze Age; some Sardinians argue that Cannonau is native and travelled to Spain, while most DNA evidence points to a Spanish origin for Garnacha, perhaps arriving with the Aragonese rulers from the 14th century. Phoenicians and Carthaginians traded wine here, and Romans grew vines on the Campidano plain. From the 14th to the early 18th century, Aragonese and Spanish rule brought many grapes (Bovale, Monica, Girò and probably Carignano and Cannonau). Phylloxera arrived in the 1880s. Piedmontese entrepreneurs founded Sella & Mosca in 1899; cooperatives dominated the 20th century; and in the 1980s and 1990s Giacomo Tachis's work with Argiolas (Turriga) and Santadi (Terre Brune) showed the island's potential.
regions.terroir: Old, varied geology: granite in Gallura and parts of the centre, schist and volcanic rock (trachyte, basalt) in the middle, limestone around Alghero and Oliena, alluvial plains in the Campidano and sand dunes in the Sulcis. The climate is hot and dry, with the mistral (*maestrale*) blowing hard from the northwest; mountains rise to 1,834 m in the Gennargentu, so inland vineyards at 400 to 700 m are much cooler.
regions.grapes: Cannonau (Grenache), Carignano, Monica, Bovale (Bovale Sardo, genetically Graciano), Cagnulari, Girò, Pascale; whites Vermentino, Nuragus, Nasco, Torbato, Semidano, Vernaccia di Oristano, Malvasia di Sardegna, Moscato.
regions.styles: Warm, spicy Cannonau reds, from fresh to powerful; saline Vermentino; dense Carignano; flor-aged Vernaccia; sweet and oxidative Malvasia, Nasco, Moscato and Girò.
regions.classification: One DOCG (Vermentino di Gallura, 1996), 17 DOCs and 15 IGTs (Isola dei Nuraghi IGT is widely used). The three island-wide DOCs are Cannonau di Sardegna (with subzones Capo Ferrato, Jerzu, Oliena or Nepente di Oliena, and a Classico for Nuoro and Ogliastra), Vermentino di Sardegna and Monica di Sardegna.

it-abruzzo.name: Abruzzo
it-abruzzo.grapes: Pecorino, Passerina, Cococciola, Montonico, Malvasia; Montepulciano
it-abruzzo.summary: A regional DOC created in 2010 mainly to give the native whites a home: Pecorino (the region's rising white), Passerina, Cococciola and Montonico, plus sparkling and passito wines. Since 2023 it has the same four provincial subzones as the other regional DOCs.

it-aglianico-del-taburno.name: Aglianico del Taburno
it-aglianico-del-taburno.summary: Aglianico from the slopes of Monte Taburno, the 'sleeping woman' mountain in the province of Benevento, a DOCG since 2011. Compared with Taurasi it is often more supple and fruity, with black cherry, spice and violets, from clay and limestone soils with volcanic deposits. It needs two years of ageing (three for Riserva); a rosato is also allowed.

it-aglianico-del-vulture.name: Aglianico del Vulture
it-aglianico-del-vulture.summary: Aglianico del Vulture comes from 15 communes on the slopes of Monte Vulture, an extinct volcano last active about 40,000 years ago. The soils of tuff and ash give the wine a smoky, mineral side to go with Aglianico's black cherry, plum, tar and violets, and its high acid and tannin make it age as well as Taurasi. The basic wine is released after about a year; the Superiore and Riserva are a separate DOCG since 2010. About 580 ha.
it-aglianico-del-vulture.terroir: Volcanic soils at 200 to 700 m, highest around Barile, Rionero and Ripacandida; the east-facing slopes toward the Ofanto valley get cool winds, and harvests run late into autumn.
it-aglianico-del-vulture.nerd_note: Elena Fucci's Titolo comes from a single 6 ha vineyard in Contrada Solagna del Titolo at Barile, at about 600 m, with vines 55 to 70 years old.

it-aglianico-del-vulture-superiore.name: Aglianico del Vulture Superiore
it-aglianico-del-vulture-superiore.summary: The DOCG tier of Aglianico del Vulture, created in 2010 and Basilicata's only DOCG: at least three years of ageing with a year in wood and a year in bottle (five years for Riserva), and 13.5% minimum alcohol. These are dark, smoky, firmly tannic wines that need a decade.

it-alba.name: Alba
it-alba.summary: One of Italy's newer DOCs and a rare case of an official blend of Piedmont's two great reds: Nebbiolo for perfume and tannin, Barbera for colour and acidity. It codifies a farmer tradition of mixing the two and covers communes in both the Langhe and Roero. It remains a niche, with only a handful of producers using it.
it-alba.terroir: Langhe marls and Roero sands around Alba.
it-alba.nerd_note: Its creation in 2011 caused friction: producers of Barbera d'Alba and Nebbiolo d'Alba objected to a new wine using the town's name alone.

it-albugnano.name: Albugnano
it-albugnano.summary: Nebbiolo from four communes on the high hills of north Asti, near the Romanesque abbey of Vezzolano. Light, fresh and acid-driven.
it-albugnano.nerd_note: Albugnano is the highest village in the province of Asti, at about 550 metres.

it-alcamo.name: Alcamo
it-alcamo.grapes: Catarratto, Inzolia, Grillo, Grecanico; Nero d'Avola, Calabrese, Frappato, Perricone
it-alcamo.summary: One of Sicily's older DOCs, on the hills between Palermo and Trapani around Alcamo and Monte Bonifato, built on Catarratto. Bianco Classico from Catarratto Bianco Lucido is the traditional style; Rapitalà is the best-known estate.

it-aleatico-di-gradoli.name: Aleatico di Gradoli
it-aleatico-di-gradoli.summary: A tiny DOC for sweet and fortified red Aleatico from the volcanic slopes above Lake Bolsena around Gradoli. Perfumed with roses and cherries. About 1 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 5,600 bottles a year.

it-aleatico-di-puglia.name: Aleatico di Puglia
it-aleatico-di-puglia.summary: A region-wide DOC for sweet and fortified Aleatico, the rose-scented red Muscat relative. Barely any is declared today, though a few producers in the Salento and Gioia del Colle still make it.

it-alezio.name: Alezio
it-alezio.summary: A tiny DOC near Gallipoli, historically known for its Negroamaro rosato; Michele Calò's Mjère is the reference. About 4 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 15,000 bottles a year.

it-alghero.name: Alghero
it-alghero.grapes: Torbato, Vermentino, Chardonnay, Sauvignon; Cagnulari, Cannonau, Cabernet, Sangiovese
it-alghero.summary: A DOC around Alghero, the Catalan-speaking town on the northwest coast, dominated by Sella & Mosca. It is the home of Torbato, a white grape of Catalan origin (Tourbat in Roussillon) that survives almost only here, and of Cagnulari, a local red. The Anghelu Ruju passito (Cannonau) and Marchese di Villamarina (Cabernet) are Sella & Mosca classics.

it-alta-langa.name: Alta Langa
it-alta-langa.summary: Piedmont's answer to Champagne and Franciacorta: metodo classico sparkling wine from Pinot Nero and Chardonnay grown in the high Langhe, Roero and Monferrato at 250 metres or more. Every wine is vintage-dated and spends at least 30 months on the lees (Riserva 36). The project goes back to 1990, when the big Asti houses (Gancia, Fontanafredda, Martini & Rossi and others) planted experimental vineyards to bring sparkling-wine grapes back to Piedmont, reviving the tradition that Carlo Gancia started in 1865.
it-alta-langa.terroir: Marls and sandstones of the upper Langhe, often at 400 to 700 metres where the cool nights keep acidity high.
it-alta-langa.nerd_note: Alta Langa is the only Italian sparkling DOCG that requires every bottle to carry a vintage.

it-alto-adige.name: Alto Adige
it-alto-adige.grapes: Schiava, Lagrein, Pinot Nero, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Gewürztraminer, Müller-Thurgau, Sylvaner, Kerner, Riesling, Moscato Giallo, Moscato Rosa and others
it-alto-adige.summary:
The Alto Adige / Südtirol DOC covers almost all the vineyards of the province of Bolzano, about 5,800 hectares, and is one of the few Italian denominations where whites outnumber reds (around 60% white). It is a varietal-led DOC with a large cast of grapes, unusually high average quality and a dominant cooperative sector that produces many of its top wines.

The DOC was created in 1975 (its 50th anniversary was celebrated at Vinitaly 2025), and it contains subzones that can appear on the label: Santa Maddalena (St. Magdalener) and Colli di Bolzano (Bozner Leiten) around Bolzano, Terlano (Terlaner), Meranese (Meraner), Valle Isarco (Eisacktaler) with its Bressanone (Brixner) and Klausen sections, Val Venosta (Vinschgau) and Lago di Caldaro classico. Since 2024 the DOC also has 86 UGAs, small named areas each with up to five permitted varieties and yields 25% lower than the DOC; a UGA symbol on the label marks these wines, which covered about 403 hectares and 6.7% of DOC production in 2025.

The white benchmarks are Terlano's long-lived Pinot Bianco and Sauvignon (some vintages released after decades on the lees), Tramin's Gewürztraminer Nussbaumer and Epokale, and San Michele Appiano's Sanct Valentin range. Lagrein, a dark native red, is grown on the hot gravels of Gries in Bolzano; Pinot Noir is at its best on the Mazon plateau above Egna and in Appiano Monte (Eppan Berg).
it-alto-adige.terroir: Vineyards climb from about 200 m on the Adige valley floor to over 1,000 m in Val Venosta and Valle Isarco. Porphyry around Bolzano and Terlano gives mineral, long-lived wines; dolomitic limestone and moraine in the Bassa Atesina (Termeno, Cortaccia, Magrè) suit Gewürztraminer and Pinot Noir; schist, quartz-phyllite and moraine in the Isarco valley give taut Sylvaner, Kerner and Riesling. Summer heat in the valley bottom contrasts with cool nights from the mountains.
it-alto-adige.nerd_note: The 86 UGAs were drawn using, among other evidence, place names from the Theresian Cadastre of the 1770s; Gries, Mazon, Eppan Berg and Brenntal are among the best known.

it-amarone-della-valpolicella.name: Amarone della Valpolicella
it-amarone-della-valpolicella.grapes: Corvina and Corvinone (45 to 95%), Rondinella (5 to 30%), plus up to 25% other local reds such as Molinara and Oseleta
it-amarone-della-valpolicella.summary:
Amarone is one of the world's most distinctive red wines: dry, powerful (often 15 to 16.5% alcohol) and opulent, made from grapes that have spent three to four months drying (*appassimento*) in airy lofts called *fruttai* until they have lost 30 to 45% of their weight. The concentrated sugars ferment fully dry, giving flavours of dried cherry, fig, chocolate, tobacco and spice with a bitter twist on the finish (*amaro* means bitter, and Amarone means 'big bitter').

It was born almost by accident. Valpolicella's traditional dried-grape wine was the sweet Recioto, and Amarone was originally a Recioto that had fermented all the way to dryness, a fault. The name is said to have been coined in 1936 by Adelino Lucchese, cellar master at the Cantina Sociale Valpolicella, when he tasted such a cask, and Bolla, Bertani and others began selling it commercially in the 1950s. It became a DOC within Recioto della Valpolicella in 1968, a separate DOC in 1990 and a DOCG in 2010 (approved December 2009).

The production zone covers 19 communes and 8,614 hectares of Valpolicella vineyard (2025). In 2025 about 13.6 million bottles of Amarone and Recioto were released, with 327,545 quintals of grapes set aside for drying. Ageing is at least two years from 1 January after harvest (Riserva four), and minimum alcohol is 14%. Giuseppe Quintarelli and Romano Dal Forno make the most sought-after, long-aged versions; Bertani's Classico, released after years in large casks, is the benchmark of the traditional style.
it-amarone-della-valpolicella.terroir: Valpolicella is a fan of north-south valleys running down from the Lessini Mountains to the Adige: in the Classico zone the Fumane, Marano and Negrar valleys, then Valpantena, then the eastern valleys of Illasi and Mezzane. Soils are limestone, marl and clay on the hills (red clays on the *marogne*, dry-stone terraces), with volcanic basalt in the east. Higher hillside sites at 300 to 500 m give fresher, more aromatic grapes, while the drying process itself, regulated by humidity and airflow in the fruttai, shapes the wine as much as the vineyard.
it-amarone-della-valpolicella.nerd_note: Before drying became mechanised in some cellars, grapes were dried on bamboo racks (*arele*) or hung from rafters; Quintarelli still dries on racks in his attic, and the consortium has proposed the ritual of 'grape-resting' for UNESCO intangible heritage.

it-amelia.name: Amelia
it-amelia.grapes: Sangiovese, Ciliegiolo, Merlot; Trebbiano, Grechetto, Malvasia
it-amelia.summary: The southernmost Umbrian DOC, around the Roman walled town of Amelia near the Lazio border. Ciliegiolo, a cherry-scented red related to Sangiovese, is a local strength (Zanchi makes a well-known one).

it-ansonica-costa-dell-argentario.name: Ansonica Costa dell'Argentario
it-ansonica-costa-dell-argentario.summary: A tiny white DOC for Ansonica from the Monte Argentario promontory, Isola del Giglio and the coast around Orbetello. On Giglio the vines grow on granite terraces above the sea and give salty, sun-baked whites, sometimes made with long skin contact by small growers.

it-aprilia.name: Aprilia
it-aprilia.summary: A DOC on land reclaimed from the Pontine Marshes in the 1930s and settled by farmers from northern Italy, who planted Merlot, Sangiovese and Trebbiano. The flat, sandy-clay coastal plain gives soft, easy wines.

it-arborea.name: Arborea
it-arborea.summary: A DOC on the reclaimed land around Arborea, south of Oristano, drained and settled in the 1920s and 1930s by farmers from the Veneto and Romagna, who planted Sangiovese and Trebbiano. It is almost dormant.

it-arcole.name: Arcole
it-arcole.summary: A plain-land DOC south of Soave, named after Napoleon's 1796 victory at the bridge of Arcole.
it-arcole.nerd_note: Napoleon's charge across the Arcole bridge is depicted in Antoine-Jean Gros's famous painting.

it-arnad-montjovet.name: Arnad-Montjovet
it-arnad-montjovet.grapes: Nebbiolo (min 70%), plus Dolcetto, Vien de Nus, Pinot Noir, Freisa
it-arnad-montjovet.summary: Nebbiolo-based reds from the lower valley around Arnad and Montjovet, near the Fort of Bard. Light, fragrant and mountain-edged.
it-arnad-montjovet.nerd_note: Arnad is also famous for its lard (Lardo d'Arnad DOP), cured in chestnut-wood tubs.

it-asolo-montello.name: Asolo Montello
it-asolo-montello.summary: Varietal DOC for the Asolo and Montello hills.

it-assisi.name: Assisi
it-assisi.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet, Pinot Nero; Grechetto, Trebbiano
it-assisi.summary: A DOC on the slopes of Monte Subasio below the city of Saint Francis, for Sangiovese-based reds, Grechetto and rosé. Small and mostly sold locally. About 57 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 211,000 bottles a year.

it-asti.name: Asti
it-asti.summary:
Asti is the sweet, aromatic sparkling wine of the Monferrato and Langhe hills, and one of Italy's largest denominations, with tens of millions of bottles a year. It comes in two styles. Asti Spumante (now usually just 'Asti') is fully sparkling, made by fermenting chilled Moscato must in pressurised tanks (the Martinotti or charmat method) and stopping at around 7% alcohol. Moscato d'Asti is *frizzante*, sealed with a regular cork, lighter in bubbles and alcohol (around 5%), and often from more careful growers. Both taste of fresh grapes, peach, sage and orange blossom.

The story begins with Carlo Gancia, who learned in Reims and in 1865 made Italy's first sparkling wine at Canelli by the traditional method, then developed the sweet Moscato Champagne that became Asti Spumante. In 2017 a dry 'Asti Secco' style was added. Small growers like Saracco, Vietti, La Spinetta and Ca' d'Gal make Moscato d'Asti of real finesse. The Canelli subzone left to become its own DOCG in 2023.
it-asti.terroir: White calcareous marls (Sant'Agata Fossil Marls) and sandstones in the Belbo and Bormida valleys, on steep slopes up to 500 metres.
it-asti.nerd_note: Moscato d'Asti is one of the few wines whose fermentation is stopped by chilling and filtration rather than fortification, so the residual sugar is pure grape sugar.

it-atina.name: Atina
it-atina.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Syrah; Sémillon
it-atina.summary: An unusual DOC in the Comino valley in southern Lazio where Bordeaux varieties were brought in the 19th century by Pasquale Visocchi, an agronomist who studied in France. Cabernet is the backbone.

it-aversa.name: Aversa
it-aversa.summary: Home of Asprinio, a sharp, low-alcohol white grape traditionally trained up poplar trees in the *alberata aversana* system, with vines reaching 15 m and harvested by pickers on tall, narrow ladders. This Etruscan-style training survives in a few hectares north of Naples, and the wine is made still or sparkling.
it-aversa.nerd_note: The alberata aversana is one of the last places in Europe where the ancient practice of marrying vines to living trees (*vite maritata*) is still used commercially.

it-bagnoli-di-sopra.name: Bagnoli di Sopra
it-bagnoli-di-sopra.summary: Varietal and blended wines from the Bagnoli plain south of Padua.

it-bagnoli-friularo.name: Bagnoli Friularo
it-bagnoli-friularo.summary: Raboso, here called Friularo, from the plain around Bagnoli di Sopra south of Padua, dry or as a passito. The Borletti family's Dominio di Bagnoli, an estate founded on Benedictine lands, is the reference.
it-bagnoli-friularo.nerd_note: Bagnoli's great estate was a Benedictine property before passing to Venetian nobility, and the Friularo name recalls the grape's reputed Friulian origin.

it-barbaresco.name: Barbaresco
it-barbaresco.summary:
Barbaresco is Barolo's smaller neighbour, made from Nebbiolo grown in the communes of Barbaresco, Neive and Treiso plus the San Rocco Seno d'Elvio hamlet of Alba, on hills north-east of Alba that sit closer to the Tanaro and slightly lower. The wines are often described as more graceful and earlier to open than Barolo, with finer tannin and more red fruit and violet, but the best (Asili, Rabajà, Montestefano, Martinenga, Pajè, Montefico) are every bit as long-lived.

The story of Barbaresco as a separate wine begins in 1894, when Domizio Cavazza, director of the Alba wine school, gathered nine growers into the Cantina Sociale di Barbaresco to make and sell wine under the village name instead of selling grapes to Barolo merchants. Fascism closed it, but in 1958 the parish priest Don Fiorino Marengo founded the Produttori del Barbaresco, which today farms roughly 100 hectares through its members, about an eighth of the appellation, and bottles nine single-MGA Riservas in good years. Angelo Gaja and Bruno Giacosa then made Barbaresco world-famous from the 1960s, Gaja with single-vineyard bottlings (Sorì San Lorenzo, Sorì Tildin, Costa Russi) and barriques, Giacosa with classic large-cask wines from bought-in crus like Santo Stefano and Asili.

Rules: 100% Nebbiolo, 26 months of ageing from 1 November after harvest with 9 months in wood (Riserva 50 months), minimum 12.5% alcohol. There are 66 MGAs, created in 2007 (65) with one added in 2010; unlike Barolo there is no commune-level mention, though the consortium proposed adding one in 2024. Vineyard area was 733 hectares in 2019, up from 484 in the early 1990s.
it-barbaresco.terroir: Barbaresco's soils are mostly Tortonian Sant'Agata Fossil Marls, blue-grey and calcareous, similar to La Morra, with sandier lenses in parts of Neive and Treiso. The vineyards lie at 200 to about 400 metres; Treiso is highest and coolest. The Tanaro's influence makes the zone slightly warmer and earlier-ripening than Barolo, which, together with the shorter legal ageing, explains Barbaresco's reputation for approachability.
it-barbaresco.nerd_note: In 1996 Angelo Gaja took his three famous single-vineyard Barbarescos out of the DOCG and sold them as Langhe Nebbiolo so he could add a little Barbera; from the 2013 vintage he returned them to Barbaresco DOCG as 100% Nebbiolo.

it-barbera-d-alba.name: Barbera d'Alba
it-barbera-d-alba.summary: Barbera grown around Alba, often on the slopes that were too cool or not south-facing enough for Nebbiolo. It tends to be richer and darker than Barbera d'Asti because the Langhe's calcareous marls and the Barolo producers' attention give it more structure. In the 1980s and 1990s modernists such as Elio Altare, Roberto Voerzio and Giacomo Conterno (Cascina Francia) showed that Barbera aged in barrique or large cask could be a serious, age-worthy wine. Superiore requires 12 months' ageing with four in wood.
it-barbera-d-alba.terroir: Tortonian and Serravallian marls of the Barolo and Barbaresco hills plus Roero sands.
it-barbera-d-alba.nerd_note: Giacomo Conterno's Barbera from Cascina Francia is grown on the same Serralunga hill as its Barolo, and Monfortino's maker ferments it in the same old casks.

it-barbera-d-asti.name: Barbera d'Asti
it-barbera-d-asti.summary: The largest red DOCG of Piedmont and Barbera's home ground. On the Monferrato hills around Asti, Barbera gives juicy, high-acid, low-tannin wines tasting of sour cherry and plum, ideal with food and usually better value than Barbera d'Alba. The modern reputation dates from 1982, when Giacomo Bologna of Braida released Bricco dell'Uccellone, a barrique-aged Barbera from Rocchetta Tanaro that showed the grape could be grand. The Superiore requires 14 months' ageing with six in wood. Its former subzones Tinella and Colli Astiani remain, while the former Nizza subzone became its own DOCG.
it-barbera-d-asti.terroir: Calcareous marls and sands of the Monferrato hills, 200 to 400 metres.
it-barbera-d-asti.nerd_note: The 1986 methanol scandal, in which cheap Barbera was laced with methanol and killed more than 20 people, nearly destroyed Barbera's reputation; the quality revolution of Braida and its peers is the story of its rebirth.

it-barbera-del-monferrato.name: Barbera del Monferrato
it-barbera-del-monferrato.summary: The everyday Monferrato Barbera, sometimes lightly fizzy (*vivace*), the wine of Piedmontese osterie.
it-barbera-del-monferrato.nerd_note: The frizzante versions recall the way Barbera was drunk in the 19th century.

it-barbera-del-monferrato-superiore.name: Barbera del Monferrato Superiore
it-barbera-del-monferrato-superiore.summary: DOCG Barbera from the Monferrato Casalese and Alessandria hills, aged 14 months with six in wood. Less known than Barbera d'Asti but often good value.
it-barbera-del-monferrato-superiore.nerd_note: Iuli's Barbera from Montaldo, near Cerrina, has a cult following among natural-wine drinkers.

it-barco-reale-di-carmignano.name: Barco Reale di Carmignano
it-barco-reale-di-carmignano.summary: The younger, earlier-release red of the Carmignano zone, named after the Medici's walled hunting park. The rosato is called Vin Ruspo, from the farm workers' tradition of 'stealing' (ruspare) juice from the press before it took colour.

it-bardolino.name: Bardolino
it-bardolino.grapes: Corvina (35 to 95%), Rondinella (5 to 40%), Molinara and others
it-bardolino.summary: Bardolino is the light, fragrant red of Lake Garda's eastern shore: pale, cherry-and-spice scented, the sort of red you chill slightly and drink with lake fish. Bardolino Chiaretto, its pink sibling, is one of Italy's most popular rosés and has been reinvented since 2014 as a pale, Provence-style wine. Three subzones, La Rocca, Montebaldo and Sommacampagna, were added in the early 2020s to recognise different soils and exposures.
it-bardolino.terroir: Glacial moraine hills around the lake; the lake moderates temperatures.
it-bardolino.nerd_note: The Bardolino Chiaretto 'Rosé Revolution' of 2014 reduced skin contact to give a paler, lighter wine, reversing decades of darker rosé.

it-bardolino-superiore.name: Bardolino Superiore
it-bardolino-superiore.summary: The DOCG tier of Bardolino with lower yields and a year of ageing; a small category.

it-barletta.name: Barletta
it-barletta.summary: A DOC around the port of Barletta on the Adriatic coast, created as Rosso Barletta in 1977 and widened in 2011, for Nero di Troia reds and Malvasia whites. In the 19th century Barletta was a busy wine port shipping deep, strong reds to France after phylloxera.

it-barolo.name: Barolo
it-barolo.summary:
Barolo is Italy's most argued-over and most collectable red, made from Nebbiolo grown on eleven communes in the hills south-west of Alba. It is a wine of paradox: pale garnet in the glass yet ferociously tannic, smelling of roses, dried cherries, tar, licorice and truffle, and built to age for decades. Its fame rests on two things, the grape's sensitivity to soil and the patchwork of steep, differently oriented slopes on which it grows, which is why Barolo talk is always about places: Cannubi, Brunate, Rocche dell'Annunziata, Monprivato, Villero, Vignarionda, Francia.

The modern dry style dates from the mid-19th century, when Juliette Colbert, Marchesa di Barolo, and Cavour's Grinzane estate began fermenting Nebbiolo fully dry and ageing it in cask. King Vittorio Emanuele II's Fontanafredda estate followed, and Barolo became 'the wine of kings and the king of wines'. In the 1980s and 1990s it was the battlefield of Italy's wine wars: modernists (Elio Altare, Roberto Voerzio, Paolo Scavino, Domenico Clerico, Luciano Sandrone) cut macerations short and used new French barriques for fruit and early charm, while traditionalists (Bartolo Mascarello, Giuseppe Rinaldi, Giacomo Conterno, Cappellano, Giuseppe Mascarello) kept long maceration and large Slavonian oak *botti*. Today most producers sit somewhere in between and the argument has moved to site.

Rules: 100% Nebbiolo, at least 38 months of ageing from 1 November of the harvest year with 18 months in wood (Riserva 62 months), minimum 13% alcohol, vineyards between 170 and 540 metres and never on north-facing slopes. The zone covers roughly 2,200 to 2,300 hectares of Nebbiolo, up from about 1,200 in 1990, and produces on the order of 14 million bottles a year. Since 2010 the label may carry one of 181 MGAs: 170 vineyard areas plus 11 commune names such as 'Barolo del Comune di Serralunga d'Alba'.
it-barolo.terroir:
The Barolo zone is a horseshoe of ridges open to the north, drained by the Talloria dell'Annunziata and Talloria di Castiglione streams that flow north to the Tanaro. A geological line runs roughly north-south through Castiglione Falletto: to the west, La Morra and Barolo sit on Tortonian Sant'Agata Fossil Marls, bluish calcareous marls that give perfume, elegance and earlier approachability; to the east, Serralunga d'Alba and much of Monforte sit on older Serravallian (formerly called Helvetian) Lequio Formation marls and Diano sandstones, poorer and more compact, giving firmer, longer-lived wines. Castiglione Falletto, on the dividing ridge, blends both.

The Tanaro matters too: it once flowed north past Bra toward the Po near Carmagnola, until, in the late Pleistocene, it was captured by a stream draining east toward Alessandria. The sudden drop in base level made every tributary cut down hard, carving the steep gullies and amphitheatres that shape today's slopes. Altitude, aspect and the cooling air from the Alps decide ripeness: south and south-west amphitheatres (*sorì*) like Cannubi and Vignarionda ripen best, while higher sites in Novello, Monforte and La Morra are prized in hot years.
it-barolo.nerd_note: In 2024 the consortium floated letting Nebbiolo for Barolo be planted on north-facing slopes, citing climate change; growers resisted and, as of the latest reports, the ban (slopes between -45 and +45 degrees of north) still stands in the disciplinare.

it-bianchello-del-metauro.name: Bianchello del Metauro
it-bianchello-del-metauro.summary: A light, zesty white from Biancame grown along the Metauro river in the north of the region. Local legend claims that in 207 BC the Carthaginian army of Hasdrubal lost the battle of the Metaurus after drinking too much of the local white.

it-bianco-capena.name: Bianco Capena
it-bianco-capena.summary: A white DOC north of Rome around Capena, Fiano Romano and Morlupo, on the volcanic tuff of the Sabatini hills above the Tiber valley. It is a Malvasia-Trebbiano blend in the Castelli Romani mould, created in 1975, but production under the name is now negligible.

it-bianco-dell-empolese.name: Bianco dell'Empolese
it-bianco-dell-empolese.summary: A Trebbiano-based white and Vin Santo DOC around Empoli and Vinci in the lower Arno valley, an area now better known for the new Chianti Terre di Vinci subzone.

it-bianco-di-custoza.name: Custoza
it-bianco-di-custoza.grapes: Garganega, Trebbiano Toscano, Bianca Fernanda (Cortese), Friulano, Malvasia, Riesling, Chardonnay, Manzoni
it-bianco-di-custoza.summary: Bianco di Custoza is a light, aromatic white blend from the moraine hills south-east of Lake Garda, between Verona and Peschiera. Fresh, floral and slightly almondy; Monte del Frà, Cavalchina and Gorgo are leading names.
it-bianco-di-custoza.terroir: Glacial moraine of the Garda amphitheatre.
it-bianco-di-custoza.nerd_note: Custoza was the site of two battles of the Risorgimento (1848 and 1866), and a war ossuary stands among the vineyards.

it-bianco-di-pitigliano.name: Bianco di Pitigliano
it-bianco-di-pitigliano.grapes: Trebbiano Toscano plus Greco, Malvasia, Verdello, Grechetto and others
it-bianco-di-pitigliano.summary: One of Italy's first DOCs (1966), from the tufa plateau around Pitigliano, the 'little Jerusalem' of the Maremma whose Jewish community made kosher wine in cellars cut into the volcanic rock. The white is light and soft; a sweet Vin Santo and Superiore exist. The tufa cellars beneath the town are still used.

it-biferno.name: Biferno
it-biferno.grapes: Montepulciano 70 to 80% with Aglianico; Trebbiano for whites
it-biferno.summary: A DOC in the Biferno river valley and the coastal hills around Campomarino and Termoli, for Montepulciano-Aglianico reds and Trebbiano-based whites. Di Majo Norante's Ramitello is the best-known wine. About 48 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 393,000 bottles a year.

it-bivongi.name: Bivongi
it-bivongi.grapes: Gaglioppo, Greco Nero, Nocera, Castiglione, Calabrese; Greco, Guardavalle, Mantonico
it-bivongi.summary: A DOC in the Stilaro valley on the Ionian coast of southern Calabria, near the Byzantine Cattolica of Stilo, for blended reds and whites from local grapes. About 12 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 60,000 bottles a year.

it-blanc-de-morgex-et-de-la-salle.name: Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle
it-blanc-de-morgex-et-de-la-salle.summary: The highest-altitude subzone in the valley, below Mont Blanc in the communes of Morgex and La Salle, at roughly 900 to 1,200 metres. Prié Blanc is an ancient, early-ripening local grape grown on ungrafted roots and trained on low pergolas supported by stone pillars, so the vines can catch the heat stored in the ground. The wine is pale, light (often under 11.5%), with green apple, alpine herbs and a salty, almost glacial freshness. It is also made as metodo classico sparkling wine. The Cave Mont Blanc cooperative makes most of it; Ermes Pavese is the leading independent grower.
it-blanc-de-morgex-et-de-la-salle.terroir: Sandy, stony morainic soils at the foot of Mont Blanc; extreme frost risk and a season of barely five months.
producers: Cave Mont Blanc de Morgex et La Salle
it-blanc-de-morgex-et-de-la-salle.nerd_note: Some growers harvest a few rows in winter for an ice wine (Chaudelune) when temperatures fall below -8 C.

it-boca.name: Boca
it-boca.grapes: Nebbiolo (70 to 90%), Vespolina and/or Uva Rara
it-boca.summary: Boca is tiny (about 20 hectares) and mountainous, on porphyry soils of the Sesia supervolcano at 400 to 550 metres. The Swiss Christoph Künzli of Le Piane, mentored by local veteran Antonio Cerri, revived it from near abandonment from 1998, and the wines (with maggiorina-trained old vines) are some of the most thrilling in Alto Piemonte.
it-boca.terroir: Acidic volcanic porphyry, the most dramatic outcrop of the Sesia Supervolcano geopark.
it-boca.nerd_note: Old Boca vineyards use the *maggiorina* system, three vines trained together on a single post into a kind of tree.

it-bolgheri.name: Bolgheri
it-bolgheri.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot (any proportion), up to 50% Syrah and 50% Sangiovese; whites from Vermentino, Sauvignon Blanc, Viognier.
it-bolgheri.summary:
Bolgheri is the Italian appellation that Bordeaux varieties built. Until the 1970s this strip of coast in the commune of Castagneto Carducci, south of Livorno, was known for cattle, cypress avenues and Carducci's poetry, not wine. Then came Sassicaia, planted by Marchese Mario Incisa della Rocchetta at Tenuta San Guido in the 1940s and released from the 1968 vintage; in 1985 his nephew Lodovico Antinori founded Ornellaia, and Piero Antinori's Guado al Tasso, Grattamacco, Le Macchiole, Michele Satta and later Gaja's Ca' Marcanda followed.

Until 1994 the reds had no DOC at all and were sold as vino da tavola, even at record prices. The 1994 rules created Bolgheri Rosso and Superiore, a red DOC built around Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Merlot, with Syrah and Sangiovese allowed up to half. Today the consorzio counts 78 members and about 1,379 ha, 99% of the vineyard. Bolgheri Superiore needs two years of ageing, one in wood; the most expensive wines (Ornellaia, Guado al Tasso, Paleo, Grattamacco) are Superiore, while some icons such as Masseto (pure Merlot) and Messorio sit outside as IGT Toscana.

The style is plush and polished: blackcurrant, cedar and Mediterranean scrub (the *macchia*), riper and fleshier than Bordeaux but with a coastal freshness. Cabernet Franc has become a local speciality (Le Macchiole's Paleo is pure Franc).
it-bolgheri.terroir: Vineyards sit between the Tyrrhenian Sea and the Colline Metallifere, from near sea level to about 400 m, in a crescent between Bolgheri and Castagneto. Soils are a mosaic of alluvial gravel and pebbles washed down from the hills (*sassi*, as in Sassicaia, 'stony place'), sand, silt and clay; the gravelly fans drain like the Médoc and suit Cabernet, while clay pockets (Masseto's blue clay) suit Merlot. Sea breezes and the hills behind moderate heat and keep disease low.
producers: Tenuta San Guido (also Guidalberto, Le Difese)
it-bolgheri.nerd_note: Bolgheri allows the vineyard name on Rosso and Superiore labels (minimum 12.5%), so a 'cru' system is quietly forming inside a DOC that is barely 30 years old.

it-bolgheri-sassicaia.name: Bolgheri Sassicaia
it-bolgheri-sassicaia.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon (minimum 80%), with Cabernet Franc; in practice about 85% Cabernet Sauvignon and 15% Cabernet Franc.
it-bolgheri-sassicaia.summary:
The only Italian DOC owned, in practice, by a single estate. Marchese Mario Incisa della Rocchetta, a Piedmontese aristocrat who married into the Gherardesca family, planted Cabernet cuttings (said to come from Château Lafite) at Tenuta San Guido in the 1940s to make a claret for family use; the wine was drunk at home for two decades. His nephew Piero Antinori and the oenologist Giacomo Tachis helped refine it, and the 1968 vintage was released commercially in 1971. In 1978 a Decanter blind tasting in London put the 1972 Sassicaia first among 33 Cabernet-based wines from 11 countries, and Italian wine was never the same.

Sassicaia became a subzone of Bolgheri in 1994 and its own DOC in 2013. About 80 ha, roughly 85% Cabernet Sauvignon and 15% Cabernet Franc, aged about two years in French barriques. Compared with its neighbours it is lean, cedar-scented and tense, a wine of finesse that needs 15 years.
it-bolgheri-sassicaia.terroir: The vineyards spread over several parcels at roughly 80 to 400 m between the coast and the hills of Castiglioncello di Bolgheri, on stony alluvial soils (the original Sassicaia plot was named for its stones) with limestone and clay higher up.
it-bolgheri-sassicaia.nerd_note: The original 1940s vineyard, Castiglioncello, sits high (about 350 m) in the hills; the estate later moved its core plantings lower toward the sea when it found the stony fans there gave riper fruit.

it-bonarda-dell-oltrepo-pavese.name: Bonarda dell'Oltrepò Pavese
it-bonarda-dell-oltrepo-pavese.summary: The Oltrepò's signature everyday red, usually lightly sparkling (frizzante), purple-black, juicy and gently tannic: made from Croatina, which locals call Bonarda (not to be confused with Piedmont's Bonarda grape). It is the classic match for salame di Varzi and Lombard cooking.
it-bonarda-dell-oltrepo-pavese.nerd_note: Croatina's local name Bonarda leads to endless confusion with the Bonarda Piemontese grape and Argentina's Bonarda (Douce Noir).

it-bosco-eliceo.name: Bosco Eliceo
it-bosco-eliceo.summary: The DOC of the sandy coastal dunes and pine woods of the Po delta near Ferrara and Ravenna, famous for Fortana, an acidic, lightly sparkling red often ungrafted on the sand.
it-bosco-eliceo.nerd_note: Fortana grows on its own roots in the delta sands, where phylloxera cannot survive.

it-botticino.name: Botticino
it-botticino.summary: A small red DOC on the hills east of Brescia, in the village famous for its marble (Botticino marble was used for Rome's Vittoriano monument). The blend of Barbera, Marzemino, Sangiovese and Schiava gives fresh, medium reds.
it-botticino.terroir: Limestone slopes beside the marble quarries.
it-botticino.nerd_note: The Vittoriano 'wedding cake' in Rome is built of Botticino marble from the same hills.

it-brachetto-d-acqui.name: Brachetto d'Acqui
it-brachetto-d-acqui.summary: A sweet, rose-scented red fizz from around Acqui Terme, low in alcohol (about 5 to 6.5%) and tasting of strawberries and roses. It is made spumante or frizzante, and there is also a sweet passito. Banfi's investment in the 1990s made it fashionable in America as a Valentine's Day wine.
it-brachetto-d-acqui.terroir: Calcareous marls of the Bormida valleys.
it-brachetto-d-acqui.nerd_note: Local legend claims Cleopatra seduced Antony and Caesar with Brachetto, a story that turns up on many back labels.

it-bramaterra.name: Bramaterra
it-bramaterra.grapes: Nebbiolo (50 to 80%), Croatina, Uva Rara and/or Vespolina
it-bramaterra.summary: Hill wine from seven communes in Biella and Vercelli provinces on volcanic porphyry, blending Nebbiolo with Croatina and Vespolina. Colombera & Garella and Le Pianelle are leading names.
it-bramaterra.nerd_note: Antoniotti's Bramaterra is still made in an old wooden press and cement tanks from the 1900s.

it-breganze.name: Breganze
it-breganze.grapes: Vespaiola, Friulano (Tai), Pinot Bianco, Cabernet, Merlot
it-breganze.summary: Breganze, on the foothills of the Asiago plateau north of Vicenza, is famous for Torcolato, a golden sweet wine from Vespaiola grapes twisted (*torcolati*) onto strings and hung from rafters to dry until January. Fausto Maculan made Torcolato and his botrytised Acininobili internationally known from the 1980s.
it-breganze.terroir: Volcanic and morainic soils on south-facing foothills.
it-breganze.nerd_note: Vespaiola is named after the wasps (*vespe*) attracted to its sweet, ripe grapes.

it-brindisi.name: Brindisi
it-brindisi.grapes: Negroamaro, Malvasia Nera, Susumaniello; whites Chardonnay, Fiano, Malvasia Bianca
it-brindisi.summary: A Salento DOC around Brindisi and Mesagne, for Negroamaro reds and rosés and, increasingly, Susumaniello, a dark, juicy local grape rescued from near extinction. Tenute Rubino and Agricole Vallone are key producers; Vallone's Graticciaia (from partially dried Negroamaro) is a classic.

it-brunello-di-montalcino.name: Brunello di Montalcino
it-brunello-di-montalcino.created: DOC 1966; DOCG 1980 (one of the first four)
it-brunello-di-montalcino.summary:
Brunello di Montalcino is Sangiovese on its own, and for many people the summit of Italian red wine. The hill town of Montalcino, 40 km south of Siena, gave its name to a wine that the Biondi-Santi family made famous: Clemente Santi showed a 'Brunello' (from the dark, brownish skins of the local Sangiovese) in the 1860s, and his grandson Ferruccio bottled pure Sangiovese for long ageing from the 1888 vintage. The story is part history, part founding myth, since other families also made Brunello, but the 1888 and 1891 Riservas still exist and they set the template: a wine built to last decades.

For most of the 20th century Montalcino was poor and nearly forgotten; in 1960 there were barely a dozen bottlers. Brunello was one of the four original DOCGs in 1980, and the arrival of the American-owned Banfi estate and a wave of new growers in the 1970s and 1980s turned it into a boom town. Today about 2,100 hectares are registered to Brunello and the zone produces roughly 9 million bottles a year (about 30% of exports go to the United States).

The rules are strict and the ageing long: at least two years in wood and release only on 1 January of the fifth year after harvest (sixth for Riserva). That long wait in wood gives the classic style: brick-tinged colour even when young, cherry and blood orange, leather, tobacco and dried herbs, high acidity and firm tannin that soften over 10 to 30 years. A debate between large Slavonian oak casks (Biondi-Santi, Soldera, Poggio di Sotto) and French barriques has largely settled toward large wood.

The 2008 'Brunellopoli' scandal, when prosecutors investigated several large houses for blending other grapes into Brunello and 6.7 million litres were impounded, ended with plea bargains, declassifications and a firm recommitment to 100% Sangiovese.
it-brunello-di-montalcino.terroir: Montalcino is a roughly square block of hills (about 24,000 ha, of which only 15% is vineyard) bounded by the Orcia, Asso and Ombrone rivers, with Monte Amiata (1,738 m) to the southeast shielding it from storms. The northern slopes near the town (Montosoli, Canalicchio, Torrenieri) are cooler, with galestro and give perfumed, fine wines. The southern flank (Sant'Angelo in Colle, Castelnuovo dell'Abate, Tavernelle) is warmer and closer to the sea's influence, with clay, sand and volcanic-derived soils toward Amiata, giving riper, rounder wines. Western sites around Castelgiocondo and Camigliano catch the sea breeze; the east near Castelnuovo dell'Abate is more sheltered. No subzones are official, but most nerds read a label by hamlet.
producers: Case Basse di Gianfranco Soldera (sold as IGT)
it-brunello-di-montalcino.nerd_note: Lisini owns a half-hectare plot of ungrafted Sangiovese that survived phylloxera; since 1985 it has been bottled in tiny quantities as 'Prefillossero'.

it-buttafuoco-dell-oltrepo-pavese.name: Buttafuoco dell'Oltrepò Pavese
it-buttafuoco-dell-oltrepo-pavese.grapes: Barbera, Croatina, Uva Rara, Ughetta di Canneto
it-buttafuoco-dell-oltrepo-pavese.summary: 'Spark of fire': a powerful red blend from seven communes around Canneto Pavese and Broni. The Buttafuoco Storico association bottles single-vineyard versions with long ageing.
it-buttafuoco-dell-oltrepo-pavese.terroir: Steep hills between the Versa and Scuropasso streams.
it-buttafuoco-dell-oltrepo-pavese.nerd_note: The name is said to come from Austrian sailors on the Po who were 'set on fire' by the wine.

it-cacc-e-mmitte-di-lucera.name: Cacc'e mmitte di Lucera
it-cacc-e-mmitte-di-lucera.grapes: Nero di Troia, Montepulciano, Sangiovese, with white Bombino and Trebbiano
it-cacc-e-mmitte-di-lucera.summary: The name, in local dialect, means roughly 'drink it up and pour again': in the old days farmers drank the wine fast so the vats could be refilled. It is a light red blend around the hill town of Lucera, whose castle was built by Frederick II.

it-cagliari.name: Cagliari
it-cagliari.summary: A DOC created in 2011 that absorbed the old Malvasia di Cagliari, Monica di Cagliari and Moscato di Cagliari DOCs, for the sweet and fortified traditions of the south. About 19 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 153,000 bottles a year.

it-calosso.name: Calosso
it-calosso.summary: A micro-DOC for Gamba di Pernice ('partridge's leg', after its red stalks), a spicy red grape found only around Calosso.
it-calosso.nerd_note: Fewer than 20 hectares of Gamba di Pernice exist.

it-campi-flegrei.name: Campi Flegrei
it-campi-flegrei.summary: The Campi Flegrei, the 'burning fields' west of Naples, are a giant active caldera with more than 20 craters, hot springs and the bradyseism that raises and lowers the ground at Pozzuoli. The vineyards grow on loose volcanic sand, many ungrafted, some inside craters (the Astroni, Agnano). The DOC (1994) is built on Falanghina, here a different biotype from Sannio's, and Piedirosso, which gives light, aromatic, smoky reds that are the region's hidden treasure.
it-campi-flegrei.nerd_note: Raffaele Moccia's Agnanum vineyards sit on the edge of the Astroni crater nature reserve inside the city of Naples, on terraces of pure volcanic sand.

it-campidano-di-terralba.name: Campidano di Terralba
it-campidano-di-terralba.summary: A red DOC on the sandy western plain south of Oristano, built on Bovale. The sands kept many vines ungrafted. About 27 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 61,000 bottles a year.

it-canavese.name: Canavese
it-canavese.grapes: Nebbiolo, Barbera, Erbaluce, Uva Rara, Neretto
it-canavese.summary: The umbrella DOC for the Canavese north of Turin, around Ivrea and Caluso, covering Nebbiolo and Barbera reds and Erbaluce whites outside Carema and Caluso.
it-canavese.terroir: Glacial moraine of the Ivrea amphitheatre.
it-canavese.nerd_note: Ivrea's moraine is so large that geologists use it as a textbook example of a glacial amphitheatre.

it-candia-dei-colli-apuani.name: Candia dei Colli Apuani
it-candia-dei-colli-apuani.summary: Steep terraces under the Apuan Alps near Massa and Carrara, within sight of the marble quarries, for Vermentino whites and rare reds from Barsaglina and Vermentino Nero. It is close in spirit to Liguria's Colli di Luni next door.

it-canelli.name: Canelli
it-canelli.summary: Italy's 78th DOCG and Piedmont's most recent, split off from Asti in 2023 after almost twenty years of lobbying. Canelli covers 18 communes in Asti and Cuneo provinces around the town that invented Italian sparkling wine, with about 100 hectares and roughly 500,000 bottles. Rules are stricter than for Asti: hand harvesting only, vineyards at 165 to 500 metres and a maximum yield of 9.5 tonnes per hectare (Asti allows 10). The style is Moscato d'Asti-like frizzante, often with more intensity and saline length, plus Riserva.
it-canelli.terroir: White calcareous marls of the Belbo valley, steep and often terraced, with famous slopes around Canelli, Calosso and Santo Stefano Belbo.
it-canelli.nerd_note: The 'underground cathedrals' of Canelli (the cellars of Gancia, Bosca, Contratto and Coppo, dug into the hill in the 19th century) form a core zone of the UNESCO Langhe-Roero and Monferrato site.

it-cannellino-di-frascati.name: Cannellino di Frascati
it-cannellino-di-frascati.summary: The traditional sweet Frascati, made from late-harvested grapes with at least 35 g/l of residual sugar. 'Cannellino' was the name Romans gave to the lightly sweet wine served with *ciambelline* biscuits. It is gently honeyed rather than heavy.
it-cannellino-di-frascati.nerd_note: Cannellino is one of the few Italian DOCGs dedicated solely to a late-harvest sweet white.

it-cannonau-di-sardegna.name: Cannonau di Sardegna
it-cannonau-di-sardegna.summary:
Cannonau is Sardinia's Grenache, and the island's most important red: about 2,100 ha in the DOC, which covers the whole island. It thrives in the mountainous east, where small growers keep old bush vines on granite and schist at 300 to 700 m. Good Cannonau is warm and spicy, with red berries, Mediterranean scrub, dried herbs and a firm, slightly bitter finish; the alcohol is often high, but altitude and the mistral give freshness. The DOC also allows rosé, Riserva, passito and fortified (liquoroso) wines.

Three subzones carry extra prestige. Jerzu, in the Ogliastra, is a village of terraced vineyards below limestone *tacchi* (cliffs) and a large cooperative, Antichi Poderi di Jerzu. Oliena, below the limestone of Monte Corrasi near Nuoro, makes 'Nepente di Oliena', the name the poet Gabriele D'Annunzio gave to its wine in 1909, comparing it to the drug of oblivion in Homer. Capo Ferrato, on the southeast coast, is warmer. Classico, from the provinces of Nuoro and Ogliastra, requires 90% Cannonau. Mamoiada, though not an official subzone, has become a byword for high-altitude, artisanal Cannonau, with dozens of tiny family producers.
it-cannonau-di-sardegna.terroir: Granite sands in the Barbagia and around Mamoiada (600 to 700 m), limestone near Oliena and Jerzu, schist in the Mandrolisai; hot, dry summers with strong winds, cold winters inland.
it-cannonau-di-sardegna.nerd_note: In the 1990s a Sardinian study claimed that Cannonau's high polyphenol content helped explain the longevity of Ogliastra's centenarians; the link is unproven, but the region's long-lived shepherds still drink it daily.

it-capalbio.name: Capalbio
it-capalbio.summary: A small DOC in the far south of the Maremma near the Lazio border, around the hill town of Capalbio. Most wines from here are now labelled Maremma Toscana. About 2 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 11,000 bottles a year.

it-capri.name: Capri
it-capri.summary: The island of Capri has its own DOC but barely a hectare of declared vines. Emperor Tiberius lived here from AD 27, and Roman villas once had vineyards; today Capri wine is a curiosity sold to visitors.

it-capriano-del-colle.name: Capriano del Colle
it-capriano-del-colle.grapes: Sangiovese, Marzemino, Barbera; Trebbiano (Trebbiano di Lugana)
it-capriano-del-colle.summary: Small DOC on Monte Netto, an isolated hill south-west of Brescia.
it-capriano-del-colle.terroir: An isolated loess and gravel hill rising from the plain.

it-carema.name: Carema
it-carema.summary: Carema is Nebbiolo in the mountains: a single village at the mouth of the Aosta Valley where vines grow on stone-and-lime pillars (*pilun*) supporting pergolas (*topie*), on terraces cut from the rock between 300 and 700 metres. The pillars soak up daytime heat and release it at night, letting Nebbiolo ripen at the edge of its range. The wines are pale, fragrant and long-lived. Ferrando's black-label Carema and the Cantina dei Produttori Nebbiolo di Carema (a co-op founded in 1960) produce almost all of it.
it-carema.terroir: Thin, sandy, acidic morainic and granitic soils over rock, on steep terraces.
it-carema.nerd_note: Carema is one of the smallest DOCs in Italy, with about 17 hectares, and the area under vine has shrunk by roughly 80% since the 1950s.

it-carignano-del-sulcis.name: Carignano del Sulcis
it-carignano-del-sulcis.summary: In the Sulcis, the southwestern corner of Sardinia, and on the islands of Sant'Antioco and San Pietro, Carignano (Carignan) grows as old bush vines on sand, many ungrafted because phylloxera cannot live in sand. The wines are dark and spicy, with blackberry, myrtle and a saline edge, far richer than most Carignan. Cantina di Santadi and the oenologist Giacomo Tachis put it on the map with Terre Brune (first vintage 1984) and Rocca Rubia.
it-carignano-del-sulcis.terroir: Sandy coastal soils and dunes around Sant'Antioco and Calasetta, with clay and limestone inland around Santadi; hot, windy and dry.
it-carignano-del-sulcis.nerd_note: Some of Sardus Pater's ungrafted Carignano on Sant'Antioco is believed to be over 100 years old.

it-carmignano.name: Carmignano
it-carmignano.grapes: Sangiovese minimum 50%, Cabernet Franc and/or Cabernet Sauvignon 10 to 20%, Canaiolo up to 20%.
it-carmignano.summary:
Carmignano, on the Montalbano ridge west of Florence and Prato, was one of the four zones in Cosimo III's 1716 edict, and its wine was a Medici favourite: the family's hunting reserve, the Barco Reale, was walled here, and the villa La Ferdinanda at Artimino looks over the vines. Cabernet has grown here since at least the 18th century (locally called *uva francesca*), so when the DOC was created in 1975 Carmignano was the first Italian appellation to require Cabernet in the blend, decades before the Super Tuscans made it fashionable.

The wine is Sangiovese-led with 10 to 20% Cabernet: medium-full, with red cherry, cassis and a herbal, slightly austere finish. Only about 117 ha are planted. The Contini Bonacossi family of Tenuta di Capezzana, whose records show wine made on the estate in 804, did most to save the name.
it-carmignano.terroir: Hills of 50 to 400 m on the southern flank of Monte Albano, with galestro, alberese and sandy clay, warmer and drier than Chianti Classico to the south.
it-carmignano.nerd_note: A rental contract dated 804, kept at Capezzana, records vines and olives on the property, one of the oldest written mentions of a specific Tuscan wine estate.

it-carso.name: Carso
it-carso.summary: The Karst plateau that runs from Trieste into Slovenia is a land of limestone, sinkholes, caves and the fierce Bora wind, where small growers carve vineyards out of rock and dig cellars into the stone. Native Vitovska and Malvasia Istriana make saline, mineral whites, often skin-macerated in amphorae; Terrano, a local Refosco, gives a sharp, iron-rich red. Edi Kante, Paolo Vodopivec, Benjamin Zidarich and Sandi Skerk have made the Carso a pilgrimage site for natural-wine lovers.
it-carso.terroir: Karst limestone with thin red *terra rossa* soils, often bulldozed and crushed by hand to make vineyards; strong winds and Adriatic influence.
it-carso.nerd_note: Pliny wrote that the Empress Livia attributed her 86 years to Pucinum, a wine from the rocky coast near Trieste, often identified with today's Prosecco and Carso area.

it-casauria.name: Casauria
it-casauria.summary: Italy's newest Abruzzo DOCG, approved in 2025 after nearly a decade of lobbying. Casauria was a subzone (Terre di Casauria) of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo from 2006; it covers the hills of the Val Pescara foothills in the province of Pescara, around Tocco da Casauria and Castiglione a Casauria, centred on the Benedictine abbey of San Clemente a Casauria (founded 871). The rules require at least 90% Montepulciano, 18 months of ageing (24 for Riserva), and vineyards no higher than 500 m (600 m facing south), and they stress place rather than grape. A local clone, also called 'Casauria', is recognised.

it-casavecchia-di-pontelatone.name: Casavecchia di Pontelatone
it-casavecchia-di-pontelatone.summary: Casavecchia ('old house') is a red grape rediscovered in the 19th century, the story goes, as a single ancient vine growing against the ruins of an old house near Pontelatone. Its DOC (2011) covers a few communes in the hills north of Caserta. The wines are dark, tannic and spicy.

it-casteggio.name: Casteggio
it-casteggio.summary: A small DOC for structured Barbera from the hills around Casteggio, the Roman Clastidium.
it-casteggio.nerd_note: Clastidium was the site of a famous Roman victory over the Gauls in 222 BC.

it-castel-del-monte.name: Castel del Monte
it-castel-del-monte.grapes: Nero di Troia, Aglianico, Montepulciano, Bombino Nero, Cabernet; whites Bombino Bianco, Pampanuto, Chardonnay
it-castel-del-monte.summary: Named after Frederick II's 13th-century octagonal castle, which sits alone on a hill of the Murge plateau, this DOC covers the hills around Andria, Corato, Minervino and Ruvo. It is the home of Nero di Troia, a late-ripening grape with firm tannin and violet, black cherry and spice aromas, and of Bombino Nero, which gives delicate rosé. Three styles have been separate DOCGs since 2011: Rosso Riserva, Nero di Troia Riserva and Bombino Nero (rosato).
it-castel-del-monte.terroir: Limestone plateau and slopes at 200 to 500 m, with thin red soils and big day-night swings; cooler and windier than the Salento.
contains: Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva

it-castel-del-monte-bombino-nero.name: Castel del Monte Bombino Nero
it-castel-del-monte-bombino-nero.summary: A rosé-only DOCG, one of the very few in Italy. Bombino Nero ripens unevenly, which keeps acidity high and makes it ideal for fresh, cherry-scented pink wine. Torrevento and Rivera make good examples.

it-castel-del-monte-nero-di-troia-riserv.name: Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva
it-castel-del-monte-nero-di-troia-riserv.summary: The top expression of Nero di Troia (Uva di Troia), a DOCG since 2011: at least 90% of the grape and two years of ageing, one in wood. Firm, dark and perfumed with violets and spice. Rivera's Puer Apuliae and Torrevento's Vigna Pedale are references.

it-castel-del-monte-rosso-riserva.name: Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva
it-castel-del-monte-rosso-riserva.grapes: Nero di Troia minimum 65%, with Aglianico, Montepulciano and others
it-castel-del-monte-rosso-riserva.summary: A Riserva red DOCG with Nero di Troia as the main grape blended with Aglianico or Montepulciano, aged two years. Rivera's Il Falcone, made since 1971, is the classic. About 46 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 316,000 bottles a year.

it-castel-san-lorenzo.name: Castel San Lorenzo
it-castel-san-lorenzo.summary: A small DOC in the hills of the Calore Salernitano valley, oddly based on Barbera for reds, plus a sweet Moscato. About 11 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 10,000 bottles a year.

it-casteller.name: Casteller
it-casteller.grapes: Schiava, Merlot, Lambrusco a foglia frastagliata (Enantio) and others
it-casteller.summary: A light red blend from the hills of Trento and Vallagarina, named after the Casteller hill above Trento.

it-castelli-di-jesi-verdicchio-riserva.name: Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva
it-castelli-di-jesi-verdicchio-riserva.summary: The Riserva tier of Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi, a DOCG since 2010. It needs 18 months of ageing including six in bottle and at least 12.5% alcohol, and it is where the grape's ability to age shows best: Villa Bucci Riserva, from old vines around Montecarotto and Serra de' Conti, is aged in large old casks and often drinks well after two decades. Classico Riserva comes from the historic core.

it-castelli-romani.name: Castelli Romani
it-castelli-romani.grapes: Malvasia, Trebbiano; Cesanese, Merlot, Montepulciano, Nero Buono, Sangiovese
it-castelli-romani.summary: An umbrella DOC over the whole Alban Hills district (the 'Roman castles', the hill towns around the old volcano), for simpler whites, reds and rosés that do not fit the local village DOCs. It accounts for a large share of the area's volume.

it-cellatica.name: Cellatica
it-cellatica.grapes: Marzemino, Barbera, Schiava gentile, Incrocio Terzi
it-cellatica.summary: Tiny red DOC in the hills north-west of Brescia, one of Lombardy's oldest delimited wines.
it-cellatica.nerd_note: Incrocio Terzi No. 1, a Barbera x Cabernet Franc cross, was bred in Brescia province.

it-cerasuolo-d-abruzzo.name: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo
it-cerasuolo-d-abruzzo.summary: Cerasuolo means 'cherry-coloured', and this is a rosé dark enough to be mistaken for a light red: Montepulciano pressed after a short maceration, giving a deep pink wine with cherry, wild strawberry and a grip of tannin. It was a style of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo until 2010, when it got its own DOC. It is the classic partner for Abruzzo's fish soups (*brodetto*). Valentini's and Emidio Pepe's Cerasuolos age for years.

it-cerasuolo-di-vittoria.name: Cerasuolo di Vittoria
it-cerasuolo-di-vittoria.summary: Sicily's only DOCG, from the southeastern corner of the island around Vittoria, Comiso and Acate in the province of Ragusa. Despite the name (*cerasuolo*, cherry-coloured), it is a red, a blend of the dark, structured Nero d'Avola with the pale, perfumed Frappato, which gives flavours of red cherry, pomegranate and violets with gentle tannin and lively acidity. The Classico area, the historic core, needs about 18 months of ageing. Two growers changed its fortunes: COS, founded in 1980 by Giambattista Cilia, Giusto Occhipinti and Cirino Strano, who later revived amphora ageing, and Arianna Occhipinti, whose Frappato became a natural-wine icon.
it-cerasuolo-di-vittoria.terroir: Red sand (*terra rossa*) over limestone tuff on a plateau at 150 to 300 m, close to the sea, with hot days and breezy nights. Sandy soils protected some vines from phylloxera.

it-cerveteri.name: Cerveteri
it-cerveteri.summary: A DOC around Cerveteri, the Etruscan city of Caere with its UNESCO necropolis, on the coast northwest of Rome. About 10 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 12,000 bottles a year.

it-cesanese-del-piglio.name: Cesanese del Piglio
it-cesanese-del-piglio.summary: Lazio's only red DOCG, from the hill towns of Piglio, Serrone, Acuto, Anagni and Paliano in the Ciociaria, southeast of Rome. Cesanese has two forms: Cesanese di Affile, small-berried and finer, and Cesanese Comune, larger-berried. The wine is medium-bodied with red cherry, pepper, rose and a touch of earth, sometimes compared to a lighter Syrah or Pinot Noir. Superiore and Superiore Riserva are aged longer. It was Lazio's first DOCG (2008).
it-cesanese-del-piglio.terroir: Apennine foothills at about 300 to 700 m, with red clay, limestone and volcanic deposits; cool nights help aroma.

it-cesanese-di-affile.name: Cesanese di Affile
it-cesanese-di-affile.summary: The tiny DOC of Affile, the mountain village (about 700 m) that gave its name to the finer Cesanese biotype. Only a few hectares remain; the wines are fresh, spicy and light-bodied.

it-cesanese-di-olevano-romano.name: Cesanese di Olevano Romano
it-cesanese-di-olevano-romano.summary: A small DOC around Olevano Romano on the hills east of Rome, which has become the most exciting place for Cesanese thanks to growers such as Damiano Ciolli, whose Cirsium from 1950s vines showed how fine and aromatic the grape can be.

it-chambave.name: Chambave
it-chambave.grapes: Moscato Bianco (Muscat de Chambave), Petit Rouge, Gamay, Pinot Noir
it-chambave.summary: Best known for Chambave Muscat, dry or as the honeyed Moscato Flétri passito from dried grapes, and for Petit Rouge-based reds. The cooperative La Crotta di Vegneron is the main producer.
it-chambave.terroir: Warm, dry slopes in the central valley around Chambave and Saint-Denis.
it-chambave.nerd_note: Chambave's Moscato Flétri was historically served to the Savoy kings when they hunted in the valley.

it-chianti.name: Chianti
it-chianti.grapes: Sangiovese (minimum 60%; 75% in the Colli Senesi), with Canaiolo, Colorino and other reds (Cabernet up to 15%) and up to 10% white grapes; a rosato was added in 2026.
it-chianti.summary:
Chianti is the big tent around Chianti Classico: a DOCG of roughly 13,700 hectares and more than 700,000 hectolitres a year across six provinces, from the Arno hills west of Florence to Arezzo and the Sienese countryside. The name spread outward in the 20th century as merchants and growers outside the historic zone fought to use it; a 1932 decree drew the seven subzones that still exist (Classico was one of them until it split off in 1996).

Most Chianti (minimum 60% Sangiovese) is fresh, cherry-fruited wine for the table, released from March after the harvest; Superiore and Riserva (24 months) add depth, and the subzones carry the character. Rùfina, in the cool, high Sieve valley northeast of Florence, makes the longest-lived wines (its producers created the TerraElectae single-vineyard mark). Colli Senesi wraps around Siena, Montalcino and Montepulciano and must contain at least 75% Sangiovese. Colli Fiorentini, Montespertoli, Montalbano (next to Carmignano), Colline Pisane, Colli Aretini and the new Terre di Vinci (2026, around Leonardo's birthplace) complete the map.

The 2026 rule change also created Chianti Rosato, made from at least 60% Sangiovese. The old *governo all'uso toscano*, refermenting young wine with a share of dried grapes for a softer, slightly prickly wine, is still allowed for the red.
it-chianti.terroir: The zone is too large for one terroir: galestro and alberese in Rùfina and the Colli Senesi, sandier Pliocene soils around Montespertoli and the Colline Pisane, and Arno-valley clays nearer Florence. Rùfina's altitude (to about 500 m) and Apennine air give acidity and long ageing.
it-chianti.nerd_note: Selvapiana's Bucerchiale Rùfina Riserva, first bottled as a single vineyard in 1979, shows how Chianti can age 30 years when the site is cool enough.

it-chianti-classico.name: Chianti Classico
it-chianti-classico.grapes: Sangiovese (minimum 80%; 90% for Gran Selezione from 2027), with Canaiolo, Colorino, Malvasia Nera, Ciliegiolo and, outside Gran Selezione, some international reds.
it-chianti-classico.summary:
Chianti Classico is the original Chianti: the hills between Florence and Siena that Cosimo III named in 1716, long before the name spread across half of Tuscany. It covers about 70,000 hectares, of which only around 10,000 are vineyard (7,200 ha registered to the DOCG); the rest is oak and chestnut forest, olive groves and stone villages, which is why the landscape still looks like a Renaissance painting. About 480 members, 342 of them bottlers, make 35 to 38 million bottles a year, every one carrying the black rooster (*gallo nero*) on the neck, a symbol taken from the medieval Lega del Chianti formed by Castellina, Gaiole and Radda.

The modern wine was rebuilt from a low point. The 1967 DOC rules froze a recipe that demanded white Trebbiano and Malvasia in a red wine, and the best producers responded by leaving the system. The consorzio fought back: 100% Sangiovese became legal in 1995, Chianti Classico became its own DOCG in 1996, and white grapes were banned from the 2006 vintage. Today the wine is Sangiovese at its most transparent: sour cherry, violets, dried herbs and a savoury, saline acidity, with tannins that can be chalky in Gaiole or silky in Panzano.

The pyramid has three levels. *Annata* is released after about a year; Riserva needs 24 months; Gran Selezione (created 2014) needs 30 months and estate-grown fruit, and is moving to a minimum 90% Sangiovese with only native partners from the 2027 vintage. Gran Selezione can also carry one of 11 UGA village names, the first legal recognition that Radda tastes different from Castelnuovo Berardenga.
it-chianti-classico.terroir: The zone runs about 50 km north to south across all or part of eight communes. Soils change ridge by ridge: galestro (crumbly schistous clay) around Gaiole, Radda and Panzano gives perfume and tension; alberese limestone gives structure; macigno sandstone in Lamole and San Casciano gives finesse; the Pliocene sands and clays near Castelnuovo Berardenga give riper, rounder wines. Vineyards climb from about 200 m to the legal limit of 700 m, and the high, cool sites have gained ground as summers warm. The Pesa, Greve and Arbia valleys and the Monti del Chianti ridge on the east frame most of the best slopes.
it-chianti-classico.nerd_note: The 2027 Gran Selezione rules allow only eight native blending partners (Canaiolo, Ciliegiolo, Colorino, Foglia Tonda, Malvasia Nera, Mammolo, Pugnitello and Sanforte) up to 10%: Cabernet and Merlot, once the secret of many 'modern' Chianti Classico, are out at the top of the pyramid.

it-chianti-colli-aretini.name: Chianti Colli Aretini
it-chianti-colli-aretini.summary: The eastern subzone, on the hills of the upper Arno around Arezzo, facing the Val d'Arno di Sopra, with cooler Apennine influence and lively, fruity wines.

it-chianti-colli-fiorentini.name: Chianti Colli Fiorentini
