it-chianti-colli-fiorentini.summary: The hills around Florence on both sides of the Arno and down the Pesa and Greve valleys toward Chianti Classico, with about 900 ha. Wines are medium-bodied and aromatic, released a little later than basic Chianti.

it-chianti-colli-senesi.name: Chianti Colli Senesi
it-chianti-colli-senesi.summary: The largest subzone, wrapping around Siena and reaching south to Montalcino, Montepulciano and San Gimignano, so many Brunello and Vino Nobile producers also make Colli Senesi from younger vines or declassified fruit. It requires at least 75% Sangiovese, more than the rest of Chianti, and the style is warm and ripe.

it-chianti-colline-pisane.name: Chianti Colline Pisane
it-chianti-colline-pisane.summary: The westernmost subzone, on the hills southeast of Pisa around Terricciola and Casciana Terme, with marine sands and clays, giving softer, rounder Chianti close to the coast.

it-chianti-montalbano.name: Chianti Montalbano
it-chianti-montalbano.summary: The slopes of Monte Albano west of Florence around Vinci, Lamporecchio and Quarrata, surrounding the Carmignano enclave. The wines are soft and fruity.

it-chianti-montespertoli.name: Chianti Montespertoli
it-chianti-montespertoli.summary: A small subzone carved out of Colli Fiorentini in 1996 around the town of Montespertoli, southwest of Florence, on sandy Pliocene soils. It has only a few dozen hectares declared.

it-chianti-rufina.name: Chianti Rùfina
it-chianti-rufina.summary: One of the smallest and the highest-regarded Chianti subzone, in the Sieve valley about 20 km northeast of Florence, with about 750 ha. Vineyards climb to 500 m and catch cold air from the Apennines through the Consuma pass, so harvests are late and the wines are tense, perfumed and long-lived. Selvapiana, Frescobaldi's Nipozzano, Colognole, Grati and I Veroni lead; since 2016 the consorzio's TerraElectae mark identifies single-vineyard Riservas. Pomino is an enclave within it.

it-chianti-terre-di-vinci.name: Chianti Terre di Vinci
it-chianti-terre-di-vinci.summary: The newest Chianti subzone, added in the 2026 rules, around Vinci, the birthplace of Leonardo, and neighbouring communes in the lower Arno hills between Empoli and Monte Albano. Its reds may be released from 1 September after the vintage.

it-cilento.name: Cilento
it-cilento.summary: The hills of the Cilento national park south of Salerno, near the Greek temples of Paestum and the ancient city of Velia. Fiano here is broader and sunnier than in Irpinia, and Aglianico is softer. Luigi Maffini and De Conciliis brought it attention in the 1990s.

it-cinque-terre.name: Cinque Terre
it-cinque-terre.summary:
The five fishing villages of Monterosso, Vernazza, Corniglia, Manarola and Riomaggiore cling to cliffs on the coast west of La Spezia, and above them rises one of the most dramatic vineyard landscapes in the world: about 7,000 km of dry-stone terraces built over a thousand years. The UNESCO World Heritage listing (1997, with Portovenere and the islands) recognises this landscape, and the national park works to stop it collapsing back into scrub.

The dry white Cinque Terre DOC, mostly Bosco with Albarola and Vermentino, is herbal, saline and crisp. The treasure is Sciacchetrà: the same grapes dried on racks for about two months, then pressed into a tiny quantity of amber, apricot-and-honey sweet wine aged at least a year (Riserva three). Grapes are carried down by hand or by small monorail trains (*trenini a cremagliera*). Production is tiny, under 100 hectares in total, and the Cantina Cinque Terre cooperative at Groppo makes much of it, alongside growers like Possa (Heydi Bonanini), Walter De Batté and Buranco.
it-cinque-terre.terroir: Sandstone (macigno) and shale on slopes up to 45 degrees, often dropping straight to the sea; terraces face south-west into the sun and sea breeze.
it-cinque-terre.nerd_note: Sciacchetrà's name is often explained as dialect for 'crush' (*sciacca*) and 'set aside' (*tra*), describing pressing the dried grapes and keeping the precious wine.

it-circeo.name: Circeo
it-circeo.summary: A coastal DOC around the promontory of Monte Circeo (home, in legend, of the sorceress Circe) and Sabaudia, on the reclaimed Pontine plain. About 66 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 587,000 bottles a year.

it-ciro.name: Cirò
it-ciro.grapes: Rosso and Rosato: Gaglioppo minimum 80%; Bianco: Greco Bianco minimum 80%
it-ciro.summary: Calabria's most important DOC, on the Ionian coast in the province of Crotone, covering Cirò, Cirò Marina, Crucoli and Melissa. Reds and rosés come from Gaglioppo, whites from Greco Bianco. The Classico Superiore Riserva reds of Cirò and Cirò Marina moved into the new Cirò Classico DOCG in 2025, so this DOC now covers the rest: fresh Cirò Rosso and Rosato, Bianco and wines from outside the Classico core.

it-ciro-classico.name: Cirò Classico
it-ciro-classico.grapes: Gaglioppo minimum 90%, Magliocco and/or Greco Nero up to 10%
it-ciro-classico.summary:
Calabria's first DOCG, recognised in 2025 and registered by the European Commission on 18 July 2025 (Regulation 2025/1518), it is one of two DOCGs created in 2025 (with Abruzzo's Casauria), which took Italy's total to 79. It covers only the communes of Cirò and Cirò Marina, the historic heart of the Cirò DOC, on hills from sea level to 462 m above the Ionian coast. The wine is a red of at least 90% Gaglioppo with up to 10% Magliocco or Greco Nero, no international varieties, aged at least three years with six months in wood, with yields capped at 8 t/ha and production and bottling inside the zone.

Gaglioppo is a paradox: pale in colour, like Nebbiolo, but with firm tannin, flavours of red cherry, orange peel, dried herbs and earth, and real ageing ability. Its modern revival owes much to Librandi and to the Cirò Revolution, a group of small growers founded around 2010 (Sergio Arcuri, A Vita of Francesco De Franco, Cataldo Calabretta, Tenuta del Conte) who went back to old bush vines, large casks and minimal intervention.
it-ciro-classico.terroir: Clay, marl and sand hills between the Ionian Sea and the Sila foothills, with mineral-rich sedimentary soils; the mountains to the west and the sea to the east shape a warm, dry climate with ventilated nights.
it-ciro-classico.nerd_note: Gaglioppo is a cross of Sangiovese and Mantonico Bianco, which may explain its Tuscan-looking colour and its southern warmth.

it-cisterna-d-asti.name: Cisterna d'Asti
it-cisterna-d-asti.summary: A small DOC on the Roero-Asti border for Croatina reds, still or frizzante.
it-cisterna-d-asti.nerd_note: Cisterna's castle houses a museum of peasant arts and trades.

it-colli-albani.name: Colli Albani
it-colli-albani.summary: A white-wine DOC on the southwestern slopes of the Alban volcano around Albano Laziale, Ariccia and Castel Gandolfo, the popes' summer residence. About 45 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 223,000 bottles a year.

it-colli-altotiberini.name: Colli Altotiberini
it-colli-altotiberini.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet, Pinot Nero; Trebbiano, Grechetto
it-colli-altotiberini.summary: The upper Tiber valley around Città di Castello and Umbertide, the coolest corner of Umbria, close to the Tuscan border. Reds are Sangiovese-based and whites light. About 31 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 48,000 bottles a year.

it-colli-asolani-prosecco.name: Asolo Prosecco
it-colli-asolani-prosecco.summary: The second Prosecco Superiore DOCG, on the Asolo and Montello hills west of the Piave around the hill town of Asolo, once home of Caterina Cornaro, Queen of Cyprus. It grew rapidly in the 2010s and is known for pioneering the drier Extra Brut style and allowing Brut Nature.
it-colli-asolani-prosecco.terroir: Gentler, sunnier slopes of sandy marl and limestone around Asolo and on the Montello.
it-colli-asolani-prosecco.nerd_note: Asolo was one of the first Prosecco zones to embrace bone-dry Extra Brut.

it-colli-berici.name: Colli Berici
it-colli-berici.grapes: Tai Rosso (Grenache), Cabernet, Carmenère, Merlot, Garganega
it-colli-berici.summary: Limestone hills south of Vicenza, home of Tai Rosso, a local form of Grenache (Cannonau), especially around Barbarano Vicentino. Inama's Carmenère and Piú show the area's Bordeaux side.
it-colli-berici.terroir: Karstic limestone and marl hills with red clays.
it-colli-berici.nerd_note: Tai Rosso was called Tocai Rosso until the EU banned the 'Tocai' name in 2007.

it-colli-bolognesi.name: Colli Bolognesi
it-colli-bolognesi.grapes: Barbera, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pignoletto, Sauvignon, Chardonnay
it-colli-bolognesi.summary: The hills south of Bologna, home to Bordeaux varieties since the 19th century; Enrico Vallania's Terre Rosse estate was an early pioneer of Cabernet in these hills.

it-colli-bolognesi-classico-pignoletto.name: Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto
it-colli-bolognesi-classico-pignoletto.summary: Pignoletto is a crisp, lightly aromatic white from the hills south-west of Bologna, made still, frizzante, spumante and passito; the grape is the same as Umbria's Grechetto Gentile. A broader Pignoletto DOC covers the plain and surrounding provinces, while the hill DOCG is registered as Colli Bolognesi Classico Pignoletto. Orsi San Vito's col fondo and Gaggioli and Manaresi's still wines are references.
it-colli-bolognesi-classico-pignoletto.terroir: Clay, sand and limestone hills of the Reno, Lavino and Samoggia valleys.
it-colli-bolognesi-classico-pignoletto.nerd_note: Pliny mentioned 'Pino Laeto' wines from the Bologna area, which some link to Pignoletto.

it-colli-d-imola.name: Colli d'Imola
it-colli-d-imola.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet, Barbera, Trebbiano, Pignoletto, Chardonnay
it-colli-d-imola.summary: Varietal and blended wines from the Imola hills, home of the Formula One circuit.

it-colli-del-trasimeno.name: Colli del Trasimeno
it-colli-del-trasimeno.grapes: Gamay del Trasimeno (Grenache), Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet; Trebbiano, Grechetto
it-colli-del-trasimeno.summary: The hills around Lake Trasimeno, where Hannibal ambushed a Roman army in 217 BC. The local speciality is 'Gamay del Trasimeno' (also called Gamay Perugino), which DNA testing has shown to be Grenache, brought by Spanish rulers or monks centuries ago. The lake moderates temperatures and the wines are juicy and spicy.
it-colli-del-trasimeno.nerd_note: Trasimeno Gamay is a cousin of Sardinia's Cannonau and Spain's Garnacha, not of Beaujolais' Gamay.

it-colli-dell-etruria-centrale.name: Colli dell'Etruria Centrale
it-colli-dell-etruria-centrale.summary: Created in 1990 as a home for wines from the Chianti zone that did not fit the Chianti rules (whites, rosé, Vin Santo, novello and international blends). The IGT Toscana has made it almost redundant.

it-colli-della-sabina.name: Colli della Sabina
it-colli-della-sabina.summary: The Sabine hills northeast of Rome, better known for olive oil (Sabina was Italy's first oil DOP), with a small wine DOC. About 8 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 19,000 bottles a year.

it-colli-di-conegliano.name: Colli di Conegliano
it-colli-di-conegliano.grapes: Cabernet, Merlot, Marzemino; Manzoni Bianco, Pinot Bianco; Verdiso; Torchiato di Fregona
it-colli-di-conegliano.summary: A small DOCG (since 2011) for still wines from the Prosecco hills: Bordeaux-variety reds and Manzoni Bianco whites, the rare sweet Torchiato di Fregona from dried grapes, and the red Refrontolo Passito from Marzemino.
it-colli-di-conegliano.nerd_note: Refrontolo's Marzemino passito is said to be the Marzemino Mozart's Don Giovanni toasts.

it-colli-di-faenza.name: Colli di Faenza
it-colli-di-faenza.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet, Merlot, Ciliegiolo, Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay, Trebbiano
it-colli-di-faenza.summary: Hill blends around Faenza, the ceramics town.

it-colli-di-luni.name: Colli di Luni
it-colli-di-luni.grapes: Vermentino (min 90% for Vermentino), Sangiovese, Ciliegiolo, Canaiolo
it-colli-di-luni.summary: A DOC straddling the Liguria-Tuscany border around Sarzana and the Magra valley, named after the Roman port of Luna. Its Vermentino is the richest and most structured in Liguria, with ripe citrus, almond and Mediterranean herbs, closer to the Tuscan coastal style. Vermentino 'Superiore' and reds based on Sangiovese and Ciliegiolo exist. Lunae Bosoni, Ottaviano Lambruschi (Costa Marina, Sarticola), La Baia del Sole and Giacomelli are leaders.
it-colli-di-luni.terroir: Alluvial terraces of the Magra plus hillside clays and marls around Castelnuovo Magra and Ortonovo; warm and protected by the Apuan Alps.
it-colli-di-luni.nerd_note: Luni's Roman wine was praised by Pliny the Elder; the ruins of the Roman town, abandoned in the Middle Ages because of malaria, lie a few kilometres from today's vineyards.

it-colli-di-parma.name: Colli di Parma
it-colli-di-parma.grapes: Malvasia di Candia Aromatica, Sauvignon, Barbera, Bonarda, Lambrusco
it-colli-di-parma.summary: The hills around Langhirano and Sala Baganza, famous for prosciutto, make Malvasia frizzante and light red sparklers to match.

it-colli-di-rimini.name: Colli di Rimini
it-colli-di-rimini.summary: Hill wines behind Rimini, including the sweet Rebola.
it-colli-di-rimini.nerd_note: Rebola is a local name for Grechetto Gentile, the same grape as Pignoletto.

it-colli-di-scandiano-e-di-canossa.name: Colli di Scandiano e di Canossa
it-colli-di-scandiano-e-di-canossa.grapes: Spergola, Malvasia, Sauvignon, Lambrusco Grasparossa, Marzemino
it-colli-di-scandiano-e-di-canossa.summary: Hill wines south of Reggio Emilia around the castle of Canossa (where Emperor Henry IV knelt before Pope Gregory VII in 1077), notably Spergola, a high-acid white now made as sparkling and still wine.
it-colli-di-scandiano-e-di-canossa.nerd_note: Spergola was long confused with Sauvignon until DNA showed it is a distinct local grape.

it-colli-etruschi-viterbesi.name: Colli Etruschi Viterbesi
it-colli-etruschi-viterbesi.grapes: Sangiovese, Montepulciano, Canaiolo, Grechetto Rosso (Violone); Trebbiano, Malvasia, Grechetto, Moscato
it-colli-etruschi-viterbesi.summary: A broad DOC covering the province of Viterbo (the ancient Tuscia), with many varietal types including the rare Grechetto Rosso and sweet Moscatello. About 89 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 123,000 bottles a year.

it-colli-euganei.name: Colli Euganei
it-colli-euganei.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet, Carmenère, Raboso; Garganega, Pinella, Serprina (Glera), Moscato
it-colli-euganei.summary: The Euganean Hills south-west of Padua are a cluster of extinct volcanic cones rising from the plain, where Petrarch spent his last years at Arquà. They make Bordeaux-style reds of surprising depth (Vignalta's Gemola, Ca' Lustra) on trachyte and volcanic soils, plus whites from local grapes like Pinella.
it-colli-euganei.terroir: Volcanic trachyte, rhyolite and latite cones with marine limestone on the lower slopes.
it-colli-euganei.nerd_note: Castello di Lispida in Monselice was one of the first Italian estates to ferment in amphorae, in the 2000s.

it-colli-euganei-fior-d-arancio.name: Colli Euganei Fior d'Arancio
it-colli-euganei-fior-d-arancio.summary: 'Orange blossom': Moscato Giallo from the Euganean Hills, made as a sweet sparkling wine, still, or passito. It tastes literally of orange flowers and apricot.
it-colli-euganei-fior-d-arancio.nerd_note: The DOCG is unusual for being dedicated to Moscato Giallo, the yellow Muscat more common in Alto Adige.

it-colli-lanuvini.name: Colli Lanuvini
it-colli-lanuvini.summary: A small Castelli Romani DOC around Lanuvio and Genzano di Roma on the southern rim of the Alban Hills, overlooking the plain toward the sea. Its whites are Malvasia-Trebbiano blends from volcanic ash soils; Genzano is known for its Infiorata, when the main street is carpeted with flowers each June.

it-colli-maceratesi.name: Colli Maceratesi
it-colli-maceratesi.grapes: Maceratino (Ribona) minimum 70%; Sangiovese and others for reds
it-colli-maceratesi.summary: The DOC of the province of Macerata, notable for Ribona (Maceratino), a local white grape related to Greco. Whites are soft and floral; reds are Sangiovese-based. About 87 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 568,000 bottles a year.

it-colli-martani.name: Colli Martani
it-colli-martani.grapes: Grechetto, Trebbiano, Sangiovese; Vernaccia di Cannara
it-colli-martani.summary: A hilly DOC between Todi, Montefalco and Assisi, best known for Grechetto. Its Cannara subzone keeps alive Vernaccia di Cannara (the Cornetta grape), a sweet red passito made in tiny quantities around Easter.

it-colli-orientali-del-friuli-picolit.name: Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit
it-colli-orientali-del-friuli-picolit.summary: Picolit is one of Italy's rarest and most romantic sweet wines, from a grape whose flowers are largely sterile, so it sets only a few berries per bunch ('picolit' means 'little'). Grapes are dried on the vine or on mats to make a delicate, honeyed wine with apricot and acacia. In the 18th century Count Fabio Asquini of Fagagna sold it to the courts of Europe in hand-blown Murano bottles; it was revived in the 20th century by Giuseppe Perusini of Rocca Bernarda. The Cialla subzone has its own label.
it-colli-orientali-del-friuli-picolit.terroir: Ponca hills of the Colli Orientali.
it-colli-orientali-del-friuli-picolit.nerd_note: Picolit's natural floral abortion (it sets as few as a dozen berries per bunch) keeps yields so low that it was nearly abandoned in the 19th century.

it-colli-perugini.name: Colli Perugini
it-colli-perugini.summary: A DOC on the hills south and west of Perugia between the Tiber and Nestore valleys, for Sangiovese-based reds and Trebbiano-Grechetto whites. It has little commercial profile.

it-colli-pesaresi.name: Colli Pesaresi
it-colli-pesaresi.grapes: Sangiovese, Pinot Nero, Cabernet; Trebbiano, Biancame, Pinot Bianco
it-colli-pesaresi.summary: The hills behind Pesaro, near the Romagna border, mostly for Sangiovese reds. Subzones include Focara (Pinot Nero), Roncaglia (whites) and Parco Naturale Monte San Bartolo, a cliff-top park on the sea.

it-colli-piacentini.name: Colli Piacentini
it-colli-piacentini.grapes: Barbera, Croatina (Bonarda), Malvasia di Candia, Ortrugo, Trebbiano, Pinot Nero
it-colli-piacentini.summary: The hills of Piacenza province, continuing the Oltrepò Pavese, form four valleys (Tidone, Trebbia, Nure, Arda). The DOC has subzones Vigoleno (for a rare Vin Santo), Val Trebbia, Val Nure and Val d'Arda. Malvasia di Candia Aromatica makes aromatic whites still, sparkling or passito; La Stoppa's Ageno, a skin-macerated Malvasia blend by Elena Pantaleoni, is one of Italy's most influential orange wines.
it-colli-piacentini.nerd_note: Vin Santo di Vigoleno is made in tiny quantities from grapes dried for months in the medieval borgo of Vigoleno.

it-colli-romagna-centrale.name: Colli Romagna Centrale
it-colli-romagna-centrale.summary: Hill blends from the central Romagna Apennines around Cesena and Forlì.

it-colli-tortonesi.name: Colli Tortonesi
it-colli-tortonesi.grapes: Timorasso, Barbera, Cortese, Croatina, Dolcetto, Freisa, Moscato and others
it-colli-tortonesi.summary: The hills around Tortona, in the far south-east of Piedmont toward Lombardy and Liguria, are now famous for one grape: Timorasso. Nearly extinct by the 1980s, it was revived by Walter Massa of Monleale from 1987, and its wines, labelled Derthona (the Roman name of Tortona), are powerful whites with honey, petrol and stone, compared to Riesling and capable of ageing a decade. Growth has been explosive: the area under the grape rose from about 100 hectares in 2016 to more than 500 by 2026, and about 1.75 million bottles were released in 2025, more than double the year before. In 2026 the consortium set new planting permissions to zero to protect prices. Barbera and Croatina reds are traditional.
it-colli-tortonesi.terroir: Grey-white calcareous marls of the Val Curone, Val Grue and Val Borbera (Sant'Agata Fossil Marls), at 200 to 500 metres.
it-colli-tortonesi.nerd_note: Langhe heavyweights like Vietti, Borgogno and Roagna bought into Timorasso in the 2010s, a sign of how seriously Barolo producers take it.

it-collina-torinese.name: Collina Torinese
it-collina-torinese.summary: Light reds from the hills around Turin, including Collina Torinese Bonarda and Malvasia.

it-colline-di-levanto.name: Colline di Levanto
it-colline-di-levanto.summary: A tiny DOC on the terraces just north of the Cinque Terre around Levanto, Bonassola and Framura, making light coastal Vermentino-based whites and Sangiovese reds.
it-colline-di-levanto.terroir: Shale and sandstone terraces above the sea.
it-colline-di-levanto.nerd_note: Levanto's terraces are the northern continuation of the Cinque Terre landscape.

it-colline-joniche-tarantine.name: Colline Joniche Tarantine
it-colline-joniche-tarantine.summary: A DOC created in 2008 on the hills that ring the Gulf of Taranto, the ancient Greek city of Taras, for Primitivo, Cabernet Sauvignon and whites from Verdeca and Chardonnay. It overlaps Primitivo di Manduria and Lizzano, and very little wine carries the name.

it-colline-lucchesi.name: Colline Lucchesi
it-colline-lucchesi.grapes: Sangiovese, Canaiolo, Ciliegiolo, Merlot, Syrah; Trebbiano, Vermentino, Chardonnay
it-colline-lucchesi.summary: The hills north of Lucca, with a long history of villa estates and mixed blends. Biodynamic pioneers such as Tenuta di Valgiano have shown that these sandstone and clay slopes can give fine Sangiovese-based reds.

it-colline-novaresi.name: Colline Novaresi
it-colline-novaresi.grapes: Nebbiolo, Vespolina, Croatina, Uva Rara, Erbaluce
it-colline-novaresi.summary: The umbrella DOC for the Novara side of Alto Piemonte, covering Nebbiolo, Vespolina and Erbaluce outside Ghemme, Boca, Fara and Sizzano.
it-colline-novaresi.terroir: Moraine and porphyry hills east of the Sesia.
it-colline-novaresi.nerd_note: Vespolina varietals labelled Colline Novaresi are a peppery cult curiosity.

it-colline-saluzzesi.name: Colline Saluzzesi
it-colline-saluzzesi.summary: Hill wines around Saluzzo at the foot of Monviso, including the rare Pelaverga and the sweet sparkling Quagliano.
it-colline-saluzzesi.nerd_note: Pelaverga di Saluzzo is a different variety from Verduno's Pelaverga Piccolo.

it-collio-goriziano.name: Collio
it-collio-goriziano.grapes: Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, Malvasia Istriana, Pinot Grigio, Pinot Bianco, Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Nero
it-collio-goriziano.summary:
Collio Goriziano, usually just Collio, is a crescent of hills between Gorizia and the Slovenian border, around Cormons, Capriva, San Floriano, Oslavia and Dolegna. With roughly 1,300 to 1,500 hectares it is small, but it has the best claim to be Italy's greatest white-wine zone. Its wines are aromatic yet structured and saline, from Friulano (pear, almond, meadow herbs), Ribolla Gialla (citrus, high acid), Malvasia Istriana, Sauvignon and Pinot Grigio, and especially from the field blend that Collio's growers call Collio Bianco, made from native grapes.

The zone was the cradle of the 1960s white revolution: Mario Schiopetto at Capriva, inspired by German and Alsatian cellars, used stainless steel and cool fermentation to make clean varietal whites; Josko Gravner and Stanko Radikon at Oslavia later went the other way, back to long skin maceration and amphorae. The Collio continues across the border as Goriška Brda in Slovenia, where growers like Movia and Marjan Simčič farm the same hills. The DOC was among the first in Italy (1968) and its consortium has spent the 2020s promoting Collio Bianco, a blend from local grapes, as the zone's signature wine.
it-collio-goriziano.terroir: Ponca: layers of Eocene marl and sandstone that weather into friable, calcareous, mineral soils on terraced slopes of 100 to 300 m. The Julian Alps shelter the hills from the north, the Adriatic is 25 km south, and wide day-night temperature swings sharpen aromatics.
it-collio-goriziano.nerd_note: Edi Keber convinced his neighbours to make a single Collio white blend from native grapes, and his estate now makes essentially only that one wine.

it-conegliano-valdobbiadene-prosecco.name: Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco
it-conegliano-valdobbiadene-prosecco.grapes: Glera (min 85%), Verdiso, Bianchetta Trevigiana, Perera, Glera lunga
it-conegliano-valdobbiadene-prosecco.summary:
The steep hills between Conegliano and Valdobbiadene in the province of Treviso are the historic heart of Prosecco and its top tier: Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore DOCG. Fifteen communes on a ribbon of ridges at 100 to 500 m, many slopes so steep (the *ciglioni*, grassy terraces) that everything is done by hand, about 600 hours per hectare a year. The landscape became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019.

Prosecco is made mostly by the Martinotti (tank or charmat) method, a second fermentation in pressurised tanks that preserves Glera's fresh pear, apple, wisteria and acacia aromas. Styles range from Extra Brut to Brut, Extra Dry (the traditional and most popular) and Dry, plus Sui Lieviti, the old *col fondo* style refermented in bottle and left cloudy on its lees. The 43 Rive are single-commune or single-hamlet wines from steep slopes with lower yields (13 tonnes/ha) and a vintage on the label; at the summit is Superiore di Cartizze, 107 hectares of steep hills in San Pietro di Barbozza, Santo Stefano and Saccol in Valdobbiadene, traditionally made Dry.

The Scuola Enologica in Conegliano, founded in 1876, and the sparkling wines of Antonio Carpenè, who founded his house in 1868, laid the foundations; Nino Franco, Bisol, Adami, Ruggeri, Bortolomiol, Col Vetoraz and Villa Sandi are leading houses.
it-conegliano-valdobbiadene-prosecco.terroir: Marine and glacial conglomerates, sandstones and marls folded into steep east-west hogbacks; the Pre-Alps shelter the hills from cold winds, and the Piave river and Adriatic breezes temper summer heat. Valdobbiadene, to the west, is higher, steeper and cooler; Conegliano, to the east, is gentler and warmer.
it-conegliano-valdobbiadene-prosecco.nerd_note: Cartizze vineyard land is among the most expensive in Italy, regularly quoted at well over a million euros per hectare, on a par with top Barolo crus.

it-conero.name: Cònero
it-conero.summary: Cònero is the DOCG for Riserva reds from Monte Conero, a limestone headland that rises 572 m straight out of the Adriatic just south of Ancona, covered in holm oak and *corbezzolo* (strawberry tree, *komaros* in Greek, which gave the mountain its name). The wine is Montepulciano, at least 85%, aged two years: dark, plush and spicy, with black cherry and Mediterranean herbs, firmer and fresher than most Abruzzo Montepulciano because of the limestone and sea air.
it-conero.terroir: A small zone of about 170 ha on the slopes of Monte Conero and the hills toward Osimo and Camerano, on limestone and calcareous clay, from sea level to about 400 m.

it-contea-di-sclafani.name: Contea di Sclafani
it-contea-di-sclafani.grapes: Nero d'Avola, Perricone, Cabernet, Syrah; Inzolia, Catarratto, Grecanico, Chardonnay
it-contea-di-sclafani.summary: A DOC on the high central plateau between Palermo and Caltanissetta, essentially defined by one estate: Tasca d'Almerita's Regaleali, owned by the family since 1830, at 400 to 900 m. Count Giuseppe Tasca made Rosso del Conte (from 1970), one of the first great modern Sicilian reds, and Regaleali showed that the cool interior could make fresh wines. The altitude and clay soils give big day-night swings.

it-contessa-entellina.name: Contessa Entellina
it-contessa-entellina.grapes: Ansonica, Catarratto, Grecanico, Chardonnay; Nero d'Avola, Syrah, Cabernet
it-contessa-entellina.summary: An inland DOC around Contessa Entellina, an Arbëreshë (Albanian-Sicilian) village. It is essentially the home of Donnafugata's Tenuta di Contessa Entellina, at 200 to 600 m, source of its Mille e una Notte and Chiarandà.

it-controguerra.name: Controguerra
it-controguerra.grapes: Montepulciano, Merlot, Cabernet; Trebbiano, Passerina, Pecorino, Chardonnay
it-controguerra.summary: A DOC in the far north of the province of Teramo near the Marche border, allowing international varieties alongside Montepulciano. Illuminati is the main producer. About 39 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 297,000 bottles a year.

it-copertino.name: Copertino
it-copertino.summary: A Negroamaro DOC around Copertino, south of Lecce, known for its large cooperative and earthy, plummy reds. About 76 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 829,000 bottles a year.

it-cori.name: Cori
it-cori.grapes: Bellone, Malvasia, Trebbiano; Nero Buono, Montepulciano, Cesanese
it-cori.summary: A DOC on the Lepini mountains around Cori, home of two local grapes: Bellone, an ancient white (possibly Pliny's *uva pantastica*), and Nero Buono di Cori, a dark, soft red. Marco Carpineti, a biodynamic grower, has made both known.

it-cortese-dell-alto-monferrato.name: Cortese dell'Alto Monferrato
it-cortese-dell-alto-monferrato.summary: Cortese from a wide zone in Asti and Alessandria provinces outside Gavi; light, fresh whites and sparklers.

it-corti-benedettine-del-padovano.name: Corti Benedettine del Padovano
it-corti-benedettine-del-padovano.summary: Plain wines from lands once farmed by Benedictine monasteries south of Padua.
it-corti-benedettine-del-padovano.nerd_note: The name recalls the *corti* (farm courtyards) of the Benedictine abbey of Santa Giustina.

it-cortona.name: Cortona
it-cortona.grapes: Syrah, Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet; Chardonnay, Grechetto
it-cortona.summary: The Etruscan hill town of Cortona, above the Val di Chiana near Lake Trasimeno, has made Syrah its signature, an unusual choice in Tuscany that works well in the warm, open valley. Stefano Amerighi (biodynamic) and Tenimenti Luigi d'Alessandro made the case for peppery, fresh Cortona Syrah.

it-costa-d-amalfi.name: Costa d'Amalfi
it-costa-d-amalfi.grapes: Falanghina, Biancolella, Fenile, Ginestra, Ripoli, Pepella; Piedirosso, Aglianico, Tintore
it-costa-d-amalfi.summary: Vineyards on the Amalfi Coast hang on terraces cut into limestone cliffs above the sea, some so steep that grapes are carried down on shoulders or by monorail. The DOC (1995) has three subzones. Furore, a village with almost no centre, is the domain of Marisa Cuomo, whose Fiorduva (from Fenile, Ginestra and Ripoli) is one of Italy's most famous coastal whites. Ravello makes whites and reds on the hills above the town. Tramonti, inland in the Lattari mountains, has ungrafted Tintore and Piedirosso vines, some 150 years old or more, trained on chestnut pergolas.
it-costa-d-amalfi.nerd_note: Tintore di Tramonti is a teinturier (red-fleshed) grape; Tenuta San Francesco's E' Iss comes from ungrafted vines more than a century old.

it-coste-della-sesia.name: Coste della Sesia
it-coste-della-sesia.summary: The umbrella DOC for the Vercelli and Biella hills of Alto Piemonte, used for Nebbiolo (Spanna) and blends that fall outside Gattinara, Lessona and Bramaterra.
it-coste-della-sesia.terroir: Volcanic and sandy soils west of the Sesia.
it-coste-della-sesia.nerd_note: Many of Alto Piemonte's best values hide under this name.

it-curtefranca.name: Curtefranca
it-curtefranca.grapes: Chardonnay and Pinot Bianco (white); Cabernet Franc, Carmenère, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot (red)
it-curtefranca.summary: The still-wine DOC of the Franciacorta zone, renamed from Terre di Franciacorta in 2008 to avoid confusion with the sparkling DOCG. Bordeaux-style reds and Chardonnay whites; Ca' del Bosco's Maurizio Zanella red started here.
it-curtefranca.terroir: Moraine hills south of Lake Iseo.
it-curtefranca.nerd_note: Franciacorta's Cabernet Franc plantings include old vines later identified as Carmenère, as happened in north-east Italy.

it-delia-nivolelli.name: Delia Nivolelli
it-delia-nivolelli.grapes: Nero d'Avola, Perricone; Grecanico, Inzolia, Grillo, Damaschino
it-delia-nivolelli.summary: A small DOC between Mazara del Vallo, Marsala and Salemi, named after the Delia river and the Nivolelli plain, with varietal wines from Sicilian and international grapes. About 2 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 13,000 bottles a year.

it-delle-venezie.name: delle Venezie
it-delle-venezie.summary: Created in 2017 (registered in the EU in 2020) to regulate Pinot Grigio from Veneto, Friuli Venezia Giulia and the province of Trento, which together make most of the world's Italian Pinot Grigio. It covers tens of thousands of hectares and is by far the largest Pinot Grigio appellation in the world.
it-delle-venezie.terroir: Plains and foothills across three regions.
it-delle-venezie.nerd_note: It is one of the few Italian DOCs that also has a Slovene name, Beneških okolišev, for the Slovene-speaking areas of Friuli.

it-dogliani.name: Dogliani
it-dogliani.summary: Dogliani is the one place where Dolcetto is treated as a grand wine. On the high, cool hills south of Monforte, the grape gives deeply coloured, violet-scented reds with grip and bitter-almond finish, built to age three to eight years. The town's most famous son was Luigi Einaudi, economist and first elected president of the Italian Republic (1948 to 1955), whose estate Poderi Luigi Einaudi still makes Dogliani. Anna Maria Abbona, San Fereolo, Pecchenino and Chionetti (whose Briccolero and San Luigi were benchmarks) are other key names. The Superiore requires a year of ageing.
it-dogliani.terroir: Marls and sandstones at 300 to 600 metres, cooler and higher than the Barolo zone, which preserves acidity in an otherwise low-acid grape.
it-dogliani.nerd_note: Dolcetto means 'little sweet one', but the wine is dry: the name refers to the grape's sweetness at table and possibly to the gentle (*dolci*) hills where it grows.

it-dolcetto-d-acqui.name: Dolcetto d'Acqui
it-dolcetto-d-acqui.summary: Dolcetto from the hills around Acqui Terme, lighter than Dogliani and Ovada. Often fresh and perfumed.
it-dolcetto-d-acqui.nerd_note: Acqui's thermal springs have been used since Roman times.

it-dolcetto-d-alba.name: Dolcetto d'Alba
it-dolcetto-d-alba.summary: The everyday red of the Langhe, drunk young with tajarin and vitello tonnato while the Barolo ages. Soft acidity, dark cherry and almond-bitter finish. Producers increasingly grub it up for Nebbiolo, so good Dolcetto d'Alba is getting rarer.
it-dolcetto-d-alba.terroir: Same marls as Barolo and Barbaresco, usually on cooler or east-facing slopes.
it-dolcetto-d-alba.nerd_note: Because it ripens weeks before Nebbiolo, Dolcetto was the cash-flow grape that paid Langhe farmers before the Barolo was sold.

it-dolcetto-d-asti.name: Dolcetto d'Asti
it-dolcetto-d-asti.summary: Dolcetto from the south of Asti province, fruity and meant for early drinking.
it-dolcetto-d-asti.nerd_note: Most Dolcetto d'Asti comes from the Langa Astigiana around Canelli and Calosso.

it-dolcetto-di-diano-d-alba.name: Dolcetto di Diano d'Alba
it-dolcetto-di-diano-d-alba.summary: A tiny Dolcetto DOCG on the hill town of Diano d'Alba, just east of Serralunga. Diano mapped its best slopes as *sorì* (the dialect word for a sunny slope) long before Barolo had MGAs, and labels can carry those names. The wines are a little fuller and riper than Dolcetto d'Alba.
it-dolcetto-di-diano-d-alba.terroir: Diano sandstone and marls; the town also sits partly inside the Barolo zone.
it-dolcetto-di-diano-d-alba.nerd_note: Diano d'Alba registered more than 70 *sorì* names, among the earliest official vineyard mentions in Piedmont.

it-dolcetto-di-ovada.name: Dolcetto di Ovada
it-dolcetto-di-ovada.summary: The DOC for Dolcetto from the Ovada hills near the Ligurian border. The higher-quality 'Ovada' or Dolcetto di Ovada Superiore is a separate DOCG. Ovada Dolcetto is darker and more tannic than the Alba version.
it-dolcetto-di-ovada.terroir: Red clays and marls of the Orba and Stura valleys.
it-dolcetto-di-ovada.nerd_note: Dolcetto from Ovada was once called the 'Dolcetto of the Genoese'.

it-dolcetto-di-ovada-superiore.name: Ovada
it-dolcetto-di-ovada-superiore.summary: DOCG Dolcetto from Ovada, requiring at least a year of ageing (Riserva and Vigna versions two). The strong red clays give deeply coloured, age-worthy wines quite unlike the light Dolcetto of popular imagination.
it-dolcetto-di-ovada-superiore.terroir: Iron-rich red clays (terre rosse) and marls on hills that catch the Ligurian sea air.
it-dolcetto-di-ovada-superiore.nerd_note: Ovada producers fought for the shorter name 'Ovada' to escape the image of Dolcetto as a light quaffer.

it-donnas.name: Donnas
it-donnas.summary: The first DOC of the valley (1971) and the gateway from Piedmont. Nebbiolo here, called Picotendro, grows on pergolas over granite terraces that continue straight into Carema. The wines are pale, firm and fragrant, aged at least two years. The Caves Coopératives de Donnas, founded in 1971, makes nearly all of it.
it-donnas.terroir: Granite and gneiss terraces at 300 to 600 m, with stone pillars and pergolas like Carema's.
it-donnas.nerd_note: The vineyards line the Roman Via delle Gallie, which was hacked through the rock at Donnas around the first century BC; a Roman milestone arch still stands in the cutting.

it-elba.name: Elba
it-elba.summary: The island DOC of Elba, off the Tuscan coast, for whites from Ansonica, Vermentino and Procanico, Sangiovese reds and sweet Moscato. The island once had several thousand hectares of vines; now only about 80 remain, on granite and schist terraces facing the sea. Arrighi has experimented with Ansonica aged in amphorae sunk in the sea.

it-elba-aleatico-passito.name: Elba Aleatico Passito
it-elba-aleatico-passito.summary: A sweet red passito from Aleatico grapes dried in the sun on the island of Elba, one of the smallest DOCGs in Italy (about 15 ha). Napoleon, exiled on Elba in 1814 and 1815, is said to have enjoyed it. The wine is deep ruby, with rose petals, cherry jam and spice, sweet but kept lively by acidity.

it-eloro.name: Eloro
it-eloro.summary: A DOC in the far southeastern tip of Sicily around Pachino, Noto and Rosolini, overlapping Noto, for varietal Nero d'Avola, Frappato and Pignatello. Its Pachino subzone is for a Nero d'Avola-based red; the area is better known for its tomatoes.

it-enfer-darvier.name: Enfer d'Arvier
it-enfer-darvier.summary: 'Hell of Arvier': a steep, rocky, south-facing bowl near the village of Arvier, west of Aosta, so called because the rock walls trap the summer heat. It gives a deeper, riper Petit Rouge than elsewhere. Its own DOC from 1972 to 1985, it is one of the oldest named wines of the Alps.
it-enfer-darvier.terroir: A natural amphitheatre of rock and moraine at 650 to 900 m with intense reflected heat.
it-enfer-darvier.nerd_note: The Enfer covers only a few hectares, making it one of the smallest named wine areas in Italy.

it-erbaluce-di-caluso.name: Erbaluce di Caluso
it-erbaluce-di-caluso.summary: Erbaluce is a high-acid white grape grown on the morainic amphitheatre of Ivrea north of Turin. Dry Erbaluce is citrusy and saline; sparkling Caluso Spumante is metodo classico; and Caluso Passito, from grapes dried until spring, is an amber sweet wine of real distinction. Orsolani and Ferrando are reference houses.
it-erbaluce-di-caluso.terroir: The Morainic Amphitheatre of Ivrea, one of the best-preserved glacial moraines in Europe: sandy, stony, acidic soils.
it-erbaluce-di-caluso.nerd_note: Legend says the grape is named after Albaluce, a nymph born of the dawn whose tears made the vines grow.

it-erice.name: Erice
it-erice.grapes: Catarratto, Grillo, Inzolia, Zibibbo; Nero d'Avola, Frappato, Perricone, Syrah
it-erice.summary: A DOC in the hinterland below the hill town of Erice near Trapani, for whites, reds and sweet Zibibbo. About 52 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 156,000 bottles a year.

it-esino.name: Esino
it-esino.summary: A catch-all DOC covering the Esino basin (the Verdicchio country) for wines outside the Verdicchio rules: lighter whites and Montepulciano-Sangiovese reds. About 8 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 40,000 bottles a year.

it-est-est-est-di-montefiascone.name: Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone
it-est-est-est-di-montefiascone.summary: The wine with the best name in Italy comes with a legend. In 1111 a German prelate, often called Bishop Johannes Defuk (or Fugger), travelled to Rome for the coronation of Emperor Henry V and sent his servant Martino ahead to mark inns with good wine by writing 'Est' (it is) on the door. At Montefiascone, on the rim of the Bolsena crater, Martino was so impressed he wrote 'Est! Est!! Est!!!'. The bishop stayed, drank and, the story goes, died there; his tomb is in the church of San Flaviano. The DOC (1966) makes light, soft whites from Trebbiano and Malvasia on the volcanic slopes above Lake Bolsena; a Classico area covers Montefiascone and Bolsena.
it-est-est-est-di-montefiascone.terroir: Volcanic soils of the Vulsini complex around Lake Bolsena, the largest volcanic lake in Europe, at 300 to 600 m.
it-est-est-est-di-montefiascone.nerd_note: The bishop's tombstone in San Flaviano reads 'Est Est Est pr(opter) nim(ium) est hic Jo(annes) de Fuc d(ominus) meus mortuus est', roughly 'Because of too much Est Est Est my master Johannes de Fuk died here'.

it-etna.name: Etna
it-etna.created: 1968 (Sicily's first DOC); contrade on labels since 2011; DOCG application pending
it-etna.grapes: Rosso and Rosato: Nerello Mascalese minimum 80%, Nerello Cappuccio (Mantellato) up to 20%; Bianco: Carricante minimum 60% with Catarratto; Bianco Superiore: Carricante minimum 80% from Milo; Spumante: Nerello Mascalese minimum 80% (classic method, 18 months on lees).
it-etna.summary:
Etna is Europe's highest active volcano (over 3,300 m) and, since the early 2000s, Italy's most dynamic wine region. Its DOC, created in 1968, was Sicily's first, but by the 1990s the old terraces were being abandoned and only a handful of families (Benanti, Barone di Villagrande, Murgo) bottled wine. Then outsiders arrived: the importer Marco de Grazia (Tenuta delle Terre Nere, 2002), the Tuscan winemaker Andrea Franchetti (Passopisciaro, 2000), the Belgian Frank Cornelissen (2001), and locals such as Alberto Graci and Giuseppe Russo. They found century-old, often ungrafted bush vines of Nerello Mascalese on north-slope terraces at 600 to 1,000 m, and wines that recalled Burgundy and Barolo more than Sicily.

The zone forms a crescent on the north, east and south slopes, in 20 communes. Growth has been explosive: about 670 ha were claimed in 2013, 1,347 in 2024 and 1,449 in 2025, with roughly 474 growers and 5.8 million bottles a year, and bottling up 13.6% in the first eight months of 2026. Since 2011 producers have been able to name one of 133 *contrade*, the traditional named districts, often defined by a single lava flow of a known age; the consorzio's 2022 map counts 142.

Etna Rosso, from Nerello Mascalese with a little Nerello Cappuccio, is pale, with red cherry, wild herbs, smoke and fine, firm tannins. Etna Bianco, from Carricante, is lean and saline, and Bianco Superiore must come from the commune of Milo on the east slope. Members voted unanimously on 10 November 2023 to seek DOCG status; signatures were still being gathered at the end of 2025 and, as of October 2026, the DOCG had not been granted. The proposed rules cut yields (8 t/ha for Etna Rosso, about 6.5 to 7 t/ha for contrada wines), set minimum vine ages for contrada bottlings, cap new planting, allow commune names, and open sparkling wine to Carricante and pas dosé.
it-etna.terroir: Each contrada sits on lava of a different age and texture, from ancient, weathered flows with deeper soils to young, coarse lava sand with almost no organic matter, all very low in clay (under about 3%) and too loose for phylloxera to thrive, which is why ungrafted vines survive. The north slope (Randazzo, Passopisciaro, Solicchiata) is the heart of red wine, between about 500 and 1,000 m, with warm days and cold nights; it lies in the rain shadow and harvests run into October. The east slope (Milo, Zafferana, Santa Venerina) faces the sea and catches most of the rain (more than 1,000 mm a year in places), perfect for Carricante. The south and southwest slopes (Viagrande, Trecastagni, Biancavilla, Santa Maria di Licodia) are warmer and drier. The DOC boundary follows contour lines, with vineyards up to about 1,100 m; some plantings now exceed it.
it-etna.nerd_note: Many Etna vineyards are planted *ad alberello* at about 10,000 vines per hectare and staked with chestnut poles, worked by hand on terraces of dry-stone lava walls (*muretti a secco*); Salvo Foti's I Vigneri is named after a 15th-century guild of Etna vineyard workers.

it-falanghina-del-sannio.name: Falanghina del Sannio
it-falanghina-del-sannio.summary: The province of Benevento is the heartland of Falanghina, Campania's most planted white: about 1,360 ha in this DOC, created in 2011 to gather the Falanghina of four older DOCs, which survive as subzones (Guardia Sanframondi or Guardiolo, Sant'Agata dei Goti, Solopaca and Taburno). The wines are bright and floral, with citrus, peach and a saline finish; the name may come from *falanga*, the stakes that supported the vines.

it-falerio.name: Falerio
it-falerio.summary: A white blend from the province of Ascoli Piceno and Fermo, named for the Roman town of Falerio Picenus. Trebbiano is blended with Passerina and Pecorino; a varietal Pecorino version exists. Light and fresh, it is the everyday white of the southern Marche.

it-falerno-del-massico.name: Falerno del Massico
it-falerno-del-massico.grapes: Rosso: Aglianico 60% or more with Piedirosso; Primitivo varietal; Bianco: Falanghina
it-falerno-del-massico.summary:
Falerno del Massico is the modern heir to Falernian, the most celebrated wine of ancient Rome. Falernian grew on the slopes of Monte Massico near the border of Latium and Campania; Pliny described three crus (Caucinian on the upper slopes, Faustian in the middle, plain Falernian below) and noted that Faustian Falernian was the only wine that would catch fire from a flame. Wine from the Opimian vintage of 121 BC was still served at banquets 60 years later.

Nobody knows which grapes made Falernian. The modern DOC (1989), on the same mountain around Sessa Aurunca, Falciano del Massico and Mondragone, makes a red from Aglianico and Piedirosso, a varietal Primitivo and a white from Falanghina. Villa Matilde, founded by the lawyer Francesco Paolo Avallone in the 1960s with the aim of recreating Falernian, did most to revive the name.
it-falerno-del-massico.terroir: Volcanic soils from the extinct Roccamonfina volcano mixed with limestone on Monte Massico (813 m), a ridge running toward the sea; vineyards at 50 to 400 m enjoy sea breezes.
it-falerno-del-massico.nerd_note: Pliny wrote that Falernian could be ignited with a flame, which suggests it was naturally very high in alcohol, perhaps from late-harvested, partly dried grapes.

it-fara.name: Fara
it-fara.summary: A tiny DOC on the moraine hills of Fara Novarese and Briona, Nebbiolo softened with peppery Vespolina.
it-fara.nerd_note: Vespolina gives the wine a striking white-pepper note from the compound rotundone.

it-faro.name: Faro
it-faro.grapes: Nerello Mascalese 45 to 60%, Nerello Cappuccio, Nocera, with Nero d'Avola, Gaglioppo, Sangiovese
it-faro.summary: Faro, named for the lighthouse at the tip of Sicily on the Strait of Messina, is one of Italy's smallest DOCs. By the 1980s it was nearly extinct, until the critic Luigi Veronelli encouraged the architect Salvatore Geraci to revive his family's vineyards; Geraci's Palari Faro, a blend of Nerello Mascalese, Nerello Cappuccio and Nocera from steep terraces above the strait, became one of Sicily's great reds in the 1990s.
it-faro.nerd_note: Faro's blend includes Nocera, an almost forgotten Sicilian red, and the vines grow on steep terraces that look across to Calabria.

it-fiano-di-avellino.name: Fiano di Avellino
it-fiano-di-avellino.summary: Fiano is one of the great white grapes of Italy, and its home is the hills around Avellino. The Latin name *Vitis apiana*, the vine loved by bees (*apis*), may refer to it, and the label may still carry the ancient name Apianum. Mastroberardino kept it alive in the mid-20th century when it nearly disappeared. Today about 430 ha in 26 communes make wines that start out reserved, with pear, hazelnut, smoke and herbs, and gain honey, beeswax and flint over 10 years or more. Unlike most southern whites, Fiano ages beautifully.
it-fiano-di-avellino.terroir: Hills of 300 to 650 m. Lapio, high above the Calore valley, gives taut, mineral wines; Summonte and the slopes of Monte Partenio give cool, fragrant ones; Montefredane, with clay, gives power and longevity. Volcanic ash layers and cold nights keep acidity.

it-franciacorta.name: Franciacorta
it-franciacorta.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Nero, Pinot Bianco (max 50%), Erbamat (max 10%)
it-franciacorta.summary:
Franciacorta is Italy's most prestigious traditional-method sparkling wine and the first Italian sparkling DOCG to require bottle fermentation. The zone covers 19 communes on the hills south of Lake Iseo, west of Brescia, with 3,634 hectares of vineyard in 2025 and about 19 million bottles shipped in 2024, overwhelmingly to Italian customers (only about 12% is exported).

The modern story begins in 1961, when the young winemaker Franco Ziliani convinced Guido Berlucchi, a local nobleman who made a dull still white, to let him try a Champagne-method sparkler: 3,000 bottles of 'Pinot di Franciacorta' went on sale and sold out. Franciacorta became a DOC in 1967, Maurizio Zanella founded Ca' del Bosco in the 1970s, Vittorio Moretti founded Bellavista, and in 1995 Franciacorta became a DOCG. Since 2003 the name 'Franciacorta' alone on the label (no 'metodo classico', no 'spumante') is the denomination, a deliberate imitation of Champagne.

Rules are stricter than Champagne's in places: non-vintage wines age at least 18 months on the lees (25 months from harvest), Satèn (a blanc de blancs of Chardonnay and Pinot Bianco at lower pressure, under 5 atmospheres) 24 months, Millesimato 30 months and Riserva 60 months. Rosé must include at least 35% Pinot Nero. Erbamat, an ancient late-ripening local white recorded since the 16th century, was admitted in 2017 to bring acidity as summers warm. The consortium has since halted new vineyard plantings until 2028 to protect prices.
it-franciacorta.terroir: The hills are an amphitheatre of glacial moraine, left by the glacier that carved Lake Iseo, with six soil types identified in a 1992 University of Milan zoning: deep fluvio-glacial gravels, fine colluvial soils, and calcareous rock on Monte Orfano. The lake moderates temperatures and the Alps to the north block cold air, so the grapes ripen fully but keep acidity; warming summers are pushing harvests into early August.
it-franciacorta.nerd_note: Franciacorta was the first wine region in Italy whose consortium made the denomination name alone mandatory, banning the word 'spumante' from the label to put itself on a par with Champagne.

it-frascati.name: Frascati
it-frascati.grapes: Malvasia Bianca di Candia and/or Malvasia del Lazio minimum 70%, with Bellone, Bombino, Greco, Trebbiano
it-frascati.summary: Frascati is Rome's house white, from the volcanic slopes of the Alban Hills 20 km southeast of the city, where popes and princes built the Tuscolo villas (Villa Aldobrandini, Villa Falconieri) among the vines. One of the first Italian DOCs (1966), it was ruined by its own success in the 1970s, when vast volumes of thin wine made the name a byword for cheap trattoria wine. The best producers have rebuilt it around Malvasia del Lazio (Malvasia Puntinata), which gives more aroma and structure than the neutral Trebbiano that dominated the volume era. Good Frascati is pale gold, with almond, white flowers and a volcanic, slightly salty finish. Superiore and the sweet Cannellino became separate DOCGs in 2011.
it-frascati.terroir: Slopes of the extinct Alban (Laziale) volcano at 100 to 400 m, with soils of volcanic ash, tufa and lapilli rich in potassium, overlooking Rome and the sea.

it-frascati-superiore.name: Frascati Superiore
it-frascati-superiore.summary: The top dry Frascati, a DOCG since 2011, with lower yields and at least 12% alcohol; Riserva ages 12 months. Fontana Candida's Luna Mater and Castel de Paolis's wines show how much more texture old-vine Malvasia Puntinata gives.

it-freisa-d-asti.name: Freisa d'Asti
it-freisa-d-asti.summary: Freisa, a close relative of Nebbiolo, makes wines with raspberry fruit, bitter tannin and often a light fizz. It can be still, frizzante, spumante or sweet.
it-freisa-d-asti.nerd_note: DNA shows Freisa is a parent or offspring of Nebbiolo.

it-freisa-di-chieri.name: Freisa di Chieri
it-freisa-di-chieri.summary: Freisa grown in the hills east of Turin around Chieri, historically the Turin aristocracy's everyday red, often lightly sparkling and sometimes sweet.
it-freisa-di-chieri.terroir: Sandy marls of the Turin hills.
it-freisa-di-chieri.nerd_note: Chieri's Freisa was the house wine of the Savoy court in Turin.

it-friuli.name: Friuli
it-friuli.summary: The regional DOC Friuli / Friuli Venezia Giulia (with Friulian and Slovene names Furlanija / Furlanija Julijska krajina), created in 2016 to give the whole region a single, recognisable name for exported varietal wines.
it-friuli.nerd_note: It is one of the only Italian DOCs with names in four languages: Italian, Friulian and two Slovene forms.

it-friuli-annia.name: Friuli Annia
it-friuli-annia.summary: A small DOC near the lagoon of Marano, named after the Roman Via Annia that ran from Aquileia to Padua.
it-friuli-annia.terroir: Clay and sandy soils by the lagoon.

it-friuli-aquileia.name: Friuli Aquileia
it-friuli-aquileia.grapes: Refosco, Merlot, Cabernet, Friulano, Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay
it-friuli-aquileia.summary: The plain around the Roman city of Aquileia toward the lagoon of Grado. Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso is the local specialty. The Basilica of Aquileia, with its fourth-century mosaic floor, is a UNESCO site.
it-friuli-aquileia.terroir: Alluvial clays and sands near the lagoon.
it-friuli-aquileia.nerd_note: Aquileia was a major wine port in Roman times and amphorae from its trade fill the local museum.

it-friuli-colli-orientali.name: Friuli Colli Orientali
it-friuli-colli-orientali.grapes: Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, Sauvignon, Verduzzo, Picolit, Refosco, Schioppettino, Pignolo, Tazzelenghe, Merlot, Cabernet
it-friuli-colli-orientali.summary: The eastern hills of the province of Udine, from Tarcento in the north through Cividale, Prepotto, Corno di Rosazzo and Buttrio to Manzano, continuing the Collio toward the north-west. Larger and more varied than Collio, the Colli Orientali are the home of Friuli's great native reds: Schioppettino (peppery, cool-climate, revived by Paolo Rapuzzi of Ronchi di Cialla in the 1970s), Pignolo (dark, tannic, rescued from the Abbey of Rosazzo's vineyards) and Refosco, as well as some of the finest Friulano and sweet Verduzzo and Picolit. Subzones include Cialla, Prepotto (for Schioppettino), Rosazzo (now a separate DOCG) and Ramandolo (DOCG). Miani, Le Due Terre, Ronchi di Cialla, Bastianich, Ronco del Gnemiz, Dorigo and Livio Felluga are leading names.
it-friuli-colli-orientali.terroir: Ponca flysch on terraced hills, with cooler, wetter conditions toward the north near the Alps.
it-friuli-colli-orientali.nerd_note: Schioppettino's name refers to the 'little shots' or pops of its crisp berries, or to the faint prickle the wine once had; the variety was not even officially authorised until the late 1970s, after the Rapuzzis' campaign.

it-friuli-grave.name: Friuli Grave
it-friuli-grave.grapes: Pinot Grigio, Friulano, Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet, Refosco
it-friuli-grave.summary: The largest DOC in Friuli, on the vast gravel plain of the Tagliamento and Cellina rivers in Pordenone and Udine provinces. Most of Friuli's volume Pinot Grigio, Merlot and Prosecco base comes from here. The village of Rauscedo hosts the world's largest grapevine nursery cooperative (Vivai Cooperativi Rauscedo), which supplies tens of millions of grafted vines a year worldwide.
it-friuli-grave.terroir: Deep, stony gravels (*grave*) that drain quickly and heat up, with strong day-night swings near the mountains.
it-friuli-grave.nerd_note: Rauscedo's nurseries produce a large share of all grafted vines planted in Italy, and many in the world.

it-friuli-isonzo.name: Friuli Isonzo
it-friuli-isonzo.grapes: Friulano, Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Malvasia, Merlot, Cabernet, Refosco
it-friuli-isonzo.summary: The plain along the Isonzo river south of the Collio, from Gradisca to Mariano and Romans, on red, iron-rich gravels. Gianfranco Gallo's Vie di Romans proved that this flat land could make whites as powerful as any in the hills, and Lis Neris and Ronco del Gelso followed.
it-friuli-isonzo.terroir: Ferrous red gravels and clays of the Isonzo terraces on the right bank; whiter calcareous gravels on the left.
it-friuli-isonzo.nerd_note: Isonzo's 'rive alte' (high banks) and 'rive basse' have different soils, which producers label separately.

it-friuli-latisana.name: Friuli Latisana
it-friuli-latisana.grapes: Friulano, Pinot Grigio, Refosco, Merlot, Cabernet
it-friuli-latisana.summary: A plain DOC on the lower Tagliamento near the Venetian border, making light varietal wines.

it-gabiano.name: Gabiano
it-gabiano.summary: A one-estate-dominated DOC around the castle of Gabiano above the Po, for Barbera-based reds.
it-gabiano.nerd_note: Castello di Gabiano has been in the Cattaneo Adorno family since the 17th century.

it-galatina.name: Galatina
it-galatina.summary: A small DOC around Galatina in the southern Salento, famous for its frescoed basilica and the tarantismo rituals. About 2 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 18,000 bottles a year.

it-galluccio.name: Galluccio
it-galluccio.summary: A DOC on the slopes of the Roccamonfina volcano in northern Campania, for Aglianico reds and Falanghina whites from volcanic soils. Galardi's Terra di Lavoro (IGT) comes from the same volcano.

it-gambellara.name: Gambellara
it-gambellara.summary: Soave's volcanic neighbour across the provincial border in Vicenza, making Garganega whites on dark basalt; Angiolino Maule's La Biancara made it a natural-wine reference. Recioto di Gambellara (DOCG) and Vin Santo di Gambellara are its sweet wines.

it-garda.name: Garda
it-garda.grapes: Garganega, Chardonnay, Pinot Grigio, Corvina, Merlot and many others
it-garda.summary: A large inter-regional varietal DOC around Lake Garda spanning Veneto and Lombardy.

it-garda-colli-mantovani.name: Garda Colli Mantovani
it-garda-colli-mantovani.grapes: Garganega, Trebbiano, Chardonnay, Merlot, Cabernet, Rondinella
it-garda-colli-mantovani.summary: Morainic hills south of Lake Garda in Mantua province, making light whites, reds and Chiaretto.

it-gattinara.name: Gattinara
it-gattinara.grapes: Nebbiolo (Spanna) min 90%, Vespolina and Uva Rara up to 10%
it-gattinara.summary: The flagship of northern Piedmont. Gattinara is Nebbiolo grown on steep slopes of volcanic porphyry above the Sesia river, aged at least 35 months (Riserva 47) and famous for its iron, rose and orange-peel aromatics and racy acidity. In the 19th century this was one of Piedmont's most important wines; by the 1990s it had shrunk to under 100 hectares. Antoniolo, Travaglini (with its distinctive curved bottle), Nervi (bought by Roberto Conterno of Giacomo Conterno in 2018) and Torraccia del Piantavigna lead the revival.
it-gattinara.terroir: Acidic, mineral soils from the Permian Sesia supervolcano (rhyolites and porphyries), rich in iron and poor in calcium, giving high acidity and fine but firm tannins.
it-gattinara.nerd_note: Roberto Conterno's purchase of Nervi in 2018 was the clearest sign that Barolo's elite now regard Alto Piemonte as Nebbiolo's next frontier.

it-gavi.name: Gavi
it-gavi.summary: Gavi is Piedmont's best-known white, made from Cortese in eleven communes around the hill town of Gavi near the Ligurian border. It is crisp, lemony and almond-finishing, a classic with the seafood of Genoa, the city whose nobles owned estates here. Wines from the commune of Gavi itself may be labelled 'Gavi del Comune di Gavi'. Villa Sparina, La Scolca (whose Gavi dei Gavi black label was the first prestige Gavi in the 1960s) and Broglia are reference producers; Riserva and spumante versions exist.
it-gavi.terroir: White marls and red clays: the north has white calcareous marls, the south redder, iron-rich clays. The Ligurian sea air arrives through the Apennine passes.
it-gavi.nerd_note: Gavi del Comune di Gavi is often mislabelled 'Gavi di Gavi', the name La Scolca registered as a trademark.

it-genazzano.name: Genazzano
it-genazzano.summary: A small DOC around Genazzano, a medieval town of the Colonna family in the hills east of Rome near Olevano Romano. Whites are Malvasia-based and reds use Sangiovese and Cesanese with a little Ciliegiolo. Little wine is declared under the name today; most local growers prefer the Cesanese DOCs or IGT.

it-ghemme.name: Ghemme
it-ghemme.summary: Ghemme faces Gattinara across the Sesia on the Novara side. Its soils are glacial moraine rather than volcanic rock, which gives a slightly rounder, softer Nebbiolo. It ages for at least 34 months (Riserva 46) with 18 in wood. Antichi Vigneti di Cantalupo, Ioppa and Torraccia del Piantavigna are the main names.
it-ghemme.terroir: Glacial moraine of the Monte Rosa glacier: pebbly, acidic clays and sands with good drainage.
it-ghemme.nerd_note: The Romans recorded vines on the Ghemme moraine hill, and the village's medieval *ricetto* (fortified storage hamlet) still holds wine cellars.

it-gioia-del-colle.name: Gioia del Colle
it-gioia-del-colle.grapes: Primitivo (varietal minimum 90%); Rosso blends with Montepulciano, Negroamaro, Malvasia Nera
it-gioia-del-colle.summary: Gioia del Colle, on the Murge plateau at 300 to 450 m between Bari and Taranto, is the cradle of Primitivo: the priest Francesco Filippo Indellicati selected the variety here around 1799. Altitude and cooler nights give a fresher, more structured Primitivo than Manduria's, with red fruit, Mediterranean herbs and firmer acidity, from limestone and red clay. Polvanera, Pietraventosa and Fatalone lead the area.
it-gioia-del-colle.nerd_note: Gioia del Colle's growers argue their Primitivo is the original, and that Manduria's came later, when the grape travelled south as a dowry in the 1880s.

it-giro-di-cagliari.name: Girò di Cagliari
it-giro-di-cagliari.summary: Girò is a rare red grape of Spanish origin used for sweet and fortified red wines around Cagliari; only a few hectares remain. Cantina di Dolianova and Meloni make it.

it-grance-senesi.name: Grance Senesi
it-grance-senesi.summary: Named after the medieval *grance*, fortified farms run by Siena's Santa Maria della Scala hospital, this DOC covers the Crete Senesi and hills south of Siena. It is very small.

it-gravina.name: Gravina
it-gravina.grapes: Malvasia, Greco, Bianco d'Alessano; Montepulciano, Primitivo
it-gravina.summary: A small DOC on the edge of the Murge around Gravina in Puglia, near the Basilicata border, mostly for whites. About 11 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 14,000 bottles a year.

it-greco-di-bianco.name: Greco di Bianco
it-greco-di-bianco.grapes: Greco Bianco (a local variety, also called Greco di Bianco) minimum 95%
it-greco-di-bianco.summary: A sweet white passito from the town of Bianco and Casignana on the Ionian coast near the tip of the boot, made from late-harvested Greco grapes dried in the sun on cane mats until shrivelled. The wine is amber, with orange blossom, candied citrus, apricot and honey, at least 17% alcohol, and is one of the most distinctive sweet wines of southern Italy. The local grape is a distinct variety (genetically the same as Malvasia di Lipari). Umberto Ceratti made it famous.
it-greco-di-bianco.nerd_note: The grape is genetically identical to Malvasia di Lipari and Malvasia di Sardegna, a Greek family of aromatic whites scattered across the southern islands.

it-greco-di-tufo.name: Greco di Tufo
it-greco-di-tufo.grapes: Greco minimum 85%, Coda di Volpe up to 15%
it-greco-di-tufo.summary: Greco, probably brought by Greek settlers, is grown in eight communes north of Avellino around the village of Tufo. The village sits on sulphur-bearing rock: sulphur mines operated here from the 19th century (the Di Marzo family) until the 1980s, and many growers find a flinty, smoky edge in the wines. Greco di Tufo is fuller, more phenolic and more structured than Fiano, with peach, almond, citrus peel and a bitter, saline finish; it can be made as a traditional-method sparkling wine too. About 670 ha.
it-greco-di-tufo.terroir: Hills of 400 to 600 m along the Sabato river, with clay, limestone, volcanic ash and veins of sulphur-rich rock in Tufo and Santa Paolina.
it-greco-di-tufo.nerd_note: Cantine Di Marzo, founded in 1648, is one of the oldest wineries in southern Italy; the Di Marzo family also ran the sulphur mines under Tufo.

it-grignolino-d-asti.name: Grignolino d'Asti
it-grignolino-d-asti.summary: Grignolino is the Monferrato's idiosyncratic pale red: almost rosé in colour but with surprising tannin from its many seeds (*grignole* in dialect), and aromas of white pepper, wild strawberry and orange peel. Drink it young and cool. Luigi Veronelli called it 'anarchic and individualist'.
it-grignolino-d-asti.terroir: Sandy-calcareous hills north of the Tanaro.
it-grignolino-d-asti.nerd_note: The grape's name probably comes from *grignole*, the dialect word for its pips.

it-grignolino-del-monferrato-casalese.name: Grignolino del Monferrato Casalese
it-grignolino-del-monferrato-casalese.summary: Grignolino from the Casale side of the Monferrato, where it may be at its finest. Accornero, Bricco Mondalino and Castello di Gabiano are key producers.
it-grignolino-del-monferrato-casalese.terroir: Pietra da Cantoni sandstone and marls of the Casalese.
it-grignolino-del-monferrato-casalese.nerd_note: The Casalese hills are dotted with *infernot*, little cellars cut into soft sandstone, protected by UNESCO since 2014.

it-grottino-di-roccanova.name: Grottino di Roccanova
it-grottino-di-roccanova.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet, Malvasia Nera; Malvasia Bianca
it-grottino-di-roccanova.summary: A small DOC around Roccanova in southern Basilicata, named for the *grottini*, small caves dug into the hillside where farmers aged their wine. About 11 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 31,000 bottles a year.

it-gutturnio.name: Gutturnio
it-gutturnio.summary: Piacenza's signature red, Barbera blended with Croatina (Bonarda), made still or frizzante; Gutturnio Riserva and Superiore are the serious versions. Named after a Roman silver drinking vessel (*gutturnium*) found near Veleia.
it-gutturnio.terroir: Clay and limestone hills of the Val Tidone and Val Nure.
it-gutturnio.nerd_note: The Roman silver jug that inspired the name was found at the Roman town of Veleia in the Piacenza hills.

it-i-terreni-di-sanseverino.name: I Terreni di Sanseverino
it-i-terreni-di-sanseverino.summary: A small DOC around San Severino Marche for reds from Vernaccia Nera, Montepulciano and Sangiovese, including a Moro red and a passito. About 2 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 4,700 bottles a year.

it-irpinia.name: Irpinia
it-irpinia.grapes: Aglianico, Piedirosso, Sciascinoso; Fiano, Greco, Falanghina, Coda di Volpe
it-irpinia.summary: A DOC covering the whole province of Avellino, for Aglianico and varietal whites that fall outside the three DOCGs, including the Campi Taurasini subzone for Aglianico from the Taurasi area with shorter ageing.

it-ischia.name: Ischia
it-ischia.summary: Ischia was the first Greek colony in the West: Pithekoussai, founded around 770 BC, where archaeologists found 'Nestor's cup', a clay drinking cup inscribed with verses about wine and love, one of the oldest examples of Greek writing. The island's DOC dates from 1966, among Italy's first. Vines grow on steep volcanic terraces held up by green tuff walls (*parracine*), worked by hand or with monorails; Biancolella and Forastera make saline, herb-scented whites. About 100 ha remain of thousands once planted.
it-ischia.nerd_note: Casa d'Ambra's Frassitelli vineyard sits on terraces at 500 to 600 m on Monte Epomeo, reached by monorail.

it-lacrima-di-morro.name: Lacrima di Morro d'Alba
it-lacrima-di-morro.summary: Lacrima ('tear') is a rare aromatic red grape found almost only around Morro d'Alba, a walled village west of Senigallia. The name may come from the teardrop shape of the berries or from the way their thin skins split and weep juice when ripe. The wine smells like a bouquet of roses and violets with strawberry and spice, an unusual perfume for a red, and is usually drunk young. Passito and Superiore versions exist. Stefano Mancinelli is credited with saving the grape in the 1980s.
it-lacrima-di-morro.nerd_note: Frederick Barbarossa is said to have demanded Lacrima as tribute when he besieged Morro d'Alba in 1167, a story locals still tell.

it-lago-di-caldaro.name: Lago di Caldaro
it-lago-di-caldaro.summary: Kalterersee, a light, soft Schiava from around Lake Caldaro (Kaltern) south of Bolzano, was once the most exported Italian red to Austria, Germany and Switzerland, drunk by the litre. The DOC is unusual in crossing the provincial border into Trentino. The Classico zone around the lake itself, often labelled Kalterersee Auslese with higher ripeness, has seen a quality revival led by Kellerei Kaltern and Manincor.
it-lago-di-caldaro.terroir: Limestone and moraine slopes around the warm basin of Lake Caldaro.
it-lago-di-caldaro.nerd_note: Lake Caldaro is the warmest lake in the Alps, and its microclimate also ripens Cabernet and Merlot on the shores.

it-lago-di-corbara.name: Lago di Corbara
it-lago-di-corbara.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet, Pinot Nero; Grechetto, Chardonnay
it-lago-di-corbara.summary: A small DOC on the hills around the artificial lake of Corbara on the Tiber, between Orvieto and Todi. The lake's mists and the warm slopes suit Bordeaux varieties and Pinot Nero; Decugnano dei Barbi and Barberani make wines here.

it-lambrusco-di-sorbara.name: Lambrusco di Sorbara
it-lambrusco-di-sorbara.summary: The palest, most elegant Lambrusco, from the plain north of Modena around Sorbara and Bomporto between the Secchia and Panaro rivers. Lambrusco di Sorbara has a flower that often fails to set (it needs Salamino nearby as a pollinator), giving small bunches of light-coloured grapes; the wine is coral pink to pale ruby, with violet, strawberry and razor acidity. It is made by tank, by the ancestral method (rifermented in bottle and left cloudy) or by metodo classico. Cleto Chiarli, Paltrinieri (Radice, Leclisse), Cavicchioli (Vigna del Cristo), Vittorio Graziano and Cantina di Sorbara are references.
it-lambrusco-di-sorbara.terroir: Sandy alluvial soils between two rivers, whose sandiness gives perfume and lightness.
it-lambrusco-di-sorbara.nerd_note: Sorbara's poor fruit set (*acinellatura*) is why growers interplant Salamino as a pollinator, a rare case of a classic wine grape that needs a partner.

it-lambrusco-grasparossa-di-castelvetro.name: Lambrusco Grasparossa di Castelvetro
it-lambrusco-grasparossa-di-castelvetro.summary: The darkest and most tannic Lambrusco, from the foothills south of Modena around Castelvetro, Maranello and Vignola. Grasparossa (named for its stems that turn red in autumn) gives deep purple, foaming wines with blackberry and a dry, slightly bitter finish, perfect with zampone and cotechino.
it-lambrusco-grasparossa-di-castelvetro.terroir: Clay and limestone foothills of the Apennines.
it-lambrusco-grasparossa-di-castelvetro.nerd_note: Castelvetro's medieval checkerboard square inspired the town's Dama Vivente (living chess) festival, held every two years.

it-lambrusco-mantovano.name: Lambrusco Mantovano
it-lambrusco-mantovano.grapes: Lambrusco Viadanese, Maestri, Marani, Salamino, Ruberti
it-lambrusco-mantovano.summary: Lombardy's own Lambrusco from the flat lands of Mantua province south of the Po, lightly sparkling and dry or off-dry, with subzones Viadanese-Sabbionetano and Oltre Po Mantovano.
it-lambrusco-mantovano.nerd_note: Lambrusco Viadanese is a local Lambrusco variety found almost only here.

it-lambrusco-salamino-di-santa-croce.name: Lambrusco Salamino di Santa Croce
it-lambrusco-salamino-di-santa-croce.summary: From the plain around Santa Croce near Carpi, Salamino (its cylindrical bunch resembles a small salami) is the most widely planted Lambrusco and gives a balance between Sorbara's fragrance and Grasparossa's body.
it-lambrusco-salamino-di-santa-croce.terroir: Clay and silt plain of the Secchia.

it-lamezia.name: Lamezia
it-lamezia.grapes: Gaglioppo, Magliocco, Greco Nero; Greco, Montonico
it-lamezia.summary: A Tyrrhenian-side DOC around Lamezia Terme on the narrow isthmus of Calabria, for reds from Gaglioppo, Magliocco and Greco Nero. Statti is the leading estate. About 10 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 93,000 bottles a year.

it-langhe.name: Langhe
it-langhe.grapes: Nebbiolo, Dolcetto, Barbera, Freisa, Arneis, Favorita, Chardonnay, Nascetta, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Pinot Nero, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and others
it-langhe.summary: The Langhe DOC is the umbrella denomination for the hills of the Langhe, covering most of the province of Cuneo south of the Tanaro. For wine lovers its most important wine is Langhe Nebbiolo, which can be declassified Barolo or Barbaresco, younger-vine fruit or deliberately fresher wine from outside the DOCG zones, and is often the best value in Piedmont. The DOC also allows varietal Chardonnay (Gaja's Gaia & Rey, planted in 1979, put Langhe Chardonnay on the map), Nascetta (the rare aromatic white of Novello, with a 'Nas-cëtta del Comune di Novello' mention), Freisa, Arneis, and blends labelled Langhe Rosso or Bianco.
it-langhe.terroir: Everything from the Tortonian and Serravallian marls of the Barolo and Barbaresco zones to the sandstone ridges of the Alta Langa at up to 800 metres.
it-langhe.nerd_note: Gaja's famous Sorì San Lorenzo, Sorì Tildin and Costa Russi were labelled Langhe Nebbiolo from 1996 to 2012 because they contained a few per cent of Barbera, which Barbaresco DOCG forbids.

it-lessini-durello.name: Lessini Durello
it-lessini-durello.summary: Durella is a fiercely acidic white grape from the volcanic Lessini hills north of Soave, perfect for sparkling wine. Lessini Durello is made by tank or traditional method; the long-aged Monti Lessini metodo classico versions (36+ months on lees) are among Italy's most underrated sparklers.
it-lessini-durello.terroir: Volcanic basalts and tuffs of the Alpone and Chiampo valleys up to 600 m.
it-lessini-durello.nerd_note: Durella's name is thought to come from its tough (*dura*) skin.

it-lessona.name: Lessona
it-lessona.summary: A small DOC near Biella on marine yellow sands, making delicate, saline Nebbiolo. Proprietà Sperino (Paolo De Marchi of Tuscany's Isole e Olena returned to his family's roots here) and Tenute Sella, family of the 19th-century statesman Quintino Sella, lead.
it-lessona.terroir: Pliocene yellow marine sands, acidic and full of fossil shells.
it-lessona.nerd_note: Tenute Sella has been bottling Lessona since 1671.

it-leverano.name: Leverano
it-leverano.grapes: Negroamaro; whites Malvasia Bianca, Chardonnay, Fiano
it-leverano.summary: A Negroamaro DOC west of Lecce, notable for Conti Zecca's wines and for a passito white. About 105 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 710,000 bottles a year.

it-lison.name: Lison
it-lison.summary: A DOCG for Friulano, called Tai here, from the plain on the Veneto-Friuli border around Lison and Portogruaro: floral, almondy whites. Lison Classico is the historic core.

it-lison-pramaggiore.name: Lison-Pramaggiore
it-lison-pramaggiore.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet, Refosco, Malbech, Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay, Verduzzo
it-lison-pramaggiore.summary: Varietal DOC across the Veneto-Friuli border, with Refosco and Malbech among its curiosities.

it-lizzano.name: Lizzano
it-lizzano.summary: A DOC east of Taranto known for Malvasia Nera di Lizzano and Negroamaro reds and rosés. About 24 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 51,000 bottles a year.

it-loazzolo.name: Loazzolo
it-loazzolo.summary: One of Italy's smallest DOCs: a passito of late-harvested, often botrytised Moscato Bianco from terraces around Loazzolo, aged two years. Forteto della Luja and Borgo Maragliano are the reference producers.
it-loazzolo.nerd_note: Forteto della Luja's vineyards are also a WWF oasis for wild orchids.

it-locorotondo.name: Locorotondo
it-locorotondo.summary: Locorotondo is a round white hill town in the Valle d'Itria, the land of *trulli*, the conical dry-stone houses. Its DOC makes light, crisp whites from Verdeca and Bianco d'Alessano on the cooler Murge plateau, a rare fresh white in hot Puglia; the cooperative Cantina di Locorotondo makes most of it.

it-lugana.name: Lugana
it-lugana.summary: Lugana is the white wine of the southern shore of Lake Garda, straddling Lombardy (Sirmione, Desenzano, Pozzolengo, Lonato) and Veneto (Peschiera). It is made from Turbiana, a local grape related to Verdicchio (and once called Trebbiano di Lugana), and grown on heavy, chalky white-grey clays left by the Garda glacier. The wines have citrus, almond and saline depth and age surprisingly well; Superiore, Riserva, Vendemmia Tardiva and Spumante versions exist. Lugana has been one of Italy's commercial success stories of the 2010s and 2020s, with plantings expanding fast.
it-lugana.terroir: Compact white and grey calcareous clays (marl-clay) from the morainic amphitheatre south of the lake; the lake moderates frosts and summer heat.
it-lugana.nerd_note: Ca' dei Frati's Brolettino and I Frati, and Ottella's Molceo, showed in the 1980s and 1990s that Lugana could age ten years.

it-malvasia-delle-lipari.name: Malvasia delle Lipari
it-malvasia-delle-lipari.grapes: Malvasia di Lipari minimum 95% (Corinto Nero up to 8%)
it-malvasia-delle-lipari.summary: The Aeolian islands north of Sicily, especially Salina, make Malvasia delle Lipari, a sweet golden wine that was famous in the 18th and 19th centuries until phylloxera and emigration emptied the islands. The Milanese designer Carlo Hauner, who settled on Salina in the 1960s, revived it in the 1970s and 1980s. The grapes are dried on cane mats for 10 to 15 days; the Passito is amber, with apricot, honey, capers and sea salt. A light, unfortified version (Naturale) and a fortified Liquoroso also exist. Only about 9 ha are declared.
it-malvasia-delle-lipari.terroir: Volcanic slopes of Salina (twin extinct volcanoes), Lipari and Vulcano, on pumice and ash, with sea winds and strong sun.
it-malvasia-delle-lipari.nerd_note: Malvasia di Lipari is genetically the same grape as Greco di Bianco in Calabria and Malvasia di Sardegna.

it-malvasia-di-bosa.name: Malvasia di Bosa
it-malvasia-di-bosa.summary: A rare wine from the Planargia hills around Bosa on the west coast, from Malvasia di Sardegna (the same grape as Malvasia di Lipari and Greco di Bianco). It is made dry or sweet, often aged under flor like Vernaccia, giving a golden, nutty, salty wine; sweet versions come from late-harvested grapes. The late Giovanni Battista Columbu kept it alive and made it famous through Slow Food.

it-malvasia-di-casorzo-d-asti.name: Malvasia di Casorzo
it-malvasia-di-casorzo-d-asti.summary: Sweet, aromatic red or rosé fizz from Malvasia Nera di Casorzo, around Casorzo and Grana in the north Monferrato.
