it-malvasia-di-castelnuovo-don-bosco.name: Malvasia di Castelnuovo Don Bosco
it-malvasia-di-castelnuovo-don-bosco.summary: Sweet red fizz from Malvasia di Schierano in the hills around the birthplace of Saint John Bosco.
it-malvasia-di-castelnuovo-don-bosco.nerd_note: Castelnuovo is also the birthplace of Saint Joseph Cafasso, earning it the nickname 'town of saints'.

it-mamertino.name: Mamertino
it-mamertino.grapes: Nero d'Avola, Nocera; Grillo, Inzolia, Catarratto
it-mamertino.summary: A DOC on the Tyrrhenian coast west of Messina around Milazzo, named after Mamertine wine, which Pliny praised and Julius Caesar served at a banquet for his third consulship in 46 BC. Today it covers Nero d'Avola and Nocera reds and Grillo-Inzolia whites.

it-mandrolisai.name: Mandrolisai
it-mandrolisai.grapes: Bovale Sardo minimum 35%, Cannonau 20 to 35%, Monica 20 to 35%
it-mandrolisai.summary: A high inland DOC in the centre of the island around Sorgono, Atzara and Samugheo, on schist and granite at 500 to 700 m. Its reds blend Bovale, Cannonau and Monica, often from old mixed vineyards, and are fresher and more structured than coastal wines.

it-maremma-toscana.name: Maremma Toscana
it-maremma-toscana.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Ciliegiolo, Alicante; Vermentino, Ansonica, Trebbiano, Viognier
it-maremma-toscana.summary: The Maremma is Tuscany's deep south, the coastal province of Grosseto that was malarial marsh until reclamation in the 19th and 20th centuries. The Maremma Toscana DOC, promoted from IGT in 2011, covers the whole province and works as a flexible umbrella for blends and varietals of almost anything: Vermentino, Sangiovese, Cabernet, Syrah, Ciliegiolo and Alicante (local Grenache). About 2,400 ha and a fast-growing reputation; many estates from Bolgheri, Chianti and Montalcino have bought land here. 23 communes and 168 frazioni can appear on labels.

it-marino.name: Marino
it-marino.grapes: Malvasia del Lazio, Malvasia di Candia, Trebbiano, Bellone, Bombino
it-marino.summary: Frascati's neighbour on the western slope of the Alban Hills, with similar volcanic whites. Marino's grape festival, the Sagra dell'Uva held since 1925, is famous for the moment the town's fountains run with wine. The Gotto d'Oro cooperative dominates volume; Paola Di Mauro's Colle Picchioni showed the area's quality.

it-marsala.name: Marsala
it-marsala.grapes: Oro and Ambra: Grillo, Catarratto, Ansonica (Inzolia), Damaschino; Rubino: Perricone, Nero d'Avola, Nerello Mascalese (up to 30% white grapes)
it-marsala.summary:
Marsala is Sicily's fortified wine and an English invention. In 1773 the Liverpool merchant John Woodhouse, sheltering from a storm in the port of Marsala, tasted the local *perpetuum*, an oxidised wine topped up year after year in casks, and shipped some to England with added spirit to survive the voyage. It sold. In 1796 he began production in earnest, and Nelson is said to have ordered it for his fleet. Benjamin Ingham of Leeds arrived in 1806 and built a rival baglio, and in 1833 Vincenzo Florio, a Calabrian-born Palermo entrepreneur, set up between the two and eventually outgrew them. Garibaldi landed his Thousand at Marsala in 1860, and a sweet 'Garibaldi Dolce' style was named after him.

The 20th century turned Marsala into a cooking wine and flavoured mixes (egg, almond); a 1984 reform removed those from the DOC and tightened the categories. Today Marsala is classified by colour (Oro and Ambra from white grapes, Ambra coloured with cooked must, Rubino from red grapes), sweetness (secco up to 40 g/l, semisecco, dolce over 100 g/l) and age: Fine (1 year), Superiore (2 years), Superiore Riserva (4), Vergine or Soleras (5) and Vergine Stravecchio or Riserva (10). Vergine is the purist's Marsala: dry, never sweetened, fortified only with spirit and aged in a solera-like system. Marco De Bartoli revived the old unfortified *perpetuum* style in the 1980s with Vecchio Samperi.
it-marsala.terroir: The flat to gently rolling coast of the province of Trapani (excluding the islands and Alcamo), with sandy, limestone-rich soils and hot, windy summers; the salt pans and lagoon of the Stagnone lie just north of the town.
it-marsala.nerd_note: Label codes survive from the English trade: I.P. (Italia Particolare) on Fine; L.P. (London Particular), S.O.M. (Superior Old Marsala) and G.D. (Garibaldi Dolce) on Superiore.

it-martina.name: Martina Franca
it-martina.summary: A twin of Locorotondo across the Valle d'Itria, around the baroque town of Martina Franca, for light Verdeca whites. In the 19th century these wines were shipped north as base for vermouth.

it-matera.name: Matera
it-matera.grapes: Primitivo, Sangiovese, Aglianico, Cabernet; Greco, Malvasia
it-matera.summary: A DOC covering the province of Matera, the city of the Sassi cave dwellings (UNESCO site), for Primitivo, Moro (a Cabernet-Primitivo-Merlot blend) and Greco whites. About 57 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 140,000 bottles a year.

it-matino.name: Matino
it-matino.summary: One of the southernmost DOCs in Italy, created in 1971 in the Salento near Gallipoli, for Negroamaro reds and rosés with Malvasia Nera. The red-earth hills of the Serre Salentine give dark, warm wines, but production under the name is now almost nil, as growers use IGT Salento instead.

it-melissa.name: Melissa
it-melissa.summary: A Ionian DOC south of Cirò around Melissa and neighbouring communes, for Gaglioppo reds and Greco whites similar to Cirò's. About 14 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 135,000 bottles a year.

it-menfi.name: Menfi
it-menfi.grapes: Chardonnay, Grecanico, Fiano, Inzolia; Nero d'Avola, Syrah, Cabernet
it-menfi.summary: A DOC on the southwest coast around Menfi, the home base of the Planeta family, whose first vintage in 1995 (with a barrel-fermented Chardonnay from the Ulmo estate) symbolised the new Sicily. Settesoli, one of Italy's largest cooperatives, is also here. Sandy limestone near the sea suits whites.

it-merlara.name: Merlara
it-merlara.summary: A small plain DOC on the Adige near the Padua-Verona border.

it-modena.name: Modena
it-modena.summary: The umbrella DOC for the province of Modena, used mostly for Lambrusco di Modena blends.

it-molise.name: Molise
it-molise.grapes: Montepulciano, Aglianico, Tintilia, Cabernet, Merlot, Sangiovese; Falanghina, Fiano, Greco, Trebbiano, Moscato
it-molise.summary: A region-wide DOC for varietal wines from many grapes, from Aglianico and Montepulciano to Falanghina and Moscato. It is the label for most of Molise's quality bottlings outside Tintilia. About 177 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 632,000 bottles a year.

it-monferrato.name: Monferrato
it-monferrato.grapes: Barbera, Dolcetto, Freisa, Nebbiolo, Cortese, Chiaretto and others
it-monferrato.summary: The umbrella DOC for the provinces of Asti and Alessandria, used for blends and international grapes (Monferrato Rosso, Bianco, Chiaretto) and for Dolcetto and Freisa outside their own DOCs.
it-monferrato.nerd_note: Braida's Il Bacialé, a Barbera-based blend, is one of the best-known Monferrato Rosso wines.

it-monica-di-sardegna.name: Monica di Sardegna
it-monica-di-sardegna.summary: An island-wide DOC for Monica, a red grape probably brought by Spanish monks, giving soft, fruity, light reds for early drinking; superiore and frizzante versions exist. The old Monica di Cagliari sweet style is now part of the Cagliari DOC.

it-monreale.name: Monreale
it-monreale.grapes: Catarratto, Inzolia, Grillo; Perricone, Nero d'Avola, Syrah
it-monreale.summary: A DOC on the hills behind Palermo around Monreale, famous for its Norman cathedral mosaics. Perricone, a tannic native red, is a local speciality. About 46 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 100,000 bottles a year.

it-montecarlo.name: Montecarlo
it-montecarlo.grapes: Trebbiano with Sémillon, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Grigio, Roussanne, Sauvignon, Vermentino; Sangiovese, Syrah, Merlot
it-montecarlo.summary: A small hill town east of Lucca where French varieties (Sémillon, Roussanne, Pinot) were planted in the 19th century, giving an unusual white blend with Trebbiano. Reds use Sangiovese with Syrah and Merlot.

it-montecompatri-colonna.name: Montecompatri Colonna
it-montecompatri-colonna.summary: A small Castelli Romani white DOC around Montecompatri, Colonna and Rocca Priora, with soils of volcanic ash similar to Frascati. About 5 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 31,000 bottles a year.

it-montecucco.name: Montecucco
it-montecucco.summary: The DOC umbrella around Montecucco Sangiovese for blends with at least 60% Sangiovese, varietal Ciliegiolo, Vermentino and Vin Santo, from the slopes of Monte Amiata between Montalcino and the Maremma.

it-montecucco-sangiovese.name: Montecucco Sangiovese
it-montecucco-sangiovese.summary: Montecucco Sangiovese is the DOCG for Sangiovese from the hills of Cinigiano, Castel del Piano and neighbouring communes on the western slopes of Monte Amiata, just across the Orcia river from Montalcino. The wines need 17 months of ageing (34 for Riserva) and show a Brunello-like profile with more Mediterranean warmth. Seven communes and 18 frazioni may appear on labels. More than 60% of the area is farmed organically, one of the highest shares in Italy.

it-montefalco.name: Montefalco
it-montefalco.grapes: Rosso: Sangiovese 60 to 80% with 10 to 25% Sagrantino; Bianco: Trebbiano Spoletino and Grechetto
it-montefalco.summary: The broader DOC of the Montefalco hills. Montefalco Rosso blends Sangiovese with a share of Sagrantino, giving a more approachable wine than the DOCG; Riserva ages 30 months. Montefalco Bianco and Grechetto use local whites, and Trebbiano Spoletino is increasingly bottled here and in the Spoleto DOC.

it-montefalco-sagrantino.name: Montefalco Sagrantino
it-montefalco-sagrantino.summary:
Sagrantino is the most tannic grape variety commonly grown anywhere, with polyphenol levels well above Cabernet Sauvignon or Nebbiolo, and it grows almost nowhere except the hills around Montefalco, the 'balcony of Umbria'. For centuries it was made sweet, as a passito for Easter and family feasts, because the sugar tamed its tannin. By the 1960s only a few hectares remained. Arnaldo Caprai, a textile industrialist, bought land here in 1971, and his son Marco pushed for a dry style: the Caprai 25 Anni (first vintage 1993) made Sagrantino famous.

Today about 374 ha are planted. The dry wine needs 37 months of ageing, including 12 in wood, and cannot be released until four years after the harvest. It is inky purple, with blackberry, black cherry, cinnamon, clove and earth, and a wall of tannin that takes a decade to relax. The Passito, also 100% Sagrantino from dried grapes, is a dark, sweet, tannic rarity. The consorzio counts 118 members and 66 member wineries (2026).
it-montefalco-sagrantino.terroir: Five communes (Montefalco, Bevagna, Gualdo Cattaneo, Castel Ritaldi and Giano dell'Umbria) on hills of roughly 220 to 470 m between the Topino and Clitunno valleys. The consorzio describes four soil zones: alluvial sands near Bevagna, clay and limestone in the centre, and stonier, more calcareous ground near Giano dell'Umbria. Hot summers and cool nights help phenolic ripeness, which Sagrantino needs badly.
it-montefalco-sagrantino.nerd_note: Paolo Bea's Sagrantinos are fermented with long skin contact and aged in large casks for years; Giampiero Bea also helped found the Vini Veri natural-wine movement.

it-montello-rosso.name: Montello Rosso
it-montello-rosso.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Carmenère
it-montello-rosso.summary: A DOCG for Bordeaux-style reds from the Montello hill near Treviso. Loredan Gasparini's Venegazzù della Casa, a Bordeaux blend first made in the 1950s, was one of the earliest Italian Cabernet-based reds of ambition.
it-montello-rosso.terroir: Red clays over karst on the Montello hill.

it-montepulciano-d-abruzzo.name: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
it-montepulciano-d-abruzzo.summary:
Montepulciano d'Abruzzo covers hills across all four provinces of the region and is one of Italy's biggest red DOCs: in 2014 about 8,700 ha and 857,000 hl, more than two-thirds of it from the province of Chieti. The grape gives deep colour, soft tannins and generous black-cherry and plum fruit, which made it the classic bulk and supermarket red, but its best wines are anything but simple. Emidio Pepe's Montepulciano, foot-trodden and aged in bottle for years before release, and Valentini's, made in tiny quantities, are cult wines that age for decades.

The 2023 reform introduced provincial subzones and reserved Superiore and Riserva for them; older subzones (Alto Tirino, Teate, Terre dei Peligni, Terre dei Vestini, San Martino sulla Marrucina) also remain. Teramo's hills have their own DOCG, Colline Teramane, and since 2025 the Casauria area near Pescara does too.
it-montepulciano-d-abruzzo.terroir: Calcareous clay hills from near the coast to 600 m (700 m facing south), under the Gran Sasso and Maiella. The province of Chieti, with the most vines, is warmer and lower; Teramo and the inland valleys (Tirino, Peligna) are cooler.

it-montepulciano-d-abruzzo-colline-teram.name: Colline Teramane Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
it-montepulciano-d-abruzzo-colline-teram.summary: Abruzzo's first DOCG (2003), for Montepulciano from the hills of the province of Teramo in the north of the region, between the Gran Sasso and the sea. The area is cooler and more exposed to mountain air than Chieti, and the wines are firmer and more structured, with two years of ageing (three for Riserva). Emidio Pepe at Torano Nuovo and Illuminati at Controguerra are the reference names.

it-monteregio-di-massa-marittima.name: Monteregio di Massa Marittima
it-monteregio-di-massa-marittima.summary: A DOC in the northern Maremma around the mining town of Massa Marittima in the Colline Metallifere, for Sangiovese reds, Vermentino and Vin Santo, including Occhio di Pernice. About 21 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 65,000 bottles a year.

it-montescudaio.name: Montescudaio
it-montescudaio.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet, Merlot; Trebbiano, Vermentino, Chardonnay
it-montescudaio.summary: A coastal DOC in the Cecina valley just north of Bolgheri, for reds based on Sangiovese and international varieties, whites from Trebbiano and Vermentino, and Vin Santo. It sits in Bolgheri's shadow but has similar soils.

it-monti-lessini.name: Monti Lessini
it-monti-lessini.grapes: Durella, Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Nero
it-monti-lessini.summary: Companion DOC to Lessini Durello for still whites and long-aged metodo classico from the Lessini mountains.

it-morellino-di-scansano.name: Morellino di Scansano
it-morellino-di-scansano.summary: Morellino is the Maremma's Sangiovese, grown in the hills around the village of Scansano between the Ombrone and Albegna rivers, a few kilometres from the sea. The local name may come from the dark colour of the grape (like a *morello* cherry) or from the dark Maremma horses. Warmer and drier than Chianti, the area gives a riper, softer, more immediate Sangiovese with plum and red cherry and gentle tannins, most of it for drinking within five years; Riserva (two years, one in wood) is more serious. About 1,100 ha and close to 9 million bottles a year.
it-morellino-di-scansano.terroir: Hills from about 100 to 500 m, with sandstone, clay and limestone; the sea 20 km away moderates temperatures and the long, dry summers ripen Sangiovese early.
producers: Cantina dei Vignaioli del Morellino di Scansano
it-morellino-di-scansano.nerd_note: Elisabetta Geppetti's Le Pupille made Saffredi (a Cabernet-Merlot IGT) in 1987 that helped put the Maremma on the fine-wine map before most Tuscans took it seriously.

it-moscadello-di-montalcino.name: Moscadello di Montalcino
it-moscadello-di-montalcino.summary: Before Brunello, Montalcino was known for a sweet, aromatic Moscato, praised by the poet Francesco Redi in his 1685 *Bacco in Toscana*. Moscadello survives as a tiny DOC for still, frizzante and late-harvest Moscato. Col d'Orcia and Il Poggione are among the few still making it.
it-moscadello-di-montalcino.nerd_note: Redi's verse calls Moscadello di Montalcino 'il leggiadretto, il sì divino', the graceful, divine one, long before anyone wrote about Brunello.

it-moscato-di-sardegna.name: Moscato di Sardegna
it-moscato-di-sardegna.summary: An island-wide DOC for sweet and sparkling Moscato, with subzones Gallura and Tempio Pausania for the spumante. About 47 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 135,000 bottles a year.

it-moscato-di-sorso.name: Moscato di Sorso-Sennori
it-moscato-di-sorso.summary: A small DOC for sweet Moscato, naturally sweet or fortified, from the hills of Sorso and Sennori north of Sassari overlooking the Gulf of Asinara. The wines are golden, with orange blossom and apricot; production is tiny.

it-moscato-di-trani.name: Moscato di Trani
it-moscato-di-trani.summary: A sweet Muscat from the coastal plain around Trani, made as a naturally sweet or fortified (liquoroso) wine. It was famous in the 19th century; today only a hectare or so is declared. Villa Schinosa and Rivera have kept it alive.

it-nardo.name: Nardò
it-nardo.summary: A small Negroamaro DOC around Nardò, near the Ionian coast of the Salento. About 24 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 119,000 bottles a year.

it-nasco-di-cagliari.name: Nasco di Cagliari
it-nasco-di-cagliari.summary: Nasco is an ancient white grape of the Campidano plain around Cagliari, with a musky, aromatic perfume (the name may come from the Latin *muscus*, musk). It is made dry, sweet or fortified; Argiolas's Iselis and Cantina di Dolianova keep it alive.

it-nebbiolo-d-alba.name: Nebbiolo d'Alba
it-nebbiolo-d-alba.summary: Nebbiolo grown in a ring of communes around Alba, mostly in the Roero and the northern Langhe, outside or overlapping with the Barolo and Barbaresco zones. It is a step up from Langhe Nebbiolo in ambition and ages for a minimum of 12 months (Superiore 18). Many Barolo houses make one from younger vines or the Roero side, and the style is fragrant, medium-bodied and approachable within three to five years.
it-nebbiolo-d-alba.terroir: Mostly sandy Roero soils plus Langhe marls around Diano, Monticello and Vezza.
it-nebbiolo-d-alba.nerd_note: The legal zone includes Barolo-area communes such as Diano and Grinzane, but not the parts already inside the Barolo or Barbaresco boundaries.

it-negroamaro-di-terra-d-otranto.name: Negroamaro di Terra d'Otranto
it-negroamaro-di-terra-d-otranto.summary: A DOC covering the provinces of Lecce, Brindisi and Taranto for varietal Negroamaro, red, rosé and sparkling, created in 2011 to give the grape a single regional name.

it-nettuno.name: Nettuno
it-nettuno.summary: A coastal DOC around Nettuno and Anzio, the Allied landing beaches of 1944, where Bellone is called Cacchione and gives a light, saline white. About 12 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 73,000 bottles a year.

it-nizza.name: Nizza
it-nizza.summary: Nizza is the summit of Barbera: 100% Barbera from 18 communes around Nizza Monferrato, at least 18 months of ageing with six in wood (Riserva 30 months with 12 in wood), and lower yields than Barbera d'Asti. The wines are dark, dense and high in acid, with the balance to age ten years. It began as a subzone of Barbera d'Asti, was promoted to DOCG in 2014 and registered as an independent denomination in 2019. 'Vigna' names are allowed.
it-nizza.terroir: Calcareous marls and sandstones; south- to south-west-facing hills at 150 to 400 metres. Vineyards must be on hillside slopes with good exposure.
it-nizza.nerd_note: The name causes confusion with Nice, which in Italian is also Nizza; producers lobbied for the full name 'Nizza Monferrato' but the DOCG is simply 'Nizza'.

it-noto.name: Noto
it-noto.summary: The baroque town of Noto gives its name to a DOC for two very different wines. Moscato di Noto was the original, a sweet, sparkling or fortified Muscat with an ancient reputation. Since the 1990s the area has become the heartland of Nero d'Avola: the grape takes its name from the nearby town of Avola, and the red sand and limestone around Noto and Pachino give its most elegant, age-worthy versions, such as Planeta's Santa Cecilia.
it-noto.nerd_note: Nero d'Avola is also called Calabrese, possibly a corruption of 'Calea-aulisi', grape of Avola in dialect, rather than a sign of Calabrian origin.

it-nuragus-di-cagliari.name: Nuragus di Cagliari
it-nuragus-di-cagliari.summary: Nuragus, named after the nuraghi, the Bronze Age stone towers that dot Sardinia, is a productive, neutral white grape possibly brought by the Phoenicians. The DOC around Cagliari makes light, fresh whites.

it-nus.name: Nus
it-nus.grapes: Vien de Nus, Pinot Gris (Malvoisie de Nus)
it-nus.summary: A small subzone east of Aosta for the red Vien de Nus and the 'Malvoisie de Nus', which is actually a local Pinot Gris, made dry or as a passito Flétri.
it-nus.terroir: Granite and moraine on the adret of the valley.
it-nus.nerd_note: Malvoisie de Nus is not Malvasia at all but a local Pinot Gris clone.

it-offida.name: Offida
it-offida.grapes: Pecorino or Passerina (minimum 85% each); Rosso from Montepulciano minimum 85%
it-offida.summary: Offida, a hill town famous for its bobbin lace, gives its name to a DOCG that rescued a grape. Pecorino (the name may come from sheep, *pecore*, nibbling the grapes along transhumance routes) had almost vanished when Guido Cocci Grifoni found old vines in the mountains around Arquata del Tronto in the early 1980s and replanted them. The result is a white with surprising acidity and weight, with flavours of green apple, sage and liquorice and a saline finish. Passerina, crisper and lighter, is the other white. Offida Rosso is a Montepulciano aged two years.
it-offida.terroir: Rolling hills of clay, sand and limestone between the Tronto and Tesino rivers in the province of Ascoli Piceno, at 100 to 500 m, with the Sibillini mountains to the west and the sea 20 km east.

it-oltrepo-pavese.name: Oltrepò Pavese
it-oltrepo-pavese.grapes: Barbera, Croatina, Uva Rara, Pinot Nero, Riesling, Moscato and others
it-oltrepo-pavese.summary: The 'beyond the Po' hills of Pavia province, Lombardy's largest wine zone with about 13,500 hectares, form a triangle wedged between Piedmont and Emilia. The umbrella DOC covers Rosso, Barbera, Riesling (Italian Riesling and Rhine Riesling), Moscato and more. Historically this was Milan's wine cellar, much of it sold in bulk or as sparkling base.
it-oltrepo-pavese.terroir: Apennine foothills of marl, clay and limestone.
it-oltrepo-pavese.nerd_note: For decades Oltrepò Pinot Noir went anonymously into the sparkling wines of big Piedmontese houses, which is why the zone's own name is still little known abroad.

it-oltrepo-pavese-metodo-classico.name: Oltrepò Pavese metodo classico
it-oltrepo-pavese-metodo-classico.grapes: Pinot Nero (min 70%), Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Grigio
it-oltrepo-pavese-metodo-classico.summary: Oltrepò Pavese has more Pinot Noir than anywhere else in Italy, about 3,000 hectares, and for a century it supplied base wine to the sparkling houses of Piedmont and beyond. Its own metodo classico DOCG requires at least 70% Pinot Nero and 15 months on the lees (24 for vintage), and the 'Cruasé' brand denotes Pinot Nero rosé. The zone around Santa Maria della Versa, Montalto and Rocca de' Giorgi grows its best sparkling grapes. Conte Vistarino, Monsupello, Ballabio, Calatroni and Mazzolino lead.
it-oltrepo-pavese-metodo-classico.terroir: Clay, limestone and marl hills of the northern Apennines, 150 to 500 m, cooler in the upper valleys (Versa, Scuropasso).
it-oltrepo-pavese-metodo-classico.nerd_note: The Giorgi di Vistarino counts planted Pinot Noir cuttings from France at Rocca de' Giorgi in the 1850s and supplied grapes for some of the first Italian sparkling wines made with Carlo Gancia.

it-oltrepo-pavese-pinot-grigio.name: Oltrepò Pavese Pinot grigio
it-oltrepo-pavese-pinot-grigio.summary: A separate DOC for Pinot Grigio in the Oltrepò hills.

it-orcia.name: Orcia
it-orcia.summary: The Val d'Orcia, the UNESCO-listed landscape of rolling wheat fields and cypresses between Montalcino and Montepulciano, has its own DOC, mostly for Sangiovese reds. The wines are often good value next to their famous neighbours, and a few estates (Podere Forte, Sante Marie) aim high.

it-orta-nova.name: Orta Nova
it-orta-nova.grapes: Sangiovese minimum 60%, with Nero di Troia, Montepulciano
it-orta-nova.summary: A small DOC south of Foggia, unusual for Puglia in using Sangiovese as its main grape. About 2 ha were declared in 2019, giving roughly 7,500 bottles a year.

it-ortona.name: Ortona
it-ortona.summary: A small DOC around the port town of Ortona in the province of Chieti, the scene of fierce fighting in December 1943, for Montepulciano reds and Trebbiano whites. About 4 ha were declared in 2021.

it-ortrugo-dei-colli-piacentini.name: Ortrugo dei Colli Piacentini
it-ortrugo-dei-colli-piacentini.summary: Ortrugo, a native white grape (its name means 'other grape'), makes light, almondy sparkling and still wines in the Piacenza hills.

it-orvieto.name: Orvieto
it-orvieto.grapes: Grechetto and Procanico (Trebbiano Toscano) minimum 60%, with Malvasia, Verdello, Drupeggio and others
it-orvieto.summary:
Orvieto is one of Italy's historic whites, from the hills around the cliff-top city that sits on a block of volcanic tufa. Underneath, Etruscans and medieval monks dug hundreds of caves, many used to ferment and store wine at a steady cool temperature. For centuries the style was *abboccato*, gently sweet, the wine of popes and the 'liquid sunlight' Signorelli asked to be paid in.

The DOC (1971, about 2,100 ha, 95% in Umbria and 5% in Lazio) makes mostly dry whites today, light, almond-scented and fresh. The Classico core around the city gives more depth, and the best producers (Palazzone, Barberani, Decugnano dei Barbi) make wines that age. Orvieto also has a rare noble-rot category, Muffa Nobile: autumn fogs off the Paglia river and Lake Corbara let *Botrytis cinerea* concentrate the grapes, as in Sauternes.
it-orvieto.terroir: Volcanic soils (tufa, ash, lapilli) from the Vulsini volcanoes near the city, with marine clay and sandy marls elsewhere; vineyards between 100 and 500 m. Humid autumns favour botrytis in the low valleys.
it-orvieto.nerd_note: Barberani's Calcaia is a Muffa Nobile Orvieto from botrytised Grechetto and Procanico near Lake Corbara, made only in years when the fog cooperates.

it-ostuni.name: Ostuni
it-ostuni.summary: A small DOC below the white town of Ostuni, notable for rare local grapes: the whites Impigno and Francavidda, and Ottavianello, the local name for Cinsault, which makes a light red.

it-pantelleria.name: Pantelleria
it-pantelleria.summary:
Pantelleria is a windswept volcanic island 100 km southwest of Sicily and only 70 km from Tunisia. Its name in Arabic, *Bint al-Riyah*, means 'daughter of the winds', and the winds shaped its viticulture: Zibibbo vines are grown as tiny bushes in hollows dug into the black soil, protected by dry-stone walls, so the leaves shade the grapes and the plants catch every drop of dew. On 26 November 2014 UNESCO inscribed the 'traditional agricultural practice of cultivating the vite ad alberello' of Pantelleria on its Intangible Cultural Heritage list, the first agricultural practice ever recognised.

Passito di Pantelleria is made by drying part of the harvest in the sun for weeks on mats, then adding the raisins to fresh must from late-picked grapes, so the wine ferments slowly into an amber, intensely sweet wine of apricot, candied orange, fig and Mediterranean herbs, balanced by acidity and minerality. About 430 ha remain, many tended by elderly growers. Moscato, dry Zibibbo and liqueur versions exist too.
it-pantelleria.terroir: Volcanic soils of ash, pumice and lava, rich in minerals and potassium but poor in organic matter; constant wind, almost no rain in summer, and vineyards from sea level to about 400 m, on terraces held up by dry-stone walls.
it-pantelleria.nerd_note: Zibibbo takes its name from the Arabic *zabib*, raisin; on Pantelleria the bushes are pruned so low that pickers work on their knees.

it-parrina.name: Parrina
it-parrina.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon; Ansonica, Vermentino, Chardonnay
it-parrina.summary: A near-monopoly DOC around the Tenuta La Parrina estate near Orbetello, on the coast facing Monte Argentario. Reds are Sangiovese-based with Merlot and Cabernet; whites use Ansonica and Vermentino. About 45 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 45,000 bottles a year.

it-penisola-sorrentina.name: Penisola Sorrentina
it-penisola-sorrentina.grapes: Piedirosso, Aglianico, Sciascinoso (Olivella); Falanghina, Biancolella, Greco
it-penisola-sorrentina.summary: The Sorrento peninsula DOC is famous for two subzones that make red frizzante: Gragnano and Lettere, dark, fruity, lightly sparkling and slightly sweet or dry, the classic wine of Neapolitan pizza. A Sorrento subzone covers still wines. The Romans praised Surrentine wine as good for convalescents.

it-pentro-di-isernia.name: Pentro di Isernia
it-pentro-di-isernia.summary: An inland DOC in the province of Isernia, named for the Pentri, a Samnite tribe. Very little wine is declared under this name. About 74 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 900 bottles a year.

it-pergola.name: Pergola
it-pergola.summary: A small DOC around Pergola in the Cesano valley where Aleatico, locally called Vernaccia di Pergola, makes dry, perfumed reds and passito. About 5 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 32,000 bottles a year.

it-piave.name: Piave
it-piave.grapes: Raboso Piave, Merlot, Cabernet, Carmenère, Tai, Verduzzo
it-piave.summary: The flat plain along the Piave river in Treviso and Venice provinces, the homeland of Raboso, a tough, high-acid red grape, and of easy Merlot and Cabernet.
it-piave.terroir: Alluvial gravels and clays of the Piave plain.
it-piave.nerd_note: Raboso is said to take its name from the river Raboso, a tributary of the Piave, or from *rabbioso* ('angry'), describing its acidity.

it-piave-malanotte.name: Piave Malanotte
it-piave-malanotte.summary: A DOCG for Raboso from the Piave, in which 15 to 30% of the grapes are dried before fermentation to tame the grape's fierce acidity and tannin. Aged at least 36 months. Named after the Malanotte borgo at Vazzola.
it-piave-malanotte.terroir: Gravel and clay of the Piave plain.
it-piave-malanotte.nerd_note: Raboso was historically shipped to Venice because its acidity let it survive long sea voyages.

it-piemonte.name: Piemonte
it-piemonte.grapes: Barbera, Bonarda, Brachetto, Chardonnay, Cortese, Dolcetto, Grignolino, Moscato, Pinot Nero and many others
it-piemonte.summary: The regional DOC covering the hills of Asti, Alessandria and Cuneo and parts of Turin province. Because Piedmont has no IGT, it is the safety net for varietal and blended wines that do not fit a local DOC, including Piemonte Moscato and Piemonte Barbera.
it-piemonte.nerd_note: Piedmont is the only major Italian region with no IGT, so Piemonte DOC does the job an IGT does elsewhere.

it-pignoletto.name: Pignoletto
it-pignoletto.summary: The broad DOC created in 2014 for Pignoletto from the plain and hills of Bologna, Modena and Ravenna provinces, mostly frizzante and spumante; the hill classic is the Colli Bolognesi Classico Pignoletto DOCG.
it-pignoletto.nerd_note: Creating the DOC made Pignoletto a protected place name, so the grape must now be called Grechetto Gentile on labels elsewhere.

it-pinerolese.name: Pinerolese
it-pinerolese.grapes: Barbera, Bonarda, Dolcetto, Freisa, Avanà, Doux d'Henry, Ramìe
it-pinerolese.summary: Mountain reds from the Pinerolo valleys west of Turin, including the rare Ramìe and Doux d'Henry.
it-pinerolese.nerd_note: Doux d'Henry is said to be named after Henry IV of France.

it-pinot-nero-dell-oltrepo-pavese.name: Pinot nero dell'Oltrepò Pavese
it-pinot-nero-dell-oltrepo-pavese.summary: Still Pinot Noir from the Oltrepò, red or vinified as white or rosé. Tenuta Mazzolino's Noir and Conte Vistarino's Pernice single vineyard show its Burgundian ambitions.
it-pinot-nero-dell-oltrepo-pavese.terroir: Cool upper valleys of the Oltrepò.
it-pinot-nero-dell-oltrepo-pavese.nerd_note: Frecciarossa's Giorgio Odero bottled Pinot Nero in the 1930s.

it-pomino.name: Pomino
it-pomino.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Grigio, Trebbiano; Pinot Nero, Sangiovese, Merlot
it-pomino.summary: Pomino is a mountain enclave inside the Chianti Rùfina zone, named in Cosimo III's 1716 edict and since the 19th century almost a Frescobaldi monopoly. The family planted French varieties here in 1855 (Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Nero), so the DOC, created in 1983, is one of the few in Tuscany built on Burgundian grapes. Vines reach about 700 m, and the cool air gives crisp whites and light reds. The Castello Pomino Bianco is the flagship, Benefizio a barrel-fermented Chardonnay.
it-pomino.nerd_note: Frescobaldi's Benefizio, first made in 1973, was one of the first barrique-fermented Chardonnays in Italy.

it-pornassio.name: Pornassio
it-pornassio.summary: The DOC of Ormeasco, Liguria's name for Dolcetto, in the mountains around Pornassio in the upper Arroscia valley. The grape reportedly arrived from Piedmont in the 14th century. Reds, Superiore, a rosé called Sciac-trà (not to be confused with Sciacchetrà) and passito are made.
it-pornassio.terroir: Mountain slopes at 400 to 800 m on the border with Piedmont.
it-pornassio.nerd_note: The Ormeasco Sciac-trà rosé shares its dialect name, meaning 'crush and draw off', with the Cinque Terre's sweet wine.

it-portofino.name: Golfo del Tigullio - Portofino
it-portofino.grapes: Vermentino, Bianchetta Genovese, Moscato, Ciliegiolo, Dolcetto
it-portofino.summary: The DOC of the Tigullio gulf from Portofino to Sestri Levante and inland valleys. Bianchetta Genovese, a delicate local white, and Ciliegiolo reds are its specialities.
it-portofino.terroir: Shale and sandstone hills behind the gulf.
it-portofino.nerd_note: Bisson ages a sparkling wine, Abissi, at the bottom of the sea in the Portofino marine park.

it-primitivo-di-manduria.name: Primitivo di Manduria
it-primitivo-di-manduria.summary:
Primitivo di Manduria is Puglia's best-known wine and one of Italy's fastest-growing DOCs, with about 3,900 ha around the town of Manduria and 17 neighbouring communes in the provinces of Taranto and Brindisi. The grape, genetically the same as Zinfandel, ripens early (hence the name), accumulates sugar fast and gives wines of 14 to 16% alcohol, with blackberry jam, dried fig, liquorice and sweet spice. Riserva needs two years including nine months in wood.

Much of the volume is soft and slightly sweet in style for export, but old bush vines on red earth near the coast, such as Gianfranco Fino's Es, show how dense and complex it can be. The sweet version has its own DOCG.
it-primitivo-di-manduria.terroir: Flat to gently rolling land between the Murge and the Ionian Sea, with red earth over limestone near the coast and deeper clay inland. Hot, dry summers; sea breezes keep nights a little cooler.

it-primitivo-di-manduria-dolce-naturale.name: Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale
it-primitivo-di-manduria-dolce-naturale.summary: A naturally sweet red from late-harvested Primitivo, often left to raisin on the vine or briefly dried, with at least 50 g/l of residual sugar and no fortification. A DOCG since 2011, it revives the old local habit of making sweet wine from the ripest grapes. Dark, port-like but unfortified, with fig, prune and chocolate.

it-prosecco.name: Prosecco
it-prosecco.grapes: Glera (min 85%); Pinot Nero (10 to 15%) for rosé
it-prosecco.summary:
The Prosecco DOC is the world's best-selling sparkling wine and Italy's largest wine appellation by value. Created in 2009, it spans nine provinces in Veneto (Treviso, Venezia, Vicenza, Padova, Belluno) and Friuli Venezia Giulia (Trieste, Gorizia, Udine, Pordenone), a defensive move: the grape was renamed Glera and the name Prosecco, taken from the village of Prosecco near Trieste, became a protected place name that no one outside the zone could use.

Production reached 667 million bottles in 2025 (607 million white and 60 million rosé, a category introduced in 2020), with the United States the largest export market. The vineyard potential of about 24,450 hectares is being raised by 6,050 hectares to 30,500, in two phases approved by both regions in late 2025. Treviso and Trieste provinces may add their names to the label ('Prosecco DOC Treviso', 'Prosecco DOC Trieste').
it-prosecco.terroir: Mostly flat alluvial plains of the Piave, Livenza and Tagliamento, with fertile gravels and clays allowing high yields (18 tonnes/ha).
it-prosecco.nerd_note: The village of Prosecco that gave its name to the wine is a suburb of Trieste in Friuli, not in the Treviso hills where the wine is most associated.

it-ramandolo.name: Ramandolo
it-ramandolo.summary: Friuli's first DOCG (2001): sweet Verduzzo from the steep, wet hills around Ramandolo and Nimis north of Udine, where the Alps rise abruptly. The grapes are late-harvested or dried; the wine is golden, honeyed and almondy, with a tannic grip unusual in a sweet white. The Dri family (Il Roncat) and Anna Berra are reference producers.
it-ramandolo.terroir: Steep ponca terraces at 350 to 500 m in one of the wettest wine zones of Italy, below Monte Bernadia.
it-ramandolo.nerd_note: Verduzzo's tannin comes from its thick skins, making Ramandolo one of the few sweet whites with noticeable grip.

it-recioto-della-valpolicella.name: Recioto della Valpolicella
it-recioto-della-valpolicella.summary: The original dried-grape wine of Valpolicella: sweet, red, rich in cherry and chocolate, made from dried grapes whose fermentation is stopped while sugar remains. It is the direct descendant of the *Acinatico* praised by Cassiodorus around AD 500. The name comes from *recie*, dialect for the 'ears' or upper lobes of the bunch that got the most sun and were selected for drying. Today Recioto is a rarity, a fraction of Amarone's volume, but Quintarelli, Dal Forno and Bussola make thrilling ones.
it-recioto-della-valpolicella.nerd_note: Recioto Spumante, a sweet sparkling red, is still permitted and occasionally made.

it-recioto-di-gambellara.name: Recioto di Gambellara
it-recioto-di-gambellara.summary: Sweet dried-grape Garganega from the Gambellara hills, still or sparkling.

it-recioto-di-soave.name: Recioto di Soave
it-recioto-di-soave.summary: Italy's first DOCG for a white sweet wine (1998), from Garganega grapes dried on racks until spring, giving a golden, apricot and almond-scented wine with bright acidity. A sparkling version also exists.
it-recioto-di-soave.terroir: Same volcanic and limestone hills as Soave Classico.
it-recioto-di-soave.nerd_note: Recioto di Soave was a favourite of the Venetian court and the papal households in the 18th century.

it-reggiano.name: Reggiano
it-reggiano.grapes: Lambrusco Salamino, Maestri, Marani, Montericco, Ancellotta
it-reggiano.summary: The Lambrusco of Reggio Emilia, typically darker and softer than Modena's thanks to Ancellotta and the Maestri and Marani varieties; most volume of 'Lambrusco Reggiano' comes from here, including much of the sweet export style. Medici Ermete's single-vineyard Concerto (from Salamino) helped show the zone's potential for dry, serious Lambrusco.
it-reggiano.nerd_note: Lini 910 is known for a long-aged metodo classico Lambrusco, a rarity in a zone dominated by the tank method.

it-reno.name: Reno
it-reno.summary: A plain DOC north of Bologna along the Reno river, known for the local Montuni white grape.

it-riesi.name: Riesi
it-riesi.grapes: Nero d'Avola, Cabernet, Syrah; Ansonica, Chardonnay
it-riesi.summary: A DOC in the province of Caltanissetta around Riesi and Butera, sulphur-mining country in the hot centre-south, mostly for Nero d'Avola-based reds; Feudo Principi di Butera (Zonin) is here. About 12 ha were declared in 2021.

it-riviera-del-brenta.name: Riviera del Brenta
it-riviera-del-brenta.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet, Raboso, Pinot Bianco, Tai
it-riviera-del-brenta.summary: Wines from the Brenta canal country between Padua and Venice, lined with Palladian villas.

it-riviera-del-garda-bresciano.name: Riviera del Garda Classico
it-riviera-del-garda-bresciano.summary: The DOC of the western shore of Lake Garda in Brescia province (formerly Garda Bresciano), for Groppello reds and Chiaretto.
it-riviera-del-garda-bresciano.terroir: Moraine and limestone on the lake's western shore.
it-riviera-del-garda-bresciano.nerd_note: The DOC was formerly Riviera del Garda Bresciano / Garda Bresciano.

it-riviera-ligure-di-ponente.name: Riviera ligure di Ponente
it-riviera-ligure-di-ponente.grapes: Pigato, Vermentino, Rossese, Ormeasco (Dolcetto), Granaccia, Moscato
it-riviera-ligure-di-ponente.summary: The umbrella DOC for the western Riviera from Ventimiglia to Genoa, best known for Pigato and Vermentino. Pigato, whose name refers to the freckles (*pighe*) on its ripe skins, is especially at home in the Albenga plain and its valleys (Arroscia, Lerrone, Neva), where it makes rich, herbal, slightly bitter whites with notes of peach, rosemary and resin; genetically it is the same as Vermentino, but growers stand by its distinct character. Subzones include Riviera dei Fiori, Albenganese, Finalese and Quiliano, plus Taggia for Moscato and Granaccia from Quiliano.
it-riviera-ligure-di-ponente.terroir: Alluvial and clay-limestone soils in the Albenga valleys; terraced flysch and limestone near Finale and Imperia.
it-riviera-ligure-di-ponente.nerd_note: Albenga's plain is an island of flat land in Liguria, and Pigato from Ortovero and Ranzo is where the variety's reputation was built from the 1980s.

it-roero.name: Roero
it-roero.grapes: Nebbiolo (min 95%) for Roero; Arneis (min 95%) for Roero Arneis
it-roero.summary:
Roero is the Langhe's mirror image across the Tanaro: Nebbiolo grown on loose Pliocene sands that make a lighter, more perfumed, earlier-drinking wine, and Arneis, the white grape that the region's growers saved from near extinction. Arneis means something like 'little rascal' in Piedmontese, a nod to its awkward habits in the vineyard; it was traditionally planted among Nebbiolo to attract birds and bees away from the red grapes and sometimes added to soften them. In the late 1960s Alfredo Currado at Vietti and Bruno Giacosa bottled it as a varietal, and by the 1990s Roero Arneis was a fashionable white with pear, chamomile and almond notes.

Roero rosso needs 20 months of ageing (Riserva 32), with six months in wood; the white comes as still, spumante and Riserva. Matteo Correggia, who died in a tractor accident in 2001, did more than anyone to show that Roero Nebbiolo could age, and estates like Malvirà, Cascina Ca' Rossa, Monchiero Carbone, Giovanni Almondo and Cascina Val del Prete followed. The consortium has mapped MGAs, and Roero is increasingly seen as a source of value-priced, elegant Nebbiolo.
it-roero.terroir: Pliocene marine sands (Sabbie d'Asti) over marls, crumbling into dramatic ravines called *rocche*. The sands warm quickly and drain freely, ripening Nebbiolo earlier and giving softer tannins; Arneis gets its freshness from the cooler, north-facing parcels and higher sites.
it-roero.nerd_note: The *rocche* ravines also mark a geological watershed: the sandy slopes are full of marine fossils, and in places you can pick scallop shells out of the vineyard soil.

it-roma.name: Roma
it-roma.grapes: Montepulciano, Cesanese, Sangiovese, Syrah; Malvasia del Lazio, Bellone, Bombino
it-roma.summary: A DOC created in 2011 to put the name of the capital on a bottle, covering much of the province of Rome. Reds must be at least 50% Montepulciano; whites at least 50% Malvasia Puntinata. Romanella is its sparkling white. A Classico area covers the historic vineyard belt around the city.

it-romagna.name: Romagna
it-romagna.grapes: Sangiovese (min 95% for Romagna Sangiovese), Trebbiano, Cagnina (Refosco), Pagadebit (Bombino Bianco)
it-romagna.summary: The Romagna DOC unites the region's historic denominations: Romagna Sangiovese (formerly Sangiovese di Romagna, DOC 1967), Romagna Trebbiano, Romagna Cagnina (a sweet red from Refosco, drunk with roast chestnuts in autumn) and Romagna Pagadebit ('pays the debts', a hardy white). Sangiovese is the core: the hills are divided into 12 sottozone (MGAs) that may appear on the label: Serra, Brisighella, Marzeno, Oriolo, Modigliana, Castrocaro, Predappio, Bertinoro, Cesena, San Vicino, Longiano and Meldola. Each has a distinct character: Modigliana on high, cool marl-sandstone at 180 to 570 m gives tense, pale wines; Predappio's red clays give silky tannin; Bertinoro's spungone gives power. Riserva ages two years. Romagna Sangiovese Superiore is the standard bearer; producers include Fattoria Zerbina, Torre San Martino, Villa Papiano, Il Pratello, Fattoria Nicolucci, Noelia Ricci, Tenuta La Viola and Giovanna Madonia.
it-romagna.terroir: Apennine foothills from Imola to Rimini: spungone, calcareous clays, red clays and marl-sandstone, at 100 to 600 m, with sea breezes from the Adriatic.
it-romagna.nerd_note: Modigliana's growers formed their own association, Modigliana Stella dell'Appennino, and argue that their cool, high, marl-sandstone valleys make Sangiovese closer to Chianti Classico than to the rest of Romagna.

it-romagna-albana.name: Romagna Albana
it-romagna-albana.summary: Albana became Italy's first white DOCG in 1987, a decision widely mocked at the time because most Albana was dull and the promotion looked political. Since then producers have made the case: Albana is a thick-skinned, tannic white grape with apricot, almond and saffron notes, made dry (secco), amabile, sweet (dolce) and above all passito from dried or botrytised grapes. Fattoria Zerbina's Scacco Matto passito and Tre Monti's skin-contact Vitalba helped change minds. The zone covers hills of Bologna, Forlì-Cesena, Ravenna and Rimini provinces, centred on Bertinoro, Dozza and Faenza.
it-romagna-albana.terroir: Calcareous clays and spungone sandstone of the Romagna foothills.
it-romagna-albana.nerd_note: Legend says Galla Placidia, daughter of Emperor Theodosius, tasted Albana at Bertinoro and said it should be drunk 'in gold', which supposedly gave the hill town its name.

it-rosazzo.name: Rosazzo
it-rosazzo.grapes: Friulano (min 50%), Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Ribolla Gialla
it-rosazzo.summary: A DOCG for white blends from the hills around the Abbey of Rosazzo in Manzano, Corno di Rosazzo, Premariacco, San Giovanni al Natisone and Buttrio. Livio Felluga's Terre Alte, first made in 1981, is the archetypal Rosazzo blend. Rosazzo Pignolo, though famous, falls under Colli Orientali rules.
it-rosazzo.terroir: Ponca hills around the abbey, well ventilated, with a warm microclimate.
it-rosazzo.nerd_note: The Abbey of Rosazzo, founded around 1070, preserved the last Pignolo vines through the 20th century.

it-rossese-di-dolceacqua.name: Rossese di Dolceacqua
it-rossese-di-dolceacqua.summary: Liguria's first DOC and its most distinctive red, from the Nervia and Verbone valleys behind Ventimiglia near the French border. Rossese (which DNA links to Tibouren of Provence) gives a pale, perfumed, spicy red with wild strawberry, rose and sea-salt notes, sometimes compared to a Mediterranean Pinot Noir. Steep terraces and old alberello vines are the norm, and in 2012 the disciplinare recognised named vineyard sites (menzioni geografiche) such as Posaú, Galeae, Beragna and Arcagna. Maccario Dringenberg, Terre Bianche, Ka*Manciné and Testalonga are reference producers.
it-rossese-di-dolceacqua.terroir: Steep terraces of marl and sandstone (flysch) at 150 to 600 m in the hinterland of the Riviera dei Fiori.
it-rossese-di-dolceacqua.nerd_note: Legend says Napoleon tasted Rossese at Dolceacqua and declared it fit for an emperor, and Pope Paul III is also said to have praised it in the 16th century.

it-rosso-conero.name: Rosso Cònero
it-rosso-conero.summary: The non-Riserva red of Monte Conero, a Montepulciano-based wine with lively acidity and dark fruit, released after a few months. When the Riserva became the Cònero DOCG in 2004, this DOC kept the younger wines.

it-rosso-di-cerignola.name: Rosso di Cerignola
it-rosso-di-cerignola.summary: A nearly dormant DOC for Nero di Troia-based reds around Cerignola on the Tavoliere. About 1 ha were declared in 2021.

it-rosso-di-montalcino.name: Rosso di Montalcino
it-rosso-di-montalcino.summary:
The younger sibling of Brunello, from the same zone and the same grape but released from 1 September after the harvest with no minimum time in wood. It was created to give growers cash flow and a way to declassify lesser lots, and the best producers now treat it as a serious wine from younger vines or specific parcels: bright cherry, fresh acidity and much of Brunello's character at a fraction of the price and wait.

In September 2024 the consorzio reassigned 352 hectares of existing vineyard to Rosso, taking its registered area to about 872 ha (no new planting), so potential output from the 2024 vintage more than doubles to about 7.3 million bottles. Producers are now debating whether Rosso is a second wine or a terroir wine in its own right.

it-rosso-di-montepulciano.name: Rosso di Montepulciano
it-rosso-di-montepulciano.summary: The early-release red of Montepulciano, sold from March after the vintage: juicy, cherry-scented Sangiovese for drinking young. About 390 ha and over 2 million bottles a year. It lets producers keep their best fruit for Vino Nobile and the new Pieve wines.

it-rosso-orvietano.name: Rosso Orvietano
it-rosso-orvietano.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet, Canaiolo, Aleatico and others
it-rosso-orvietano.summary: The red-wine companion to Orvieto, covering the same zone. It allows blends and varietals from Sangiovese and international grapes; production is small. About 14 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 53,000 bottles a year.

it-rosso-piceno.name: Rosso Piceno
it-rosso-piceno.summary: Rosso Piceno, named for the ancient Piceni people, is the broad Montepulciano-Sangiovese red of southern and central Marche, about 765 ha. Superiore comes only from a delimited southern area around Ascoli Piceno and Offida and is the more serious wine. Velenosi and Saladini Pilastri make widely exported versions.

it-rubino-di-cantavenna.name: Rubino di Cantavenna
it-rubino-di-cantavenna.summary: A historic blend from three communes near the Po in the Casalese, now made by very few producers.
it-rubino-di-cantavenna.nerd_note: One of the rarest DOC wines in Italy; production is tiny.

it-ruche-di-castagnole-monferrato.name: Ruchè di Castagnole Monferrato
it-ruche-di-castagnole-monferrato.summary: A tiny DOCG for Ruchè, an aromatic red grape grown in seven communes around Castagnole Monferrato. It smells of rose petals, violets, white pepper and cinnamon, with moderate tannin. Its revival is credited to the parish priest Don Giacomo Cauda, who replanted it in the 1960s and 1970s. Montalbera and Luca Ferraris are the main producers.
it-ruche-di-castagnole-monferrato.terroir: Calcareous clay and sandy marls in the hills north-east of Asti.
it-ruche-di-castagnole-monferrato.nerd_note: Don Cauda's parish vineyard is still known as the 'Vigna del Parroco'.

it-s-anna-di-isola-capo-rizzuto.name: S. Anna di Isola Capo Rizzuto
it-s-anna-di-isola-capo-rizzuto.grapes: Gaglioppo with Nocera, Nerello, Malvasia Nera
it-s-anna-di-isola-capo-rizzuto.summary: A small coastal DOC south of Crotone near the Capo Rizzuto marine reserve, for Gaglioppo-based reds and rosés. About 3 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 8,700 bottles a year.

it-salaparuta.name: Salaparuta
it-salaparuta.grapes: Nero d'Avola, Merlot, Cabernet, Syrah; Catarratto, Inzolia, Grillo, Chardonnay
it-salaparuta.summary: A small DOC around Salaparuta in the Belice valley. The town gave its name to the Duca di Salaparuta family, whose Corvo brand (founded 1824 at Casteldaccia near Palermo) was Sicily's most famous wine label for a century.

it-salice-salentino.name: Salice Salentino
it-salice-salentino.grapes: Negroamaro minimum 75% (often with Malvasia Nera); whites from Chardonnay, Fiano, Verdeca
it-salice-salentino.summary: The best-known Negroamaro DOC, about 1,700 ha in the flat heart of the Salento between Lecce and Brindisi. Negroamaro ('black-bitter') gives dark, soft reds with plum, tobacco, earth and a bitter, almond finish, often blended with a little Malvasia Nera. Rosato has a special place: Leone de Castris, based in Salice, bottled Five Roses in 1943, said to be the first rosé bottled in Italy, after American officers asked for a pink wine.
it-salice-salentino.terroir: Flat red earth and sandy clay over limestone, swept by winds from both seas (the hot sirocco and the cooler tramontana); bush-trained vines resist heat and drought.
it-salice-salentino.nerd_note: Cosimo Taurino's Patriglione, from late-harvested Negroamaro in Guagnano, was one of the first Puglian wines to be taken seriously abroad in the 1980s.

it-sambuca-di-sicilia.name: Sambuca di Sicilia
it-sambuca-di-sicilia.grapes: Ansonica, Chardonnay, Grillo; Nero d'Avola, Cabernet, Syrah
it-sambuca-di-sicilia.summary: A small DOC around Sambuca di Sicilia and Lake Arancio, where Planeta's Ulmo estate is located.

it-san-colombano-al-lambro.name: San Colombano al Lambro
it-san-colombano-al-lambro.grapes: Croatina, Barbera, Uva Rara; Chardonnay, Pinot Nero
it-san-colombano-al-lambro.summary: The only DOC in Milan's metropolitan province, on an isolated hill rising above the Po plain near Lodi. Light reds of Croatina and Barbera.
it-san-colombano-al-lambro.terroir: An isolated hill of marine sediments and loess in the flat plain.
it-san-colombano-al-lambro.nerd_note: The hill is named after the Irish monk Saint Columbanus, who passed by on his way to found the abbey of Bobbio in 614.

it-san-gimignano.name: San Gimignano
it-san-gimignano.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Pinot Nero; Vin Santo from Trebbiano and Malvasia
it-san-gimignano.summary: The red, rosé and Vin Santo companion DOC to Vernaccia, covering the same commune. It is small and mostly used for Sangiovese-based reds and international blends; most producers sell their reds as Chianti Colli Senesi or IGT instead.

it-san-ginesio.name: San Ginesio
it-san-ginesio.grapes: Sangiovese with Vernaccia Nera, Cabernet, Merlot, Ciliegiolo
it-san-ginesio.summary: A tiny DOC in the Sibillini foothills around San Ginesio, for Sangiovese-based reds and a sparkling Vernaccia Nera, close to Serrapetrona in style. About 7 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 40,000 bottles a year.

it-san-martino-della-battaglia.name: San Martino della Battaglia
it-san-martino-della-battaglia.summary: A tiny DOC south of Lake Garda for Friulano, here called Tuchì, dry or as a liqueur wine. It overlaps Lugana's zone around the Risorgimento battlefield of San Martino (1859).
it-san-martino-della-battaglia.nerd_note: The battle of Solferino and San Martino in 1859 inspired Henry Dunant to found the Red Cross.

it-san-severo.name: San Severo
it-san-severo.grapes: Bombino Bianco, Trebbiano; Montepulciano, Sangiovese, Nero di Troia
it-san-severo.summary: One of Puglia's oldest DOCs, on the Tavoliere plain north of Foggia, for Bombino Bianco whites (including sparkling) and Montepulciano reds. About 121 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 720,000 bottles a year.

it-san-torpe.name: San Torpè
it-san-torpe.summary: Named after the Roman officer Torpè, martyred under Nero, this DOC in the Pisan hills is for Trebbiano-based whites and Vin Santo. It is nearly extinct in practice, with well under a hectare declared.

it-sangue-di-giuda.name: Sangue di Giuda
it-sangue-di-giuda.summary: 'Blood of Judas': a sweet, lightly sparkling red from the same area as Buttafuoco, low in alcohol and drunk with desserts.
it-sangue-di-giuda.nerd_note: Legend says Judas, resurrected in the Oltrepò, cured the vines of disease and the wine was named for him.

it-sannio.name: Sannio
it-sannio.grapes: Aglianico, Piedirosso, Sciascinoso, Barbera; Coda di Volpe, Fiano, Greco, Malvasia, Moscato
it-sannio.summary: The umbrella DOC for the province of Benevento, with varietal wines from nearly every Campanian grape and subzones such as Solopaca and Guardia Sanframondi. Mustilli at Sant'Agata de' Goti was the first to bottle a varietal Falanghina, in 1979.

it-sant-antimo.name: Sant'Antimo
it-sant-antimo.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Nero, Sangiovese, Chardonnay and others
it-sant-antimo.summary: A catch-all DOC covering the whole commune of Montalcino, named after the Romanesque abbey of Sant'Antimo near Castelnuovo dell'Abate. It exists for wines that cannot be Brunello or Rosso: international varieties, blends and Vin Santo. Banfi and Castello Romitorio have used it, but most producers now prefer IGT Toscana.

it-santa-margherita-di-belice.name: Santa Margherita di Belice
it-santa-margherita-di-belice.grapes: Ansonica, Catarratto, Grecanico; Nero d'Avola, Sangiovese, Cabernet
it-santa-margherita-di-belice.summary: A tiny DOC in the Belice valley, where the 1968 earthquake destroyed the town that Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa's family palace (Donnafugata in *The Leopard*) once dominated. Barely 0.5 ha were declared in 2019, so the name is close to dormant.

it-sardegna-semidano.name: Sardegna Semidano
it-sardegna-semidano.summary: A DOC for Semidano, a rare aromatic white grape that once covered much of central Sardinia. Its Mogoro subzone, around the village of Mogoro in the Marmilla, holds most of the remaining vines; the cooperative Il Nuraghe keeps it going.

it-savuto.name: Savuto
it-savuto.grapes: Gaglioppo, Magliocco, Greco Nero, Nerello, Sangiovese
it-savuto.summary: A small DOC on the steep terraces of the Savuto river valley between Cosenza and Lamezia, one of Calabria's oldest, for blended reds; it has a Classico area. About 6 ha were declared in 2021.

it-scanzo.name: Moscato di Scanzo
it-scanzo.summary: Italy's smallest DOCG, about 31 hectares in the single commune of Scanzorosciate near Bergamo. Moscato di Scanzo is a red Muscat whose grapes are dried for at least 21 days, giving an aromatic sweet red with rose, sage, cherry jam and spice, aged at least two years. Local tradition holds that it was shipped to London and the Russian court in the 18th and 19th centuries and fetched prices to rival the finest wines.
it-scanzo.terroir: Sass del Luna, a local friable marly limestone, on south-facing hills at 250 to 500 m.
it-scanzo.nerd_note: Moscato di Scanzo is a distinct red Muscat variety found only here; it is not Moscato Rosa or Moscato Nero.

it-scavigna.name: Scavigna
it-scavigna.grapes: Aglianico, Gaglioppo, Nerello; Trebbiano, Chardonnay, Greco
it-scavigna.summary: A small DOC on the Tyrrhenian coast near Nocera Terinese and Falerna, with blends of local and international grapes. Little is produced.

it-sciacca.name: Sciacca
it-sciacca.grapes: Inzolia, Catarratto, Grecanico, Chardonnay; Nero d'Avola, Merlot, Cabernet, Sangiovese
it-sciacca.summary: A small DOC around the spa town of Sciacca, below Monte Kronio, where Copper Age jars with wine residues (about 4000 BC) were found. Its Rayana subzone is for a Catarratto-Inzolia white Riserva.

it-serrapetrona.name: Serrapetrona
it-serrapetrona.summary: The still, dry red version of Vernaccia Nera from Serrapetrona, created when the sparkling wine became a DOCG in 2004. Peppery and juicy, sometimes with a share of dried grapes for depth (Terre di Serrapetrona's Collequanto).

it-sforzato-di-valtellina.name: Sforzato di Valtellina
it-sforzato-di-valtellina.summary: Sforzato (in dialect Sfursat, 'forced') is Valtellina's answer to Amarone: Nebbiolo grapes picked in October and dried in airy lofts (*fruttai*) until at least December or January, losing around 30 to 40% of their weight, then fermented dry. The result is a powerful red of 14 to 16% alcohol with dried cherry, fig, tar and spice, but still with Nebbiolo's acidity and tannin. It ages at least 20 months (12 in wood). Nino Negri's 5 Stelle Sfursat, first made by Casimiro Maule in the 1980s, made the category famous.
it-sforzato-di-valtellina.terroir: Grapes come from the best terraces of the Valtellina Superiore subzones; the drying lofts use the cold, dry Alpine air.
it-sforzato-di-valtellina.nerd_note: Sforzato was the first dried-grape dry red to win DOCG status in Italy (2003), six years ahead of Amarone (2009).

it-sicilia.name: Sicilia
it-sicilia.grapes: Nero d'Avola, Grillo, Catarratto, Inzolia, Frappato, Nerello, Perricone, Carricante, Zibibbo and international varieties
it-sicilia.summary: An island-wide DOC created in 2011 from the old Sicilia IGT, about 24,600 ha and 800,000 hl a year, which makes it one of Italy's biggest denominations. It was designed to protect the names Nero d'Avola and Grillo, which until then could be used on wines bottled anywhere: since 2017 those varietal names on labels are reserved for DOC Sicilia. The quality ranges from supermarket wine to estate bottlings, and Salemi was added as the first UGA.

it-siracusa.name: Siracusa
it-siracusa.summary: Moscato di Siracusa, sometimes linked by enthusiasts to the ancient Pollio wine of Greek Syracuse, had almost disappeared when the Pupillo family revived it in the 1990s. The DOC was expanded in 2011 to include reds and whites.

it-sizzano.name: Sizzano
it-sizzano.grapes: Nebbiolo (50 to 70%), Vespolina and/or Uva Rara
it-sizzano.summary: One of the smallest DOCs in Italy, on the moraine between Ghemme and Fara. Cavour reportedly compared it to Burgundy.
it-sizzano.nerd_note: Only a handful of producers bottle Sizzano.

it-soave.name: Soave
it-soave.grapes: Garganega (min 70%), Trebbiano di Soave and Chardonnay
it-soave.summary:
Soave is one of Italy's great white wines and, after its 1970s and 1980s reputation as a cheap supermarket staple, one of its great comeback stories. It is made mainly from Garganega, a late-ripening, thick-skinned grape that gives almond, chamomile, yellow plum and a saline, smoky mineral finish, especially from the volcanic hills. The DOC covers about 7,000 hectares east of Verona, but the heart is Soave Classico, the hills around the medieval walled town of Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone.

In 2019 the consortium mapped 33 UGAs (Unità Geografiche Aggiuntive), covering about 2,660 hectares (38% of the area): 28 in the Classico zone, three in the limestone west (Broia, Paradiso, Monte di Colognola) and two volcanic sites in the east (Duello, Roncà-Monte Calvarina). The names, which can appear on labels from the 2019 vintage, include Foscarino, Froscà, Castelcerino, Fittà, Monte Grande, Pressoni, Carbonare, Volpare and Costalunga. Pieropan (Calvarino, La Rocca), Anselmi, Inama, Gini, Prà, Coffele, Suavia, Filippi and Cantina di Soave are key producers. The Soave hills were also recognised in 2018 by the FAO as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System for their traditional pergola training.
it-soave.terroir: Two very different soils meet in the Classico zone. East of the Alpone and on the Monte Foscarino and Castelcerino ridges are dark volcanic basalts and tuffs from Eocene eruptions, giving smoky, saline, structured wines; west, toward Soave and Colognola, are white limestones (Calvarino, La Rocca) giving finer, more floral wines. The vines are traditionally trained on the Veronese pergola, which shades the grapes from summer heat.
it-soave.nerd_note: Roberto Anselmi left the DOC in 2000 in protest at its rules and now sells his famous Capitel Foscarino and I Capitelli as IGT Veneto.

it-soave-superiore.name: Soave Superiore
it-soave-superiore.summary: The DOCG tier of Soave, with lower yields and longer ageing (Riserva a year). In practice most top producers bottle their best wines as Soave Classico DOC rather than Superiore, so the DOCG remains marginal.
it-soave-superiore.nerd_note: One of the few cases in Italy where the DOCG is less prestigious in practice than the DOC beneath it.

it-sovana.name: Sovana
it-sovana.grapes: Sangiovese, Ciliegiolo, Aleatico, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot
it-sovana.summary: The red counterpart to Bianco di Pitigliano, from the same volcanic tufa country around Sovana, Pitigliano and Sorano. Ciliegiolo and Aleatico are local specialities; the Etruscan necropolis of Sovana lies among the vineyards.

it-spoleto.name: Spoleto
it-spoleto.summary: A white-wine DOC created in 2011 to rescue Trebbiano Spoletino, a distinct local grape once trained on maple trees along the Spoleto valley (some vines are a century old). It is high in acidity and ages into a waxy, citrus and herb-scented white that has become a cult wine. Superiore, spumante and passito versions exist.

it-squinzano.name: Squinzano
it-squinzano.summary: A Negroamaro DOC north of Lecce around Squinzano, close to Salice Salentino in style. About 52 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 147,000 bottles a year.

it-strevi.name: Strevi
it-strevi.summary: A tiny DOC for passito Moscato from the commune of Strevi near Acqui Terme, separated from Asti in 2005.
it-strevi.nerd_note: Strevi is one of only a few Italian communes with a DOC solely for dried-grape Moscato.

it-suvereto.name: Suvereto
it-suvereto.created: subzone of Val di Cornia 1989; separate DOCG 2011
it-suvereto.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot (blends or varietal), Sangiovese
it-suvereto.summary: Suvereto, a medieval village south of Bolgheri named for its cork oaks (*sughere*), became one of Tuscany's newest DOCGs in 2011. Its reds, built on Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot (with varietal versions of each and of Sangiovese), are warmer and denser than Bolgheri's, from iron-rich, stony soils on the hills above the Cornia valley. Tua Rita's Redigaffi, a pure Merlot first made in 1994, gave the area cult status.

it-tarquinia.name: Tarquinia
it-tarquinia.summary: A coastal DOC around Tarquinia, another Etruscan city famous for the painted tombs of its necropolis, which show banquets with wine. About 12 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 47,000 bottles a year.

it-taurasi.name: Taurasi
it-taurasi.summary:
Taurasi is the 'Barolo of the South', a nickname that captures its tannin, acidity and longevity, if not its flavour. It was the first DOCG of southern Italy (1993), and for decades it was almost synonymous with one producer: Mastroberardino, whose 1968 Taurasi Riserva is one of the legendary Italian wines of the 20th century.

The wine comes from 17 communes in the hills of Irpinia, east of Avellino, around the village of Taurasi and the Calore river valley. Aglianico ripens very late here, often into November, and must be aged three years (one in wood) before release, four for Riserva. Young Taurasi is dark and severe, with black cherry, plum, tar, tobacco and volcanic smoke; with 15 years it turns savoury, earthy and fine. Styles range from traditional large-cask wines to modern barrique-aged versions.
it-taurasi.terroir: Hills of about 300 to 700 m on both sides of the Calore. The northern and central communes (Taurasi, Castelfranci, Montemarano, Paternopoli, Lapio) have clay, limestone and layers of volcanic ash from Vesuvius; Montemarano and Castelfranci, higher and colder, give the most acidic, slow-ageing wines. The continental climate, with snow in winter and big day-night swings, is unusual for the south.
it-taurasi.nerd_note: Phylloxera reached Irpinia late, in the 1920s and 1930s, and some old Aglianico vines in Taurasi are still ungrafted; Guastaferro's Primum comes from pre-phylloxera vines said to be over 200 years old.

it-tavoliere-delle-puglie.name: Tavoliere delle Puglie
it-tavoliere-delle-puglie.summary: A DOC created in 2011 for Nero di Troia on the Tavoliere, the great plain of the province of Foggia, Italy's second-largest after the Po valley. About 21 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 30,000 bottles a year.

it-teroldego-rotaliano.name: Teroldego Rotaliano
it-teroldego-rotaliano.summary:
Teroldego is the 'prince of Trentino', a dark, juicy red grown almost exclusively on the Campo Rotaliano, a triangular gravel plain where the Noce river meets the Adige between Mezzolombardo, Mezzocorona and San Michele all'Adige. It is deep purple, with blackberry, violet and tar, and lively acidity.

Its modern reputation is the work of Elisabetta Foradori, who took over her family estate in Mezzolombardo in 1984, spent years selecting old clones from the vineyards to restore diversity lost to productive modern clones, converted to biodynamics in the 2000s and now ferments single-vineyard Teroldegos (Sgarzon, Morei) in clay amphorae from Spain. DNA work in the 2000s showed that Lagrein is probably Teroldego's offspring, that Marzemino belongs to the same family, and that Teroldego is closely related to Dureza, one of Syrah's parents.
it-teroldego-rotaliano.terroir: Deep alluvial gravels and sands of the Noce fan, well-drained, warm, sheltered by mountain walls on three sides.
it-teroldego-rotaliano.nerd_note: Through its close kinship with Dureza, a parent of Syrah, Teroldego is a distant Alpine cousin of the great Rhône grape.

it-terra-d-otranto.name: Terra d'Otranto
it-terra-d-otranto.grapes: Primitivo, Aleatico, Malvasia Nera; Fiano, Verdeca, Chardonnay, Malvasia Bianca
it-terra-d-otranto.summary: A broad Salento DOC (2011) covering the old Terra d'Otranto, the historic name of the southern heel, for many varietal wines. About 28 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 43,000 bottles a year.

it-terracina.name: Terracina
it-terracina.summary: A DOC for Moscato di Terracina, a distinctive local Muscat grown near the sea around Terracina and Monte San Biagio, made dry, amabile, sparkling and passito. About 42 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 256,000 bottles a year.

it-terratico-di-bibbona.name: Terratico di Bibbona
it-terratico-di-bibbona.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet, Syrah; Trebbiano, Vermentino
it-terratico-di-bibbona.summary: A small coastal DOC around Bibbona, immediately north of Bolgheri. Its gravel and sand soils are much like Bolgheri's, but it has little commercial presence. About 6 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 25,000 bottles a year.

it-terre-alfieri.name: Terre Alfieri
it-terre-alfieri.summary: A small DOCG approved in October 2020 for Arneis and Nebbiolo from eleven communes straddling Asti and Cuneo provinces: Antignano, Celle Enomondo, Cisterna d'Asti, Revigliasco, San Damiano, San Martino Alfieri and Tigliole in Asti, and Castellinaldo, Govone, Magliano Alfieri and Priocca in Cuneo. Named after the Alfieri family (the poet Vittorio Alfieri's line), it extends the Roero style eastward.
it-terre-alfieri.terroir: Sandy marine soils similar to the eastern Roero.
it-terre-alfieri.nerd_note: It was one of the last DOCGs approved before Canelli in 2023.

it-terre-del-colleoni.name: Terre del Colleoni
it-terre-del-colleoni.grapes: Schiava, Marzemino, Incrocio Manzoni, Franconia, Merlot, Cabernet
it-terre-del-colleoni.summary: Named after the condottiero Bartolomeo Colleoni, this Bergamo DOC covers the hills around Bergamo with a range of varietals including Franconia (Blaufränkisch).

it-terre-dell-alta-val-d-agri.name: Terre dell'Alta Val d'Agri
it-terre-dell-alta-val-d-agri.summary: A small DOC in the high Agri valley around Viggiano and Grumento Nova, for Merlot and Cabernet-based reds, a legacy of plantings by local aristocrats. About 16 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 13,000 bottles a year.

it-terre-di-casole.name: Terre di Casole
it-terre-di-casole.summary: A small DOC around Casole d'Elsa, west of Siena, for Sangiovese-based reds and Chardonnay-based whites. About 9 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 20,000 bottles a year.

it-terre-di-cosenza.name: Terre di Cosenza
it-terre-di-cosenza.grapes: Magliocco, Gaglioppo, Greco Nero, Aglianico; Greco, Pecorello, Mantonico, Guarnaccia
it-terre-di-cosenza.summary: A big DOC created in 2011 covering the province of Cosenza, absorbing the former DOCs Donnici, Pollino, San Vito di Luzzi and Verbicaro as subzones (with Colline del Crati, Condoleo and Esaro). It is the home of Magliocco, a dark, tannic red, and Pecorello, a rare white revived by Cantine Spadafora and others.

it-terre-di-offida.name: Terre di Offida
it-terre-di-offida.summary: The old Offida DOC, renamed when Offida became a DOCG, now covering Passerina sparkling, passito and Vin Santo from the Offida hills. About 5 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 33,000 bottles a year.

it-terre-di-pisa.name: Terre di Pisa
it-terre-di-pisa.summary: A red-only DOC covering the hills of the province of Pisa, for Sangiovese and international varieties alone or blended. It overlaps the Chianti Colline Pisane subzone and the old San Torpè area.

it-terre-tollesi.name: Terre Tollesi
it-terre-tollesi.summary: A DOCG limited to the single commune of Tollo in the province of Chieti, named after its Latin name, Tullum. It covers Montepulciano reds (Rosso and Riserva), Pecorino and Passerina whites and sparkling and passito wines, one of the smallest DOCGs in Italy by area.

it-tintilia-del-molise.name: Tintilia del Molise
it-tintilia-del-molise.summary: Tintilia is Molise's own grape and the region's calling card. Small-berried and low-yielding, it was almost abandoned by the 1970s; growers began replanting it in the 1990s and the DOC followed in 2011, with about 80 ha today and vineyards required to sit above 200 m. The wine is medium-bodied with dark berries, black pepper, Mediterranean herbs and a touch of liquorice, with fresh acidity; Riserva ages two years. A rosato is also made.
it-tintilia-del-molise.nerd_note: Molise once called Tintilia 'the wine of the transhumance', drunk by shepherds moving flocks along the *tratturi*, the ancient grass highways to Puglia.

it-todi.name: Todi
it-todi.grapes: Grechetto (the Todi biotype, G5), Sangiovese, Merlot
it-todi.summary: A DOC around the hill town of Todi built on Grechetto di Todi, a biotype genetically identical to Emilia's Pignoletto and distinct from Orvieto's Grechetto. The whites are textured and nutty; Superiore and passito versions exist. Roccafiore and Todini are leading producers.

it-torgiano.name: Torgiano
it-torgiano.grapes: Sangiovese, Canaiolo, Cabernet, Merlot, Pinot Nero; Trebbiano, Grechetto, Chardonnay
it-torgiano.summary: One of Umbria's first DOCs, around the village of Torgiano. Lungarotti's Rubesco (Rosso) and Torre di Giano (Bianco, Trebbiano and Grechetto) are the reference wines; the estate's MUVIT wine museum (1974) and olive oil museum make Torgiano the region's wine-culture centre.

it-torgiano-rosso-riserva.name: Torgiano Rosso Riserva
it-torgiano-rosso-riserva.grapes: Sangiovese 70% or more, with Canaiolo and other reds
it-torgiano-rosso-riserva.summary: A DOCG that is essentially the work of one family. Giorgio Lungarotti modernised the estate near the medieval village of Torgiano, where the Chiascio and Tiber meet south of Perugia, and his Rubesco Riserva Vigna Monticchio (first made in 1964) became the model for the DOCG, granted in 1990. The wine is Sangiovese-based, aged three years, and evolves for decades into a savoury, leathery, tobacco-scented red. Only a handful of hectares are declared each year.
it-torgiano-rosso-riserva.nerd_note: Lungarotti releases Vigna Monticchio Riserva only after years in bottle; the estate's library holds vintages back to the 1960s.

it-torrette.name: Torrette
it-torrette.grapes: Petit Rouge (min 70%), plus Fumin, Cornalin, Mayolet, Vien de Nus and others
it-torrette.summary: The most important red subzone, covering several communes west of Aosta (Saint-Pierre, Aymavilles, Sarre, Quart and others). Torrette is Petit Rouge-based, light to medium-bodied, with cherry, violet and almond; the Supérieur has more alcohol and ageing.
it-torrette.terroir: Moraine and schist on the sunny side of the central valley.
it-torrette.nerd_note: The name comes from the Torrette hamlet near Saint-Pierre, close to the medieval castle of Saint-Pierre.

it-trebbiano-d-abruzzo.name: Trebbiano d'Abruzzo
it-trebbiano-d-abruzzo.grapes: Trebbiano Abruzzese and/or Trebbiano Toscano (Bombino Bianco also historically allowed) minimum 85%
it-trebbiano-d-abruzzo.summary:
Most Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is a neutral, cheap white from high-yielding tendone vines. A few wines are among the greatest whites in Italy. Edoardo Valentini (died 2006), at Loreto Aprutino, selected the true Trebbiano Abruzzese, kept yields low and made a wine of extraordinary depth and longevity; his son Francesco Paolo continues, releasing only what meets the family standard. Emidio Pepe's Trebbiano, foot-trodden and aged in glass-lined cement, is equally legendary, and growers such as Tiberio (Fonte Canale, from vines planted around 1960) and Cataldi Madonna have proved the local variety's potential.

The 2023 reform added provincial subzones for Superiore and Riserva. The challenge is that the name covers several different grapes: true Trebbiano Abruzzese, Trebbiano Toscano and Bombino Bianco (locally also called Trebbiano).
it-trebbiano-d-abruzzo.nerd_note: Valentini never used consultants or new oak; he made wine in large old casks and simply refused to bottle vintages he did not like. Bottles from the 1970s and 1980s are still alive.

it-trentino.name: Trentino
it-trentino.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Grigio, Müller-Thurgau, Nosiola, Marzemino, Teroldego, Lagrein, Merlot, Cabernet and many others
it-trentino.summary: The umbrella DOC for the province of Trento, mostly varietal wines from the Adige valley, the Valle dei Laghi and Vallagarina. Most volume comes from big cooperatives (Cavit, Mezzacorona, La-Vis). Its gems include Marzemino from Isera (the wine Don Giovanni orders in Mozart's opera), Nosiola, the native white, and Vino Santo Trentino, a rare sweet wine from Nosiola grapes dried until Holy Week in the Valle dei Laghi, aged for several years before release.
it-trentino.terroir: Alluvial valley floors and limestone, porphyry and moraine slopes.
it-trentino.nerd_note: Trentino's Vino Santo grapes are dried on racks (*arele*) until Easter week, and the wine spends years in small casks before release.

it-trento.name: Trento
it-trento.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Nero, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Meunier
it-trento.summary:
Trento DOC was Italy's first DOC dedicated to metodo classico sparkling wine (1993) and is the second most important Italian traditional-method appellation after Franciacorta. Vineyards on the slopes of the Adige valley and its side valleys, often at 300 to 800 m, give Chardonnay with high acidity and a mountain freshness. Rules require at least 15 months on the lees (24 for millesimato, 36 for Riserva). The brand 'TrentoDOC' groups about 60 houses.

Giulio Ferrari, who studied in Montpellier and Geisenheim and worked in Champagne, founded his company in 1902 and planted Chardonnay in Trentino; in 1952 he sold it to Bruno Lunelli, whose family built Ferrari into Italy's leading sparkling-wine brand. Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore is one of Italy's great wines. Rotari (Mezzacorona), Cesarini Sforza, Letrari, Revì, Maso Martis, Abate Nero and Altemasi (Cavit) are other names.
it-trento.terroir: Limestone, dolomite and porphyry slopes on the hills around Trento, the Valle di Cembra, Valsugana and Vallagarina; mountain altitude preserves acidity.
it-trento.nerd_note: Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore comes from the Lunelli family's Maso Pianizza Chardonnay vineyard at around 550 to 600 m and spends about a decade on the lees.

it-val-d-arbia.name: Val d'Arbia
